questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In determining nutrient requirements for a population, which of the following nutrients is not included in the calculation for Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for 97.5% of the population?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Energy

Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is the daily nutrient intake level sufficient to meet the requirements of 97.5% of healthy individuals in a particular age and sex group.

However, energy requirements are not expressed as RDA because:

• Excess intake of energy can lead to obesity
• Energy needs vary widely depending on physical activity and metabolism
• Therefore, energy is estimated as the Average Requirement rather than an intake covering 97.5% of the population

Nutrients commonly expressed as RDA:

• Protein
• Vitamins (eg, Vitamin A)
• Minerals (eg, Iron)
questions.learning: Energy Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) is the daily nutrient intake level sufficient to meet the requirements of 97.5% of healthy individuals in a particular age and sex group.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A girl with a history of schizophrenia presents to a Primary Health Centre (PHC). Which of the following online government portals should the doctor use to book an appointment with a psychiatrist?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tele - MANAS

Tele-MANAS (Tele Mental Health Assistance and Networking Across States) is the flagship online platform that provides access to mental health services, enabling doctors and frontline health workers to connect patients directly to psychiatrists and trained mental health professionals for consultation.

Tele MANAS, a 24/7 mental health support helpline, launched its mobile app and video consultation services to enhance access to mental health support.

The Tele MANAS app is a user-friendly platform that offers a range of mental health resources. Users can access self-care tips, stress management techniques, and tools for recognizing early signs of distress. The app also features interactive activities, including mind challenges, games, and mindfulness practices. Additionally, Tele MANAS provides free, confidential counseling with trained mental health professionals from across India.

Video consultations enhance the already existing audio call services, enabling mental health professionals to conduct thorough assessments through direct observation. This feature facilitates history taking, clarification of concerns, and brief physical or Mental State Examinations (MSE) when needed. The service is initially available in Karnataka, Jammu & Kashmir, and Tamil Nadu, with plans for nationwide expansion.

Tele MANAS services include:

* Immediate tele-counselling by trained professionals.

* Referral support to psychiatrists for severe cases.

* Mental health awareness campaigns via digital platforms.

* Mobile-based mental health interventions ensure accessibility in rural and remote areas.

Other Options:

Option A: NIKSHAY is a digital platform for the management of tuberculosis cases.

Option C: U-WIN is a digital platform for recording all vaccination-related activities and tracking the administration of vaccines under Universal Immunization Programme (UIP).

Option D: Nikusth is the web-based solution for monitoring of Leprosy patients

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child presents with recurrent upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) and laboratory findings reveal absence of B cells, T cells, and NK cells, along with ADA deficiency. What is the most likely underlying immunodeficiency disorder responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Severe combined immunodeficiency disorder

Adenosine deaminase deficiency causes accumulation of toxic purine metabolites leading to lymphocyte apoptosis.

This results in absence of B cells, T cells, and NK cells with severe combined immune dysfunction.

ADA deficiency

↓

↑ Deoxyadenosine → ↑ dATP

↓

Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase

↓

↓ DNA synthesis

↓

Failure of lymphocyte development

↓

↓ T cells + ↓ B cells + ↓ NK cells

↓

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)

Patients present early with recurrent, severe infections involving multiple systems.

Bruton disease lacks B cells only, DiGeorge has T-cell deficiency, and MPO deficiency does not cause combined lymphocyte loss.

| Disorder | Defect | B cells | T cells | NK cells

| -------- | ------ | ------- | ------- | --------

| Bruton's | BTK mutation |  ↓ | ✔️ Normal | ✔️ Normal

| MPO deficiency | Neutrophil enzyme | ✔️ Normal | ✔️ Normal | ✔️ Normal

| SCID (ADA) | Purine metabolism |  ↓ |  ↓ |  ↓

| DiGeorge | Thymic aplasia | ✔️ Normal |  ↓ | ✔️ Normal

| Type | Cells affected

| ---- | --------------

| ADA deficiency | ↓ T, ↓ B, ↓ NK

| IL-2R mutation | ↓ T, ↓ NK, normal B

| RAG mutation | ↓ T, ↓ B, normal NK

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the primary identification made by a CBNAAT/gene expert?
questions.explanation: CBNAAT (Cartridge Based Nucleic Acid Amplification Test), commonly known as GeneXpert, is a revolutionary molecular test for tuberculosis. Its primary function is the simultaneous identification of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) genome and the presence of mutations in the rpoB gene, which indicates Rifampicin resistance. Because Rifampicin is a surrogate marker for multi-drug resistance (MDR-TB), this test provides rapid, critical information for treatment planning. While it identifies the bacteria itself (Option A), its most significant clinical advantage is the rapid resistance testing. Standard GeneXpert does not identify resistance to Isoniazid (Option C) or Ethambutol (Option D); those require more advanced molecular tests or traditional cultures. GeneXpert is highly sensitive, providing results in less than two hours, making it the first-line diagnostic tool in the National TB Elimination Programme of India for both pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculosis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 55-year-old female with a prolonged history of systemic lupus erythematosus, treated with multiple medications is being evaluated on autopsy. Records from the patient's most recent office visit show an elevated blood pressure and examination findings of facial plethora, truncal obesity, and skin ecchymoses. The patient's adrenal glands is most likely to reveal which of the following findings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bilateral cortical atrophy

Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy (commonly used to treat autoimmune diseases like SLE) causes iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.

Mechanism:

• Exogenous steroids suppress hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH via negative feedback.
• ↓ ACTH leads to reduced stimulation of the adrenal cortex.
• Over time, this causes bilateral adrenal cortical atrophy, particularly of the zona fasciculata and zona reticularis.
questions.learning: Bilateral cortical atrophy Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid therapy (commonly used to treat autoimmune diseases like SLE) causes iatrogenic Cushing syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Calculate the dependency ratio in this family. Mr J, age 68 years, Mrs J age 59, their son’s age 30 years, his wife’s age is 27 years and grandson is 5 years old.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 66.6%

The dependency ratio for this family will be 66.6%.

The dependent population includes children Population under 15 years and above 65 years are part of the numerator used to calculate the total dependency ratio. This is because this population is considered the dependent population.

Here,

Family members under 15 years = 1

Family members above 65 years = 1

Total population under 15 years and above 65 years = 1+1 = 2 (Numerator)

Total population in 15-65 years group = 3

Total dependency ratio = 2/3 x 100 = 66.6%

The total dependency ratio is the ratio of the combined dependent population to those in the age group of 15–65 years. It is also called the societal dependency ratio. It can also be divided into the young-age and old-age dependency ratios.

Note: As of mid-year 2020, the dependency ratio of India is 48.7%.
questions.learning: 66.6% The dependency ratio for this family will be 66.6%. The dependent population includes children Population under 15 years and above 65 years are part of the numerator used to calculate the total dependency ratio.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient undergoes parotid gland surgery and subsequently develops loss of cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible and the lower part of the external ear. Which of the following nerves is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
options: Temporofacial branch of the facial nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Great auricular nerve

The great auricular nerve (C2–C3), a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, ascends superficially across the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply cutaneous sensation over the angle of the mandible, parotid region, mastoid process, and the lower part of the auricle (external ear). Because it runs superficially over the parotid gland, it is commonly injured during parotidectomy, resulting in postoperative numbness over these areas.

Why not the other options?

• A. Marginal mandibular nerve: A motor branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) supplying muscles of the lower lip (depressor anguli oris, depressor labii inferioris, mentalis). Injury causes asymmetry of the lower lip, not sensory loss.
• B. Temporofacial branch of the facial nerve: A motor branch supplying muscles of facial expression in the upper face (frontalis, orbicularis oculi, etc.). Injury causes facial weakness, not cutaneous sensory loss.
• C. Auriculotemporal nerve: A sensory branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplying the anterior auricle, external acoustic meatus, temporal region, and TMJ. It does not supply the angle of the mandible or lower ear. It also carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland and is involved in Frey syndrome after parotid surgery.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the listed arteries is palpable on physical examination in the given image?
questions.explanation: The image shows palpation being performed behind the medial malleolus of the ankle. This is the classical anatomical location where the posterior tibial artery is palpated. The artery runs posterior to the medial malleolus, between it and the Achilles tendon, and is a key site for assessing peripheral circulation in the lower limb. Clinically, palpation of the posterior tibial pulse is important in evaluating peripheral arterial disease, especially in diabetic patients. It is one of the two main pulses checked in the foot, the other being the dorsalis pedis artery. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Anterior tibial artery → Not directly palpable at the ankle; continues as dorsalis pedis (C) Dorsalis pedis artery → Palpated on the dorsum (top) of the foot, not behind medial malleolus (D) Popliteal artery → Palpated in the popliteal fossa (behind knee)
questions.learning: The image shows palpation being performed behind the medial malleolus of the ankle. This is the classical anatomical location where the posterior tibial artery is palpated.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the condition in the image given below:
questions.explanation: The image shows classic "Leonine facies" — diffuse thickening and nodular infiltration of facial skin giving a lion-like appearance, pathognomonic of Lepromatous leprosy (LL). Key Clinical Features visible: 1. Diffuse nodular infiltration of entire face 2. Leonine facies — thickened, coarse facial features 3. Loss of eyebrows (madarosis) 4. Nodular thickening of ears and nose 5. Diffuse symmetric skin involvement Why other options are wrong: (A) Tuberculoid leprosy is incorrect because tuberculoid leprosy presents with few, well-defined, hypopigmented anesthetic patches with raised borders — no nodular facial infiltration occurs due to strong host immunity containing the bacilli. (B) Leishmaniasis is incorrect because cutaneous leishmaniasis presents as ulcerating nodular lesions typically at exposed sites — it does not produce the diffuse symmetric leonine facial infiltration seen here. (C) Borderline tuberculoid leprosy is incorrect because BT leprosy shows few to several hypopigmented plaques with partial sensation loss — it does not produce the extensive diffuse nodular facial infiltration characteristic of lepromatous disease
questions.learning: The image shows classic "Leonine facies" — diffuse thickening and nodular infiltration of facial skin giving a lion-like appearance, pathognomonic of Lepromatous leprosy (LL).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which method of measurement of scoliosis has been depicted in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cobb's angle

The given image depicts the measurement of the curvature of scoliosis using the Cobb's angle.

Scoliosis is characterized by the lateral curvature of the spine in the coronal plane when the patient is upright. Confirmation of the diagnosis is achieved through full-length lateral and posteroanterior X-rays of the spine. A Cobb's angle greater than 10% on the radiograph is diagnostic of scoliosis.

The measurement of Cobb's angle consists of three steps:

• Locating the superior-end vertebra of the curve.
• Locating the inferior-end vertebra of the curve.
• Drawing perpendicular lines from the superior surface of the superior-end vertebra and from the inferior surface of the inferior-end vertebra and making them intersect.

The angle formed by these perpendiculars represents the degree of spinal curvature, referred to as Cobb's angle.

Nash and Moe's method and Perdriolle and Vidal method are tools for assessing the vertebral rotation in scoliosis.

Other options:

Option B: Baumann's angle is the angle formed between a line drawn through the lateral epiphysis and the long axis of the humerus. Normally, it measures less than 80 degrees but increases in cases of supracondylar fractures.

Option C: Ferguson's angle is measured between the upper endplate of the S1 vertebra and a horizontal line. A normal Ferguson angle is typically around 34 degrees. A decreased Ferguson angle can be observed in advanced spondylolisthesis.

Option D: Bohler's angle is the angle formed by two lines tangent to the highest points of the anterior and posterior facets of the calcaneus. This angle is decreased in calcaneal fractures.
questions.learning: Cobb's angle — The given image depicts the measurement of the curvature of scoliosis using the Cobb's angle. Scoliosis is characterized by the lateral curvature of the spine in the coronal plane when the patient is upright.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An elderly male patient who is a known case of COPD, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus visits the OPD to review his medications. Which of the following criteria should be followed by the physician during the review?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Beer's criteria

Beer's criteria is widely used for reducing the use of potentially inappropriate medications and polypharmacy in the geriatric population.

American Geriatric Society came up with Beer's criteria to review potentially inappropriate medications and avoid polypharmacy and deprescribe irrational medications due to the increased adverse effects of many drugs in the geriatric age group. This includes:

* Explicit list of drugs that should be avoided in older adults

* Drugs that should be avoided or be used at lower doses in patients with reduced kidney function

* Specific drug-disease and drug-drug interactions that are known to be harmful in older adults

Long-acting benzodiazepines, proton pump inhibitors, antipsychotics, aspirin, dipyridamole, propoxyphene, and amitriptyline were among the most frequently prescribed inappropriate medications.

Medications like glimepiride, rivaroxaban, tramadol, and certain antipsychotic medications in patients with Parkinson's disease are recently added to the use-with-caution list.

Other options:

* The Light's Criteria is used to differentiate between different causes of pleural effusions (transudative vs exudative).

* The Jones Criteria is used for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever.

* The Duke's Criteria is used for the diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis (IE)
questions.learning: Beer's criteria Beer's criteria is widely used for reducing the use of potentially inappropriate medications and polypharmacy in the geriatric population.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: How is a broken vaccine vial disposed, according to biomedical waste management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Puncture proof blue bin

A broken vaccine vial is disposed of in a puncture-proof blue bin, according to biomedical waste management (BMW).

According to BMW, broken or discarded contaminated glass materials such as vials, ampules, etc are disposed of in boxes marked with blue color. It is then disinfected either by washing with detergent, autoclaving, or microwaving and sent for recycling.

The methods used for treatment and disposal of healthcare waste are:

• Incineration: This is a dry oxidation process done using high temperatures.
• Chemical disinfection: Chemicals are added to waste to kill or inactivate the microorganisms.
• Wet and dry thermal treatment: Shredded infectious waste is exposed to high temperature, high-pressure steam and it resembles an autoclave sterilization process.
• Microwave irradiation: Microorganisms are killed using high-frequency microwave.
• Land disposal.
• Inertization: Waste is mixed with cement and other substances before disposal to reduce toxicity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Based on the MRI findings, identify the medical condition seen in the lower back of the newborn that presents as an abnormal lump.
questions.explanation: The MRI shows a cystic swelling in the lumbosacral region of a newborn that appears well-defined and fluid-filled (bright on T2-weighted image). Importantly, there is no evidence of neural tissue (spinal cord or nerve roots) within the sac. This finding is characteristic of a meningocele. In meningocele, there is herniation of meninges filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) through a vertebral defect, but the spinal cord remains in its normal position. Clinically, it presents as a soft, fluctuant swelling over the lower back and may have minimal or no neurological deficits. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Myelomeningocele → Would show neural elements inside the sac (neural placode), which is not seen (C) Spina bifida occulta → No external swelling; only bony defect (D) Bone cyst → Intraosseous lesion, not a CSF-filled sac
questions.learning: The MRI shows a cystic swelling in the lumbosacral region of a newborn that appears well-defined and fluid-filled (bright on T2-weighted image). Importantly, there is no evidence of neural tissue (spinal cord or nerve roots) within the sac.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following criteria should be satisfied to start MDT?

1. Hypopigmented patch with sensory loss

2. Peripheral nerve thickening

3. Peripheral nerve thickening with sensory loss

4. Skin biopsy demonstrating bacilli
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,3

To start multidrug therapy (MDT), the criteria that should be satisfied are a hypopigmented patch with sensory loss and peripheral nerve thickening with sensory loss.

Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It mainly affects the skin and peripheral nerves. The disease has two polar forms, lepromatous leprosy, and tuberculoid leprosy, lying at the two ends of a long spectrum of the disease.

Leprosy is diagnosed by the detection of at least one of the following cardinal signs:

• Definite loss of sensation in a pale hypopigmented patch
• Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve, with loss of sensation and/or weakness of the muscles supplied by that nerve (statement 2)
• Presence of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear.

However, a skin smear is not a prerequisite for implementing MDT. Since MDT has been introduced, many procedures have been simplified, so that leprosy patients can be detected by health workers in the field and MDT can be immediately started.
questions.learning: 1,3 To start multidrug therapy (MDT), the criteria that should be satisfied are a hypopigmented patch with sensory loss and peripheral nerve thickening with sensory loss.

• Hydroureter / hydronephrosis
• Exact location + size
• Detects even radiolucent stones (e.g., uric acid)

| -------- | ---- | ----------

| NCCT KUB | Best diagnostic test | Radiation

| USG KUB | Screening (pregnancy) | Misses ureteric stones

| CECT KUB | Tumor evaluation | Masks stones

| Ureteroscopy | Diagnostic + therapeutic | Invasive

USG may miss stones, CECT obscures them, ureteroscopy is therapeutic not diagnostic.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: During psychotherapy, the therapist had mixed conscious and unconscious feelings towards his patient. This is known as_____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Countertransference

In the given clinical scenario, the therapist has mixed conscious and unconscious feelings towards his patient. This is known as counter-transference.

Counter-transference is the positive and negative feelings/emotions expressed by healthcare professionals towards their patients. It is the process of the physician unconsciously displacing onto the patient patterns of behaviors or emotional reactions as if he/she were a significant figure from earlier in the physician's life. Psychiatrists should be alert to signs of countertransference issues like missed appointments by the psychiatrist, boredom, or sleepiness during a session. Supervision and personal therapy can help the psychiatrist recognize and deal with these issues.

Transference is the positive and negative feelings expressed by the patients towards the healthcare professional. It is the process of the patient unconsciously displacing onto individuals patterns of behavior and emotional reactions that originated with significant figures from the past (generally in childhood). This displacement is onto the psychiatrist in a clinical scenario, who is a parent surrogate. The patient may be angry, hostile, demanding, or obedient to an extreme degree because of former relationships and patterns of behaviors. Failure to recognize this can make the psychiatrist react to the patient's behavior like a personal attack.

These are not defense mechanisms but are commonly encountered during clinical practice or while giving psychotherapy. In an interview, transference and counter-transference are very significant expressions of unconscious processes.

Option C: Dissociation is an immature defense mechanism. In this, involuntary splitting/suppression of mental functions occurs from the rest of the personality in a way that allows the expression of forbidden unconscious impulses without having a sense of responsibility for actions.
questions.learning: Countertransference — In the given clinical scenario, the therapist has mixed conscious and unconscious feelings towards his patient. This is known as counter-transference.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs interferes with the action of interleukin-2 (IL-2) without inhibiting calcineurin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Sirolimus

Sirolimus (rapamycin) suppresses T-cell proliferation by inhibiting the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), thereby blocking the cellular response to interleukin-2 (IL-2). Unlike calcineurin inhibitors (cyclosporine and tacrolimus), sirolimus does not inhibit IL-2 synthesis; instead, it prevents IL-2-mediated signal transduction, thereby inhibiting T-cell activation and proliferation.

Why not the other options?

• A. Tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor; prevents transcription and production of IL-2 by inhibiting T-cell activation.
• B. Mycophenolate mofetil: Inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH), blocking de novo purine synthesis and selectively suppressing T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation; does not act on the IL-2 pathway.
• D. Azathioprine: Purine analog that inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, including lymphocytes; no direct effect on IL-2 signaling.
questions.learning: Sirolimus Sirolimus (rapamycin) suppresses T-cell proliferation by inhibiting the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), thereby blocking the cellular response to interleukin-2 (IL-2).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In postpartum period, the intrauterine device may be inserted in the woman:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Up to 48 hours of delivery

A postpartum intrauterine contraceptive device (PPIUCD) can be inserted:

• Post-placental: within 10 minutes of placental delivery.
• Immediate postpartum: after 10 minutes but within 48 hours of delivery.
• Intracesarean: after placental removal and before closure of the uterine incision.
• If >48 hours postpartum, interval insertion is generally deferred until ≥6 weeks postpartum.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old morbidly obese patient develops respiratory distress on the third day after major surgery. What is the most likely initial differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A morbidly obese patient who develops sudden respiratory distress on postoperative day 3 is at extremely high risk for Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Obesity and major surgery are potent risk factors for DVT and subsequent PE (as established in Question 161). The timing is also characteristic, as PE most commonly occurs between days 3 and 7 post-op. Atelectasis (Option C) is the most common cause of fever and mild distress in the first 24-48 hours, but day 3 with "respiratory distress" strongly favors PE. Air embolism (Option B) occurs during the procedure or line insertion. Pneumothorax (Option D) usually presents immediately after trauma or a procedure. Clinicians must immediately order a CTPA or V/Q scan and start anticoagulation if clinical suspicion is high. This case highlights the critical importance of post-operative mobilization and prophylactic anticoagulation in high-risk patients to prevent this common and potentially fatal surgical complication
questions.learning: A morbidly obese patient who develops sudden respiratory distress on postoperative day 3 is at extremely high risk for Pulmonary Embolism (PE). Obesity and major surgery are potent risk factors for DVT and subsequent PE (as established in Question 161).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A G2P1 woman with a previous lower segment cesarean section presents with bleeding per vaginum and is diagnosed with placenta previa. During cesarean delivery, the placenta is noted to be invading into the bladder wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Placenta percreta

Placenta Accreta Spectrum occurs when the placenta attaches abnormally deep into the uterus due to absence of decidua basalis.

| Type | Depth of invasion

| ---- | -----------------

| Placenta accreta | Placenta attaches to myometrium

| Placenta increta | Invades into myometrium

| Placenta percreta | Penetrates through myometrium to serosa or adjacent organs

Previous cesarean scar

↓

Defective decidua basalis

↓

Placenta attaches deeply

↓

Placenta invades uterine wall

In placenta percreta, invasion may extend into:

• Bladder (most common)
• Broad ligament
• Bowel (rare)

Clinical Features

• Antepartum hemorrhage
• Difficult placental separation
• Massive postpartum hemorrhage

Management

Definitive management: Cesarean hysterectomy with placenta left in situ

Reason:

• Attempting placental removal causes catastrophic hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient undergoing chemotherapy was given an antiemetic, after which he developed symptoms like acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors. Which of the following drugs would have caused these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Metoclopramide

In the above scenario, the patient has developed extrapyramidal adverse effects like acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors. This is likely due to the antagonist action on dopamine receptors by metoclopramide.

Metoclopramide is a prokinetic and antiemetic. It has the following pharmacological actions:

* Dopamine receptor antagonist

* Serotonin (5HT4) receptor agonist

* Serotonin (5HT3) antagonist

* Sensitization of muscarinic receptors on smooth muscle. This results in increased lower esophageal sphincter tone and stimulates gastric antral contractions.

Metoclopramide acts on both the gastrointestinal system and central nervous system. It is used as an upper antiemetic for many types of vomiting, especially migraine, drug-induced, and chemotherapy-induced. It is also used as a prokinetic in gastroparesis to increase gastric emptying.

Adverse effects of metoclopramide are mainly extrapyramidal effects, and these include acute dystonia, Parkinson-like symptoms (tremors, bradykinesia, rigidity), tardive dyskinesia, galactorrhea due to hyperprolactinemia, and methemoglobinemia in neonates.

Extrapyramidal symptoms can be treated by discontinuation of metoclopramide and administration of anticholinergics or antihistaminics.

Other options:

Option A: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist. It blocks impulses at the peripheral origin in GIT. It is most commonly indicated for the treatment of postoperative and chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. Headache and dizziness are the common adverse effects.

Option C: Meclizine is a long-acting H1 antihistaminic drug. It is used for seasickness. It is less sedative and less anticholinergic.

Option D: Scopolamine (hyoscine) is a muscarinic antagonist. It blocks neural pathways from the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear to the emetic center in the brainstem. A transdermal patch of scopolamine is used as an antiemetic in motion sickness. Constipation, drowsiness, dry mouth, and blurred vision are the common adverse effects.
questions.learning: Metoclopramide — In the above scenario, the patient has developed extrapyramidal adverse effects like acute dystonia, bradykinesia, and tremors. This is likely due to the antagonist action on dopamine receptors by metoclopramide.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True regarding mitochondrial DNA is:
options: It has a higher mutation rate than nuclear DNA
It codes for more than 25% of oxidative phosphorylation proteins
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It has a higher mutation rate than nuclear DNA

The true statement is that mitochondrial DNA has a high mutation rate.

Mitochondrial DNA is circular and double-stranded. It has 16,569 bp (that makes up approximately 1% of total cellular DNA) while nuclear DNA has 3.3 billion bp. It has 37 genes that encode 13 protein subunits of the respiratory chain (out of a total of 67 proteins) i.e. about 20%. It mutates at a rate 5-10 times that of nuclear DNA. Mitochondrial DNA is transmitted by maternal non-mendelian inheritance.
questions.learning: It has a higher mutation rate than nuclear DNA — The true statement is that mitochondrial DNA has a high mutation rate. Mitochondrial DNA is circular and double-stranded.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10 year old boy was brought for psychiatric evaluation for intellectual disability. On examination, his IQ was 45. He has a long face, large ear ,large testis and a cardiac murmur and A history of poor intellectual function is present in the paternal family.What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fragile X syndrome

The given clinical vignette along with the family history is suggestive of fragile X syndrome.

* Fragile X syndrome is the second most common genetic cause of mental retardation (Down syndrome being the most common).

* It is caused by a trinucleotide mutation in the familial mental retardation-1 (FMR1) gene.

* When the cells were cultured in a folate-deficient medium, the cytogenetic alteration was discovered as a break in the staining in the long arm of the X chromosome. As it appeared that the chromosome was “broken” at this locale, it was named as a fragile site.

* In fragile X syndrome, the affected males are mentally retarded, with an IQ in the range of 20 to 60.

* The characteristic phenotypic features includes:

* Long face with a large mandible

* Large everted ears

* Large testicles (macro-orchidism)

* In some cases, hyperextensible joints, a high arched palate, and mitral valve prolapse may also be noted.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common site of branchial cyst is ______.
options: Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle
Junction of middle and lower third of the sternomastoid muscle
Between the two heads of the sternomastoid muscle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle

The most common site of a branchial cyst is at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border.

The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.

Branchial cyst develops due to the persistence of the cervical sinus. The cervical sinus is formed when the 2nd arch mesoderm overgrows the succeeding arches and overhangs them as shown in the image. The space between the overhanging 2nd pharyngeal arch and the 3rd, 4th, and 6th arches is called the cervical sinus. The cavity of the cervical sinus is lined by ectoderm and normally gets obliterated.

Branchial cysts are usually lined by squamous epithelium and contain thick, turbid fluid full of cholesterol crystals. It is fluctuant and may transilluminate when it contains clear fluid.

A branchial fistula may be acquired or congenital. The congenital fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid (option B). An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete surgery for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture, and it is seen at the same site as the cyst.
questions.learning: Junction of upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle The most common site of a branchial cyst is at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which biochemical cycle/process is used by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Purine salvage pathway

It is the purine salvage pathway that is utilized by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology.

Monoclonal antibodies refer to the antibodies produced by a group of lymphocytes that produce antibodies against a single antigen. These antibodies are produced by hybridoma technology.

In this technology, the B-lymphocytes of mice spleen are immunized with an antigen to produce a specific antibody. These specific antibody-producing B lymphocytes are then fused with myeloma cells that can multiply indefinitely.

The myeloma cells are deficient in the hypoxanthine-guanine-phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) gene and do not produce immunoglobulins. Therefore, the resulting hybrid cell is producing antibodies against a single antigen indefinitely. These hybrid cells are cultured in a HAT medium (containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine) and the monoclonal antibodies are obtained. It is well-established that nucleotides present in DNA and RNA consist of purine and pyrimidine bases. The synthesis of these nucleotides can occur through either the De novo pathway or the salvage pathway. Consequently, the inclusion of aminopterin in the HAT medium effectively inhibits the De novo pathway, thereby rendering the synthesis of purine dependent on the salvage pathway. However, it should be noted that the salvage pathway exclusively takes place in the presence of the enzymes HGPRT and thymidine kinase. The hybridoma cell is uniquely capable of proliferating on the HAT medium due to its distinct composition. Specifically, the myeloma component of the hybridoma possesses the capacity for repetitive cellular division, while the plasma cell component contains the enzyme HGPRT. Consequently, the hybridoma cells can sustain growth and viability over an extended period when cultivated on the HAT medium.

Hybridoma technology is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (monoclonal antibodies).

Hybridomas are somatic cell hybrids produced by fusing the antibody-forming spleen cells with myeloma cells. The resultant hybrid thus has both the antibody-producing ability of the B-cell and the ability to multiply indefinitely of the myeloma.

The following are the steps involved in hybridoma technology:

• Mice are immunized with an antigen.
• After several weeks of immunization, blood samples are obtained from mice for measurement of serum antibodies.
• When the antibody titer is high enough, mice are commonly boosted by injecting antigen without adjuvant, intraperitoneally or intravenously.
• Then the mice are euthanized and their spleens removed for in vitro hybridoma cell production.
• Fusing antibody-producing spleen cells, which have a limited life span, with myeloma cells (derived from an immortal tumour of lymphocytes) results in a hybridoma that is capable of unlimited growth.
• The cells are cultured in a medium containing hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine (HAT medium) which allows only the fused cells to survive in culture.
• Monoclonal antibodies are then harvested.

Applications of hybridoma technology

• Listing lymphocyte subpopulations
• Specific cell quantitative preparation
• As an immunosuppressant in therapeutic settings
• Blood component nephelometric assays
• ELISA testing
• Quantitative purification of antigens.
• Common therapeutic applications for monoclonal antibodies
questions.learning: Purine salvage pathway — It is the purine salvage pathway that is utilized by monoclonal antibodies in hybridoma technology. Monoclonal antibodies refer to the antibodies produced by a group of lymphocytes that produce antibodies against a single antigen.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient who presented with a scrotal swelling underwent an orchidectomy. The image below shows the histopathology findings. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Seminoma

Based on the gross and microscopic appearance of the specimen, the diagnosis is seminoma.

The gross specimen shows a well-circumscribed, pale, gray-white, fleshy, homogenous mass, with a lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. Histopathology shows uniform tumor cells with abundant clear cytoplasm, distinct cell borders, and large central nuclei. There is a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate. Classically, they have a fried egg appearance.

Other options:

Option B: Yolk-sac tumor has a yellowish-white, mucinous appearance. Histologically, they are typically composed of a lace-like (reticular) network of medium-sized cuboidal, flattened, or spindled cells, which generally show less cytologic atypia than embryonal carcinoma. In approximately 50% of tumors, structures resembling endodermal sinuses (Schiller-Duval bodies) may be seen; these consist of a mesodermal core with a central capillary and a visceral and parietal layer of cells resembling primitive glomeruli.

Option C: Embryonal cell carcinoma appears variegated with foci of hemorrhage or necrosis.  Histologically, the cells grow in alveolar or tubular patterns, sometimes with papillary folds. More undifferentiated lesions may display sheets of cells with cleft-like spaces. The neoplastic cells have an epithelial appearance, are large and anaplastic, and have hyperchromatic nuclei with prominent nucleoli. The cell borders are usually indistinct, and there is considerable variation in cell and nuclear size and shape (pleomorphism). Mitotic figures and tumor giant cells are frequently seen.

Option D: Teratomas also have a variegated appearance but have cysts reflecting the multiplicity of tissue types. Histologically, collections of differentiated cells or organoid structures originating in all 3 germ layers can be seen. Elements may be mature (resembling various adult tissues) or immature (sharing histologic features with fetal or embryonic tissue).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is least likely to cause postmenopausal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding is any vaginal bleeding occurring 12 months or more after the final menstrual period and must always be investigated. An ovarian follicular cyst (Option D) is a physiological cyst that occurs only during active ovulation in the reproductive years; therefore, it is least likely to be found or cause bleeding in a postmenopausal woman. Endometrial carcinoma (Option A) is the most concerning cause, and Granulosa cell tumors (Option B) of the ovary can cause postmenopausal bleeding by secreting excess estrogen. Genital tract trauma (Option C), such as atrophic vaginitis leading to tearing, is a common benign cause of postmenopausal spotting. Atrophic endometrium is actually the most common overall cause of postmenopausal bleeding, followed by endometrial polyps. Any postmenopausal patient presenting with bleeding must undergo transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy to rule out malignancy, particularly when risk factors like obesity or tamoxifen use are present

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following organs has the least arteriovenous oxygen difference?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kidney

The organ with the least arteriovenous oxygen difference is the kidney.

The arteriovenous oxygen difference is the amount of oxygen the tissues take up from the blood. If the amount of oxygen utilized by the tissues is more, the greater the arteriovenous oxygen difference.

The renal cortical blood flow is comparatively greater as the main function is to filter large volumes of blood through the glomeruli. Here, the oxygen extracted from the blood is relatively less. The arteriovenous oxygen difference for the kidney is only 14 mL/L of blood, which is very less when compared to the brain and heart.

Organs

Arteriovenous Oxygen Difference (mL/L)

Brain
62

Kidney
14

Skin
25

Liver
34

Heart muscles
114

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is the most dangerous lesion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. B/L Complete RLN lesion

Bilateral complete RLN (recurrent laryngeal nerve) lesion is the most dangerous lesion among the given options.

In bilateral RLN paralysis

• Both the cords lie in the median or paramedian position, the airway is inadequate causing dyspnea and stridor. This may lead to death if untreated.
• The voice is good.
• Dyspnea and stridor become worse on exertion or during an attack of acute laryngitis.

All laryngeal muscles are supplied by the ipsilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN), except cricothyroid which is supplied by the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN). Both SLN and RLN are branches of the vagus nerve.

The recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN) on the right and the left side follow different courses-

• Right RLN takes origin in the root of the neck, winds around the first part of the subclavian artery, and then ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove.
• Left RLN takes origin in the thorax, winds around the arch of the aorta, and then ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. Since it has a longer course, it is more likely to be injured.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: What is your diagnosis from the below X-ray images?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell tumor

The given radiographs show the anteroposterior and lateral views of the wrist, demonstrating a solitary lytic lesion with cortical expansion and a soap-bubble appearance in the epiphysis of the distal radius, suggestive of a giant cell tumor (GCT).

GCT usually affects young adults aged 20 to 40 years, with slight female predominance. It is a benign but locally aggressive tumor. It is exclusively seen in adults and affects the ends of long bones, typically involving the epiphysis. The most common location of the tumor is the distal femur followed by the proximal tibia. Involvement of the distal end of the radius is also seen and the tumor is more aggressive in this location.

Important X-ray features of a GCT:

• A solitary, possibly loculated, lytic lesion in the epiphysis
• Eccentric location, most often sub-chondral
• Expansion of the overlying cortex
• Soap bubble appearance (the tumor is homogenously lytic with trabeculae of the remnants of bone traversing it, giving it a loculated appearance).
• No calcification within the tumor
• No or minimal reactive sclerosis around the tumor
• Thinned out cortex, may be perforated

The classical "soap bubble" appearance of a giant cell tumor (GCT) is shown below:

Other options:

Option A: A solitary bone cyst is most commonly occurs in the metaphysis of the bone. On an X-ray, a bone fracture fragment may be observed resting in a dependent portion of the cyst, referred to as the fallen fragment or fallen leaf sign. This sign is considered pathognomonic of a simple bone cyst.

The image below shows a bone cyst in the humerus along with a pathological fracture and fallen leaf sign:

Option B: On an X-ray, an aneurysmal bone cyst is seen as an eccentric, expansile, lytic lesion with well-defined margins in the metaphysis.

Option D: Osteoblastoma is a benign bone tumor usually occurring in the jaw and spine. On X-ray, a radiopaque central nidus with a surrounding radiolucent halo is seen. If occurring in the long bones, it involves the diaphysis or metaphysis, but never in the epiphysis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Adverse effect of Lamotrigine?
questions.explanation: Lamotrigine is a commonly used antiepileptic drug, but it is notorious for causing dermatological side effects. A skin rash occurs in approximately 10% of patients. While many of these rashes are mild, there is a significant risk of progression to life-threatening hypersensitivity reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) or Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN). To minimize this risk, clinicians must adhere to a slow dose titration schedule. While diplopia (Option A) can occur as a dose-related neurotoxic effect, and tremors (Option B) or neutropenia (Option C) are rare idiosyncratic reactions, the "rash" is the most characteristic and clinically important adverse effect emphasized in medical examinations. Patients are advised to stop the medication immediately and seek medical attention if any skin lesions develop during the initiation phase. Therefore, monitoring for a rash is the highest safety priority for patients starting lamotrigine therapy
questions.learning: Lamotrigine is a commonly used antiepileptic drug, but it is notorious for causing dermatological side effects. A skin rash occurs in approximately 10% of patients.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient came to the hospital after a road traffic accident. He had severe muscle injury and his serum K+ level was found to be 5.5 mEq/L. What will happen to the resting membrane potential in this patient?
options: First becomes more positive then negative
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Becomes more positive

In the given clinical scenario, the patient has hyperkalemia. It would result in the resting membrane potential becoming more positive.

The resting membrane potential represents an equilibrium situation where the concentration gradient of ions across the membrane is equal and opposite to the electrical gradients. At a normal potassium concentration of 3.5–5.0 mEq/L, the equilibrium potential for potassium is −90 mV. This is close to the resting membrane potential of neurons, which is about –70 mV.

A decrease in the extracellular sodium concentration reduces the size of the action potential but has little effect on the resting membrane potential. However, the intracellular and extracellular potassium (K+) concentrations are the major determinants of the RMP.

This is because

• At rest, there are more open K+ channels compared to Na+ channels; therefore, the membrane permeability of K+ is greater.
• The RMP is close to the equilibrium potential of K+.

In hyperkalemia, the extracellular level of K+ is increased. Thus, the RMP moves closer to the threshold to elicit an action potential, leading to a more excitable nerve. This means the RMP has become more positive.

In hypokalemia, the extracellular level of K+ is reduced. Thus, the RMP is reduced or becomes more negative and the nerve is hyperpolarized.

Hyperkalemia can lead to various clinical manifestations depending on the severity of the condition. Mild to moderate hyperkalemia may be asymptomatic or cause nonspecific symptoms such as fatigue, muscle weakness, and paresthesias. Severe hyperkalemia can lead to life-threatening complications such as cardiac arrhythmias and paralysis. The management of hyperkalemia includes treating the underlying cause, administering medications to stabilize the cardiac membrane (e.g., calcium gluconate), promoting the movement of potassium into cells (e.g., insulin and glucose, beta-agonists), and enhancing the removal of potassium from the body (e.g., diuretics, ion-exchange resins, or hemodialysis).
questions.learning: Becomes more positive — In the given clinical scenario, the patient has hyperkalemia. It would result in the resting membrane potential becoming more positive.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What objective tests are utilized to assess an individual's hearing ability?
questions.explanation: Objective hearing tests are those that do not require the active cooperation or subjective response of the patient, making them essential for infants and non-cooperative individuals. BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry), OAE (Otoacoustic Emissions), and Tympanometry are all categorized as objective tests. BERA measures the electrical activity of the auditory nerve. OAE measures the sound generated by the outer hair cells of the cochlea. Tympanometry (Option D) evaluates middle ear function and pressure. In contrast, PTA (Pure Tone Audiometry, Option C) is a subjective test because it requires the patient to signal when they hear a specific sound. Therefore, any option including PTA is technically incorrect when specifically asked for "objective" tests. Thus, the combination of BERA, OAE, and Tympanometry (Option A) is the definitive set of objective auditory diagnostic tools. Understanding this classification is fundamental for planning neonatal hearing screenings and evaluating adult patients with suspected malingering
questions.learning: Objective hearing tests are those that do not require the active cooperation or subjective response of the patient, making them essential for infants and non-cooperative individuals.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: As a junior resident monitoring a patient on mechanical ventilation, arterial blood gas analysis reveals hypoventilation with respiratory acidosis. Which modification in the ventilator settings would be most effective in correcting this abnormality?
questions.explanation: Respiratory acidosis in a ventilated patient results from alveolar hypoventilation, which causes retention of carbon dioxide (CO₂). Correction requires increasing minute ventilation to enhance CO₂ clearance. Minute ventilation equals tidal volume × respiratory rate; therefore, increasing the respiratory rate is the most direct way to “wash out” excess CO₂. Decreasing FiO₂ (Option A) reduces oxygenation without correcting CO₂ retention. Increasing PEEP (Option C) improves oxygenation by preventing alveolar collapse but does not directly treat hypercapnia. Increasing plateau pressure (Option D) is unsafe due to the risk of barotrauma and ventilator-induced lung injury. Hence, raising the respiratory rate is the standard intervention for ventilation-induced respiratory acidosis
questions.learning: Respiratory acidosis in a ventilated patient results from alveolar hypoventilation, which causes retention of carbon dioxide (CO₂). Correction requires increasing minute ventilation to enhance CO₂ clearance.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following forms the lateral boundary of the anatomical snuff box?
options: Extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus
Extensor pollicis longus and abductor pollicis brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and abductor pollicis brevis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus

The lateral boundary of the anatomical snuff box is formed by extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus.

Boundaries of the anatomical snuffbox:

• Lateral wall:

• Abductor pollicis longus (APL)
• Extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)

• Medial wall:

• Extensor pollicis longus (EPL)

• Roof:

• Cephalic vein
• Superficial branch of the radial nerve

• Floor:

• Radial styloid, scaphoid, trapezium, and 1st metacarpal

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: What does a linear accelerator (LINAC) produce in radiation therapy?
questions.explanation: A linear accelerator (LINAC) is the standard device for external beam radiation therapy. It functions by accelerating electrons to high energies using microwave technology. These high-energy electrons can be used directly to treat superficial tumors or directed onto a metal target to generate high-energy X-rays (photons) for treating deep-seated malignancies. Alpha and beta rays (Option A) are products of natural radioactive decay. Gamma rays (Option B) are emitted from isotopes like cobalt-60, not generated by a LINAC. Neutrons and positrons (Option D) are utilized in specialized neutron therapy or PET imaging, respectively. Therefore, the primary therapeutic outputs of a modern LINAC are precisely controlled X-ray beams and electron beams tailored to the tumor's depth
questions.learning: A linear accelerator (LINAC) is the standard device for external beam radiation therapy. It functions by accelerating electrons to high energies using microwave technology.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which types of cancer are associated with exposure to ionizing radiation? 1. Leukaemia 2. Lung cancer 3. Breast cancer 4. Lymphoma Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Ionizing radiation is a well-established carcinogen that causes DNA damage through direct strand breaks and free radical formation. The risk of malignancy depends on the radiation dose, age at exposure, and tissue radiosensitivity. Hematopoietic tissues and rapidly dividing cells are particularly susceptible.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Leukaemia ✅

• One of the earliest and best-established malignancies associated with ionizing radiation exposure, especially acute leukemia (except CLL).

• 2. Lung cancer ❌

• Although high-dose radiation can increase the risk of lung cancer, lung cancer is classically associated with smoking, radon, and asbestos, and is not considered one of the characteristic radiation-induced cancers in this context.

• 3. Breast cancer ✅

• Exposure to ionizing radiation, particularly during childhood or adolescence, significantly increases the risk of breast cancer.

• 4. Lymphoma ✅

• Ionizing radiation is associated with an increased risk of lymphomas, especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Ionizing radiation is a well-established carcinogen that causes DNA damage through direct strand breaks and free radical formation. The risk of malignancy depends on the radiation dose, age at exposure, and tissue radiosensitivity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding Ascaris lumbricoides?
options: Larvae in the lungs produce asthma-like symptoms
High larval load can cause rectal prolapse
Unembryonated eggs in stool are not infective and embryonated eggs in soil are infective
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High larval load can cause rectal prolapse

A high larval load can cause rectal prolapse is not true regarding Ascaris lumbricoides.

Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) reside in the small intestine and not the large intestine to cause rectal prolapse. Trichuris Trichura (whipworm) cause rectal prolapse.

Ascaris lumbricoides is an intestinal nematode that causes ascariasis. Infection occurs through food or water contaminated with nightsoil or human faeces having eggs of Ascaris that contain the infective rhabditiform larva. Man is the only natural host. There is no intermediate host. Most infected humans are asymptomatic. (Option A)

The life cycle is as follows:

• Adult worms live in the lumen of the small intestine. A female produces eggs, which are passed with the faeces.
• Unfertilized eggs in the stool may be ingested but are not infective. The infective form of Ascaris is the embryonated egg in the soil (Option D). Infection typically arises from consuming food or water contaminated with embryonated eggs. These eggs harbour the rhabditiform larva.
• After infective eggs are swallowed, the larvae hatch.
• The larvae invade the intestinal mucosa and are carried through the portal system, then systemic circulation to the lungs.
• The larvae mature further in the lungs (10 to 14 days), penetrate the alveolar walls, ascend the bronchial tree to the throat, and are swallowed. This may present with asthma-like symptoms (Option B).
• Upon reaching the small intestine, they develop into adult worms. Between 2 and 3 months are required from ingestion of the infective eggs to oviposition by the adult female.
• Adult worms can live for 1 to 2 years.
• Adult worms can be occasionally detected in the stool or sputum of the patient. A definitive diagnosis is made by demonstration of eggs in faeces. Fertilised eggs are always bile-stained.

Effective and safe drugs for the treatment of ascariasis are Pyrantel pamoate 11 mg/kg once, Albendazole 400 mg once, Mebendazole 100 mg twice daily for 3 days, Ivermectin 150-200 mcg/kg once.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 78-year-old man presents with fatigue, dyspnea, and palpitations. Echocardiography reveals features of restrictive cardiomyopathy. Cardiac biopsy stained with Congo red demonstrates apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with symptoms of restrictive cardiomyopathy, a condition where the heart chambers are stiff and cannot fill properly. The definitive diagnostic clue is the biopsy finding: "Congo red stain" showing "apple-green birefringence" under polarized light. This is the pathognomonic marker for Amyloidosis, a disease caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils. When these fibrils accumulate in the myocardium, it leads to Cardiac Amyloidosis. Heart failure (Option A) is the clinical outcome of this disease but is not the primary histological diagnosis. Hemosiderosis (Option C) would show blue granules with a Prussian blue stain. Dystrophic calcification (Option D) involves calcium deposits in damaged tissues and would appear black on Von Kossa stain. Cardiac amyloidosis often results in thickened ventricular walls and a "granular" or "sparkling" appearance on ECHO. Management is challenging and depends on the specific protein type (e.g., AL or ATTR amyloid)

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: The compound given in the image below can be used in the treatment of which of the following poisonings?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phophorus

The compound given in the image is copper sulphate. It can be used in the treatment of phosphorus poisoning.

The initial stage of acute phosphorus poisoning through ingestion involves severe abdominal discomfort, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Excreta and breath have a garlicky odour. Luminescent faeces and vomit are characteristically seen (smoky stool syndrome). Direct contact with the skin can result in second and third-degree burns. Shock, hematemesis due to liver failure, and renal insufficiency are potential causes of death.

Regular inhalation of phosphorus fumes, leading to chronic phosphorus poisoning, results in necrosis of the lower jaw around a decayed tooth. This condition is known as phossy jaw and is associated with the discharge of foul-smelling pus from multiple sinuses.

Gastric lavage with potassium permanganate oxidizes phosphorus into phosphoric acid and phosphates. Activated charcoal can be used to adsorb the poison.

Stomach wash with 0.2% copper sulphate solution or 0.2 g of copper sulphate every 5 minutes until vomiting occurs. It coats the particles of phosphorus with a film of copper phosphide, which is relatively harmless. As copper has caustic properties and can cause acute poisoning, adequate care should be taken. Copper sulphate was also used for topical application in phosphorus poisoning. It is not recommended now.

Other options:

Option A: Aluminium Phosphide has no antidote. Magnesium sulphate is given in ALP poisoning to correct hypomagnesemia and arrhythmias and reduce organ toxicity.

Option B and D: British anti-Lewisite (BAL), also known as Dimercaprol, is used as an antidote for Mercury poisoning (except non-alkyl mercury) and Arsenic poisoning.
questions.learning: Phophorus — The compound given in the image is copper sulphate. It can be used in the treatment of phosphorus poisoning.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding the management of patients who have achieved return of spontaneous circulation following CPR?
options: Initiate targeted temperature management of <33°C, if the patient is confused
Perform emergent cardiac intervention if ST elevation is present in the ECG
Maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) above 65 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Initiate targeted temperature management of <33°C, if the patient is confused

After successful CPR, the patient may develop Post–Cardiac Arrest Syndrome, which includes:

• Brain injury
• Myocardial dysfunction
• Systemic ischemia-reperfusion injury
• Persistent precipitating pathology (e.g., MI)

Immediate management focuses on oxygenation, circulation, neuroprotection, and treating the cause. Post–cardiac arrest care includes maintaining SpO₂ >94%, MAP ≥65 mmHg, and urgent coronary intervention if STEMI is present.

Current guidelines (AHA 2020 and the post-TTM2 trial era) recommend targeted temperature management between 32–36°C, with a strong shift toward simply maintaining normothermia and actively preventing fever (≤37.5°C). A target of "<33°C" is not the standard — aggressive hypothermia below 33°C showed no benefit over 36°C or fever prevention in major trials (TTM, TTM2). The underlying concept: after successful CPR, patients develop post-cardiac arrest syndrome — anoxic brain injury, myocardial stunning, systemic ischemia-reperfusion injury, plus the precipitating pathology. Management bundles target oxygenation (94%+), perfusion (MAP ≥65), temperature control (prevent fever; cool only if comatose), and treating the cause (e.g., PCI for STEMI).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A one-month-old child presents with recurrent pneumonia and no cyanosis. On examination, a continuous murmur is heard below the left clavicle and a bounding pulse is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus)

Patent ductus arteriosus is a congenital left-to-right shunt in which the ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth, leading to continuous blood flow from the aorta to the pulmonary artery.

• Continuous “machinery” murmur best heard below the left clavicle
• Bounding pulses and wide pulse pressure due to runoff of blood into pulmonary circulation
• Recurrent respiratory infections and signs of heart failure due to increased pulmonary blood flow
• Usually no cyanosis initially (acyanotic congenital heart disease)

Pathophysiology:

• Persistent connection between aorta and pulmonary artery → left-to-right shunt
• Increased pulmonary blood flow → pulmonary congestion → recurrent pneumonia

Contrast:

• ASD: fixed split S2, no continuous murmur
• VSD: pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal border
• Coarctation of aorta: radio-femoral delay, upper limb hypertension, weak lower limb pulses

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A baby presents with diarrhea and characteristic skin lesions involving the perioral and perianal regions, as shown in the image. Which nutritional deficiency is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of perioral and perianal rashes combined with chronic diarrhea in a baby is a hallmark of zinc deficiency. This condition, known as acrodermatitis enteropathica, presents with characteristic acral and periorificial dermatitis featuring erythematous, scaly plaques. Other symptoms include growth retardation, alopecia, poor wound healing, and immune dysfunction. Niacin deficiency (Option B) causes pellagra, which involves the "3 Ds" (dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia), but the rash is typically photosensitive and occurs in sun-exposed areas like the neck (Casal's necklace), not primarily perioral. Selenium deficiency (Option C) primarily affects the cardiovascular system, leading to Keshan disease, and does not cause this specific rash pattern. Magnesium deficiency (Option D) presents with neuromuscular symptoms such as tetany, muscle cramps, or seizures rather than dermatological findings. Diagnosis is confirmed by low serum zinc levels, and treatment involves oral zinc supplementation

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with chronic kidney disease underwent a nephrectomy. Which of the following can be administered as a postoperative analgesic in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acetaminophen

Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options.

Analgesia in CKD patients:

Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients. For more severe pains opioid analgesics like tramadol or fentanyl are used.

Even though acetaminophen is considered safe, with chronic high dosage it can also become nephrotoxic.

NSAIDs like naproxen, indomethacin, diclofenac, etc are not used in CKD patients because of their direct nephrotoxic effects. In healthy normal individuals, NSAIDs have little effect on renal function and blood pressure. But in conditions where the regulatory systems are impaired as hypovolemia, congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, or other conditions where the renin-angiotensin system is activated, renal function by the formation of prostaglandins are very important.

NSAIDs cause impairment of prostaglandin-induced inhibition of chlorine reabsorption and antidiuretic hormone action. This will cause salt and water retention. It also inhibits COX-2 derived prostaglandins which regulate the renal medullary blood flow and would lead to a rise in blood pressure, increased cardiovascular thrombotic events, and cardiac failure. It can also cause electrolyte abnormalities like hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.
questions.learning: Acetaminophen Acetaminophen can be given as an analgesic for the patient as it is the least nephrotoxic among the given options. Analgesia in CKD patients: Acetaminophen is considered a safer non-narcotic analgesic in chronic kidney disease (CKD) patients.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In the demographic cycle, which phase is characterized as the low stationary phase?
questions.explanation: The demographic cycle represents the stages of population change over time. Phase 1 is the "high stationary" stage (high birth and death rates). Phase 2 is "early expanding" (birth rates remain high, death rates fall). Phase 3 is "late expanding" (birth rates start to fall). Phase 4 is correctly identified as the "low stationary phase". In this stage, both birth rates and death rates have stabilized at a very low level, resulting in zero or very slow population growth. Many developed nations are currently in Phase 4. Phase 5 is "declining" (birth rates fall below death rates). Understanding these phases is vital for long-term health planning, as the transition from Phase 2/3 to Phase 4 usually correlates with increased urbanization and better access to family planning. A nation's economic and social development can often be predicted by its current position in this demographic cycle
questions.learning: The demographic cycle represents the stages of population change over time. Phase 1 is the "high stationary" stage (high birth and death rates).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A urine sample from a 4-year-old child appeared normal at first but gradually darkened on standing, with the discoloration becoming more intense over time, as seen by the laboratory technician. This finding suggests deficiency of which enzyme as the underlying cause?
questions.explanation: The phenomenon where clear urine turns dark or black upon standing is the classic presentation of alkaptonuria. This rare autosomal recessive disorder is caused by a deficiency of the enzyme homogentisic acid oxidase (Option D) in the phenylalanine-tyrosine metabolic pathway. This deficiency leads to the accumulation of homogentisic acid, which is excreted in the urine and oxidizes into a black pigment (alkapton) when exposed to air. Beta-carotene (Option A) is a precursor to Vitamin A and does not cause urine darkening. Tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency (Option B) leads to Tyrosinemia Type II, characterized by eye and skin lesions but not black urine. L-ascorbic acid (Option C) is Vitamin C, which is sometimes used as a treatment adjunct but is not the cause of the disease. Therefore, based on the pathognomonic finding of urine darkening upon oxidation, the deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase is the causative enzyme defect

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following statements is true about palliative care?

A. Disease is the centre of concern
B. The patient is sovereign
C. Death should neither be prolonged nor hastened
D. The aim is to improve the quality of life
E. The intention is to cure
F. Imperative to do something than passively observe
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. B,D

True statements are:

• The patient is sovereign
• The aim is to improve the quality of life

Palliative care helps patients and their families cope with physical, psychological, social, and spiritual obstacles of life-threatening disease. It is interesting to note that even the quality of life of the caregiver also improves. Palliative care is needed by 56.8 million individuals annually, including 25.7 million in their final year according to WHO, while only 14% of palliative care patients worldwide receive it.

Palliative care improves the quality of life of life-threatening illness patients and their families. Early detection, assessment, and treatment of physical, psychosocial, and spiritual suffering and additional concerns diminish discomfort. Addressing suffering goes beyond physical symptoms. Palliative care supports patients and caregivers collaboratively. This includes practical assistance and bereavement counselling. It supports patients to live as fully as possible till death.

The human right to health includes palliative care. Patient-centred and integrated health services should focus on individual needs and preferences.

Many diseases require palliative care. Most palliative care patients have chronic conditions like cardiovascular disease (38.5%), cancer (34%), respiratory disease (10.3%), AIDS (5.7%), and diabetes (4.6%). Kidney failure, chronic liver illness, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's, rheumatoid arthritis, neurological disease, dementia, congenital defects, and drug-resistant TB may require palliative care.

Most common and serious symptoms that patients undergoing palliative care experience are pain and respiratory difficulties. Almost 80% of AIDS, cancer, and 67% of cardiovascular and COPD patients would experience moderate to severe agony at death.

Opioids also relieve dyspnea and diminish the increased pain experienced by patients. Early symptom control is ethical to reduce suffering and respect the dignity of the patient.
questions.learning: B,D True statements are: • — The patient is sovereign • The aim is to improve the quality of life Palliative care helps patients and their families cope with physical, psychological, social, and spiritual obstacles of life-threatening disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Seizures are seen in what percentage of RTA patients with brain contusion/loss of consciousness?
options: No relation between trauma and seizures.
questions.explanation: Post-traumatic seizures (PTS) are a well-recognized complication of Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI). For patients who have sustained significant head trauma in a road traffic accident, characterized by brain contusion or a prolonged loss of consciousness, the incidence of developing seizures is approximately 17%. These are classified as "early" if they occur within the first week and "late" if they occur after seven days. Options B and C (45% and 75%) significantly overestimate the clinical risk for most contusion cases. Statement D is incorrect as the relationship between brain trauma and epilepsy is well-established. Because of this risk, prophylactic anticonvulsants like Levetiracetam or Phenytoin are often administered for the first 7 days following severe TBI to prevent early PTS, which can worsen secondary brain injury. Accurate knowledge of these statistics helps clinicians counsel families and plan appropriate neurological follow-up
