questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: All of the following oncogenic viruses can integrate with the human genome to initiate carcinogenesis except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HTLV

HTLV - Human T cell lymphotropic virus causes microbial carcinogenesis by indirect mechanisms. Even, Hepatitis C virus, a flavivirus, does not generate a provirus and appears to induce cancer indirectly.

Oncogenic viruses:

Integration of viral genome into the host cell thereby leading to the formation of a pro-virus is commonly a mechanism of viral microbial carcinogenesis. DNA tumor viruses encode viral oncoproteins that are important for viral replication. Some portion of this may become integrated into the host cell chromosome. For RNA tumor viruses that mostly belong to the retrovirus family are known to cause microbial carcinogenesis by indirect mechanisms.

Note:

HPV causes carcinogenesis by both integrations and by the E6, E7 protein systems.
questions.learning: HTLV HTLV - Human T cell lymphotropic virus causes microbial carcinogenesis by indirect mechanisms. Even, Hepatitis C virus, a flavivirus, does not generate a provirus and appears to induce cancer indirectly.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 28-year-old lactating female presents 2 weeks after delivery, with a 3 cm subareolar mass in her right breast. The mass is associated with redness, tenderness, and mild warmth. She reports no fever but mentions difficulty in breastfeeding from the affected breast. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lactation Mastitis

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lactational mastitis.

Lactational mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Mastitis occurs due to a combination of factors such as inadequate milk drainage and the introduction of bacteria present on the skin. The cracks in the nipple serve as an entry point, thus resulting in infection. The most common organism causing acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess).

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses. Signs and symptoms of this condition involve:

* Fever and malaise

* Localized pain and tenderness

* Redness and swelling of the affected breast

* Fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess. It is a late sign.

Management includes analgesia, continued expression from the breast, antibiotics such as amoxiclav, and repeated aspiration of pus. In case of aspiration and antibiotics failure, incision and drainage can be done.

Other Options:

Option A: Mondor’s disease is characterized by thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast and anterior chest wall.

Option B: Breast abscess is a sequela of untreated bacterial mastitis, which occurs due to the growth of staphylococcus or streptococcus due to breast milk stasis. Patients usually present with fever and malaise, localised pain and tenderness, redness and swelling of the affected breast and fluctuation test positive due to pus in the abscess, which is a late sign of breast abscess.

Option C: A galactocele is a milk-filled cavity in the breast of a woman who is usually lactating. It can be caused due to lactation problems, prolactin stimulation by drugs, or duct obstruction. It presents as a palpable, round, well-circumscribed, and freely mobile mass with no fever, pain, or inflammation. It is usually subareolar and unilateral.
questions.learning: Lactation Mastitis — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of lactational mastitis. Lactational mastitis is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. What is the probable diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mallory Weiss Tear

The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear as the patient's vitals are stable.

Mallory Weiss Syndrome:

* It is a common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to the presence of longitudinal superficial mucosal lacerations (Mallory-Weiss tears).

* They occur primarily in the lower esophagus close to the gastroesophageal junction.

* It mainly occurs in patients with repetitive forceful retching and vomiting and is associated with heavy alcohol intake.

* The concurrent presence of portal hypertension with esophageal varices and hiatal hernia in patients with Mallory Weiss syndrome is not uncommon.

Boerhaave syndrome:

* It is a transmural perforation of the esophagus (while the Mallory Weiss tear is a mucosal tear).

* Clinical presentation:

* Mackler's Triad:

* Vomiting

* lower thoracic pain

* subcutaneous emphysema

* Other classical findings include deranged vitals tachypnea, tachycardia, fever, and hypotension.

* Diaphoresis and abdominal rigidity can also be present
questions.learning: Mallory Weiss Tear — The most probable diagnosis for the above-mentioned clinical presentation is Mallory Weiss tear as the patient's vitals are stable.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: As per NCEP- ATP III, which of the following is not a criterion for metabolic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. High LDL

As per NCEP- ATP III, high LDL is not included in the definition criteria of metabolic syndrome.

Metabolic syndrome is present if three or more of the following five criteria are met, which is given by NCEP-ATP III (National Cholesterol Education Program and Adult Treatment Panel III). It includes:

• Central obesity: waist circumference >102 cm (M), >88 cm (F)
• Hypertriglyceridemia: triglyceride level ≥ 150 mg/dL
• Low HDL cholesterol: <40 mg/dL and <50 mg/dL for men and women, respectively.
• Hypertension: blood pressure ≥130 mmHg systolic or ≥ 85 mmHg diastolic.
• Fasting plasma glucose level: ≥100 mg/dL or previously diagnosed type 2 diabetes.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A man suffered damage to his right knee's lateral side. He complains of having trouble walking two days later because his toes continue to drag on the floor. Additionally, he observes numbness over the dorsum of the foot and upper lateral aspect of the leg. What is the most likely injured nerve?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Common peroneal nerve

The clinical scenario, combined with a high-stepping gait (foot drop), indicates common peroneal nerve injury. This is associated with loss of sensation over the dorsum of the foot and the first interdigital space.

The nerves supplying the marked areas are shown below.

The common peroneal nerve is derived from the dorsal branches of the 4th and 5th lumbar and 1st and 2nd sacral ventral rami. It runs obliquely along the lateral side of the popliteal fossa to the fibular head. It lies between the biceps femoris and the lateral head of the gastrocnemius. It then curves laterally around the neck of the fibula and gets divided into superficial and deep fibular nerves.

The first interdigital space is supplied by the deep fibular nerve, while the dorsum of the foot (except the lateral and medial borders) is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.

Superficial fibular nerve
Deep fibular nerve

Motor innervation

• Peroneus longus
• Peroneus Brevis

• Extensor digitorum longus
• Extensor hallucis longus
• Tibialis anterior
• Peroneus tertius

Sensory innervation

• Lateral aspect of the lower leg
• Dorsum of the toes except for the lateral side of the 5th toe and the first interdigital webspace

• The first interdigital space

Injury to the common peroneal nerve at the level of the neck of the fibula causes foot drop. Ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, and eversion of the foot are lost, while the inversion and plantar flexion are usually preserved. Sensory innervation to the dorsum of the foot, including the first web space, is lost. The ankle reflex is usually preserved.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Killian's dehiscence is located between which two structures?
questions.explanation: Killian's dehiscence is a triangular area of relative muscular weakness located in the posterior wall of the lower pharynx. It is specifically situated between the oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus muscle and the transverse fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle, both of which are parts of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. This area is clinically significant because it is the most common site for the formation of a Zenker's diverticulum. Increased pressure during swallowing can cause the mucosa to herniate through this weak point. Options A, B, and D are incorrect as they involve the palatopharyngeus or salpingopharyngeus, which are internal muscles of the pharynx and do not form this specific anatomical landmark. Patients with a Zenker's diverticulum often present with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis. Surgical or endoscopic management often requires the division of the cricopharyngeus muscle (cricopharyngeal myotomy) to relieve the pressure at Killian's dehiscence

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: An 18-year-old boy has recurrent episodes of involuntary body jerking without loss of consciousness, tongue biting, or post-episode confusion, and all investigations are normal. Which condition should be considered in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The 18-year-old presents with "pseudoseizures" or jerk-like movements. The absence of classic epileptic signs—such as confusion (post-ictal state), tongue biting, or urinary incontinence—along with normal medical tests (EEG, CT), suggests that the behavior is not an organic seizure. If the patient is consciously and intentionally producing these symptoms to achieve a specific external gain (like avoiding school, work, or legal trouble), the correct term is malingering (Option A). Factitious disorder (Option B) also involves intentional symptom production, but the goal is to play the "sick role" rather than for external gain. Somatization syndrome (Option C) involves involuntary symptoms in response to psychological stress. Hypochondriasis (Option D) is an excessive preoccupation with having a serious disease . Malingering is not a psychiatric illness but a behavior. Given the age and the non-epileptic nature of the movements, malingering for secondary gain is a key forensic and clinical consideration

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true about Japanese encephalitis?
options: Vaccinating pigs is helpful in disease control
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Man acts as the reservoir

Humans are the dead-end hosts for the Japanese encephalitis virus.

Japanese encephalitis is an endemic viral infection transmitted by mosquitoes. There is an increased risk in travelers to rural areas. JE has an inactivated vero culture-derived vaccine, given as 2 primary series to adults who are travelling to endemic areas.

Other options:

Option A: The disease is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus and Culex vishnui (common in India) species.

Option B: Herons act as reservoir hosts and pigs as amplifier hosts.

Option D: The control measures include mosquito control, locating piggeries away from the human dwellings and vaccinating pigs.

The image below shows the life cycle of the Japanese B encephalitis virus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The image given below shows neuromuscular monitoring of the patient after anesthesia. What is the most commonly used nerve for monitoring?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The following image shows neuromuscular monitoring and the most commonly used nerve for monitoring is the ulnar nerve.

The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve. This assesses the contraction of the adductor pollicis muscle to monitor neuromuscular activity.

Monitoring of neuromuscular blockade is required to monitor the blockade intraoperatively, ensure its complete reversal postoperatively, and prevent residual blockade. To monitor the neuromuscular function, a peripheral motor nerve is supramaximally stimulated and the response of the muscle is assessed.

The most commonly assessed nerve-muscle unit is the ulnar nerve-adductor pollicis muscle. This is because it is easily accessible, has the lowest risk of direct muscle stimulation, and the response can be evaluated visually, by tactile methods, or by objective methods. To stimulate the ulnar nerve, the electrodes are best applied to the volar aspect of the wrist.

Other nerve-muscle units that can be assessed include:

• Posterior tibial nerve- flexor hallucis brevis muscle
• Facial nerve- orbicularis oculi muscle
• Facial nerve- corrugator supercilii muscle

Many methods can be used for objective monitoring of neuromuscular function:

• Mechanomyography (MMG)
• Electromyography (EMG)
• Acceleration of the muscle response (AMG)
• Kinemyography (KMG)
• Cuff pressure modality (CPM)
• Compressomyography (CMG)
• Phonomyography (PMG)
questions.learning: Ulnar nerve — The following image shows neuromuscular monitoring and the most commonly used nerve for monitoring is the ulnar nerve. The mechanosensor with electrodes is placed over the region of the ulnar nerve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 27-year-old man has an asymptomatic retraction pocket of the tympanic membrane without keratin debris. The TM is mobile on Valsalva. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Wait and watch

• Mild retraction pockets without keratin accumulation are managed conservatively.
• Normal TM mobility indicates preserved Eustachian tube function.
• Observation with periodic otoscopic follow-up is recommended.
• Surgery is indicated if:

• Progressive retraction
• Keratin debris
• Cholesteatoma
• Hearing loss

• Ventilation tubes are reserved for persistent middle-ear effusion or dysfunction.
• Tympanoplasty is unnecessary in an asymptomatic mobile membrane.
• Retraction pockets can remain stable for years.
• Regular follow-up prevents delayed cholesteatoma.
• No keratin + mobile TM = Observe.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the communication barrier if interpretation of a words are understood in a different manner?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Semantic barrier

The communication barrier that occurs when the interpretation of words is understood differently is called a semantic Barrier.

Semantic barriers arise from misunderstandings due to differences in the meaning of words, phrases, or symbols. These barriers can cause confusion and misinterpretation, leading to ineffective communication.

example: In a public health campaign, "herd immunity" may be misunderstood by some as meaning they don’t need vaccination or as related to animals. This confusion can reduce vaccination rates and is a perfect example of a semantic barrier.

other options:

Option A: Linguistic Barrier: This barrier occurs when the language or dialect used in communication is not understood by one or more parties. It can include differences in language, vocabulary, or grammar, making it difficult to convey the intended message.

Option C: Psychological Barrier: Psychological barriers involve emotions, attitudes, or mental states that affect communication. These could include stress, fear, anger, or low self-esteem, which can hinder the ability to send, receive, or interpret messages accurately.

Option D: Cultural Barrier: Cultural barriers arise when differences in cultural backgrounds, beliefs, values, or practices lead to misunderstandings. These barriers can affect how messages are interpreted and can lead to miscommunication if cultural contexts are not considered.
questions.learning: Semantic barrier — The communication barrier that occurs when the interpretation of words is understood differently is called a semantic Barrier. Semantic barriers arise from misunderstandings due to differences in the meaning of words, phrases, or symbols.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true about Factories Act?
options: Children under 14 years of age must not be employed in factories
A child of 16 years can be employed only between 6 AM and 8 PM
The maximum working hours for an adult is 72 hours per week
A child of 16 years can work till 5 hours per day
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Children under 14 years of age must not be employed in factories

Factories act prohibits children of <14 years from being employed.

Children between 15–18 years can be employed only in certain industries and work only between 6 AM–7 PM. They should not be made to work for more than four and a half hours.

The maximum working hours for an adult industrial worker should be not more than 48 hours per week, not exceeding 9 hours a day; if overtime is paid, then it should be not more than 60 hrs per week.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is least likely to suggest a medical cause of her mental illness?
questions.explanation: In psychiatric evaluation, it is essential to distinguish between primary mental disorders and those secondary to a general medical condition. Auditory hallucinations (Option C) are a hallmark feature of primary psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia and are least likely to suggest an underlying medical cause. Conversely, the other options are significant "red flags" for organic (medical) brain syndromes. Elderly age (Option A) of onset for first-time psychiatric symptoms strongly suggests dementia or metabolic issues. A history of loss of consciousness (Option B) points toward trauma, epilepsy, or hypoxia. An acute onset (Option D) of confusion or behavioral changes is typical of delirium caused by infections, drug toxicity, or electrolyte imbalances. Primary psychiatric conditions usually have an insidious onset in younger adulthood and do not typically involve fluctuations in consciousness. Clinicians must always rule out these "medical" indicators before concluding that a patient's symptoms are purely functional or psychiatric in nature
questions.learning: In psychiatric evaluation, it is essential to distinguish between primary mental disorders and those secondary to a general medical condition. Auditory hallucinations (Option C) are a hallmark feature of primary psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia and…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During forensic analysis of a semen sample obtained in a rape case, distinctive yellow, needle-shaped crystals are observed. Which specific test is used to confirm the presence of sperm?
questions.explanation: The identification of distinctive yellow needle-like crystals (spermine picrate) during a forensic semen analysis is the hallmark of the Barberio test. This is a preliminary chemical test used to identify spermine, a component of seminal fluid. The Florence test (Option D) also produces crystals, but they are brown, rhombic crystals of choline periodide. The Acid Phosphatase test (Option B) is a very sensitive colorimetric screening test for semen but does not involve crystal formation. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear (Option C) is a staining technique used for cytological examination to visualize actual sperm cells under a microscope. While Barberio is a useful screening tool, the confirmatory test for semen in a rape investigation remains the microscopic visualization of spermatozoa. Understanding these forensic tests is critical for the medico-legal documentation of sexual assault and the identification of the perpetrator
questions.learning: The identification of distinctive yellow needle-like crystals (spermine picrate) during a forensic semen analysis is the hallmark of the Barberio test.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the B tympanogram seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serous otitis media

Type B tympanogram is seen with serous otitis media.

Pearl PF1067: Types of curves in tympanogram

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: What is the causative agent in a 55-year-old man presenting with fever, progressive fatigue, hypotension, tachycardia, and the peripheral blood smear findings shown?
questions.explanation: The peripheral blood smear provides two definitive diagnostic clues for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. First, the presence of multiple delicate ring-form trophozoites within single red blood cells is characteristic. Second, the pathognomonic finding is the banana-shaped (crescentic) gametocyte, which is unique to P. falciparum. Plasmodium vivax (Option A) would show enlarged RBCs with Schuffner's dots and more amoeboid trophozoites. Plasmodium malariae (Option D) classically shows "band-form" trophozoites. Plasmodium ovale (Option C) shows oval-shaped RBCs with fimbriated edges. Clinically, P. falciparum is the most dangerous species, capable of causing cerebral malaria, hypotension, and rapid systemic failure as seen in this febrile patient. Therefore, because the crescent-shaped gametocyte is a definitive morphological marker for this species, Plasmodium falciparum is the correct etiological factor
questions.learning: The peripheral blood smear provides two definitive diagnostic clues for Plasmodium falciparum malaria. First, the presence of multiple delicate ring-form trophozoites within single red blood cells is characteristic.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department and is found to have a corneal abrasion, corneal ulcer, corneal perforation, and foreign body. Which of the following will not cause hypotonic maculopathy in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Suprachoroidal haemorrhage

Suprachoroidal hemorrhage will not cause hypotonic maculopathy in this patient.

Maculopathy is common in eyes developing hypotony, which is defined as IOP <6 mmHg. The most common cause is excessive drainage following glaucoma filtration surgery (Option D). Other causes include trauma such as cyclodialysis of the uvea (Option B), penetrating injury (Option C), chronic uveitis, retinal detachment, and other systemic causes such as dehydration, uncontrolled diabetes, uremia, and treatment with hyperosmotic agents. They usually cause bilateral hypotonic maculopathy.

Suprachoroidal hemorrhage is a bleed into the suprachoroidal space that results from the rupture of the posterior ciliary artery. When the bleed is severe it causes extrusion of intraocular contents that is termed as expulsive hemorrhage. It is a rare but dreaded complication of the phacoemulsification procedure. Signs seen in suprachoroidal hemorrhage are:

• Progressive increase in intraocular pressure
• Prolapse of iris
• Loss or partial obscuration of the red reflex
• In severe cases there can be extrusion of the posterior segment contents into the anterior chamber and through the incision such as vitreous extrusion

Immediate treatment involves rapid closure of the incision followed by administration of IOP-lowering medications such as oral acetazolamide and topical or systemic steroids to reduce inflammation. Standard post-operative antibiotics can be added in these patients.
questions.learning: Suprachoroidal haemorrhage Suprachoroidal hemorrhage will not cause hypotonic maculopathy in this patient. Maculopathy is common in eyes developing hypotony, which is defined as IOP <6 mmHg.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain consistent with a cluster headache. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
questions.explanation: High-flow 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min) administered via a non-rebreather mask is the gold standard for the acute abortive treatment of a cluster headache attack. It typically provides rapid relief within 15–20 minutes and is highly effective with a superior safety profile. Verapamil (Option A) is the first-line choice for long-term prophylaxis to prevent future attacks but is ineffective for stopping an acute episode once it has started. Lithium (Option C) and Topiramate (Option D) are also used as prophylactic agents in chronic or refractory cases rather than for acute relief. Cluster headaches are characterized by severe, unilateral, retro-orbital pain accompanied by autonomic symptoms like lacrimation or nasal congestion. Because the attacks are short-lived but excruciating, rapid-acting treatments like oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan are prioritized. Therefore, high-flow oxygen is the most appropriate immediate intervention
questions.learning: High-flow 100% oxygen (12–15 L/min) administered via a non-rebreather mask is the gold standard for the acute abortive treatment of a cluster headache attack.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 36-year-old woman (P2L2) who previously underwent tubectomy and surgical management of endometriosis (adhesiolysis and excision of lesions), now presents with recurrence of the symptoms. What is the definitive treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy

Endometriosis is a chronic estrogen-dependent condition.

Common sites:

• Ovary
• Uterosacral ligaments
• Pelvic peritoneum
• Rectovaginal septum

Definitive Treatment : Total Hysterectomy with Bilateral Salpingo-Oophorectomy (TAH + BSO)

Removes uterus ; Removes ovaries → eliminates estrogen source

A) Hysterectomy alone

Ovaries remain → estrogen production continues → recurrence possible.

C) LNG-IUS

Used for symptom control, not definitive treatment.

D) Resection of nodules

Conservative surgery may lead to recurrence.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes is dependent on Vitamin C for its activity?
questions.explanation: Prolyl hydroxylase is a key enzyme in collagen synthesis, responsible for the hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen. This post-translational modification is essential for the stability of the collagen triple helix. The enzyme requires vitamin C (ascorbic acid) as a cofactor to keep iron (Fe²⁺) in its reduced, active state at the catalytic site. In the absence of vitamin C, prolyl hydroxylase (and lysyl hydroxylase) cannot function effectively, leading to defective collagen formation, which is the biochemical basis of scurvy. Lysyl oxidase (Option B) is also involved in collagen maturation, but it is copper-dependent, not vitamin C–dependent, and is responsible for cross-linking collagen and elastin fibers. Lysyl dehydrogenase (Option A) and hydroxyprolyl kinase (Option D) are not key enzymes in the vitamin C–dependent collagen synthesis pathway. Thus, the enzyme whose activity depends on vitamin C is prolyl hydroxylase, explaining the classic features of vitamin C deficiency such as bleeding gums and impaired wound healing
questions.learning: Prolyl hydroxylase is a key enzyme in collagen synthesis, responsible for the hydroxylation of proline residues in procollagen. This post-translational modification is essential for the stability of the collagen triple helix.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What hormone levels are typical during days 21–25 of a 28-day cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Estrogen ↑, Progesterone ↑ ; FSH ↓, LH ↓

Days 21–25 correspond to the mid-luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is fully functional. Progesterone peaks, and estrogen remains moderately elevated. High steroid levels exert negative feedback on the pituitary, suppressing FSH and LH, matching option A.
questions.learning: Estrogen ↑, Progesterone ↑ ; FSH ↓, LH ↓ Days 21–25 correspond to the mid-luteal phase, when the corpus luteum is fully functional. Progesterone peaks, and estrogen remains moderately elevated.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text:
A patient presented with breathing difficulty and nasal polyposis when he took aspirin for fever. He faced this issue previously too when he took aspirin. Which among the following is not true about this?

COX -  Cyclooxygenase
options: There is no allergic sensitization to aspirin and its metabolites
Occur on exposure to only aspirin
Occurs with exposure to other NSAIDs too that block COX 1
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Occur on exposure to only aspirin

The diagnosis for this patient with breathing difficulty and nasal polyposis, triggered by aspirin, a COX-1 inhibitor is aspirin-induced asthma, also known as Samter's triad. The statement that is not true is that "it occurs on exposure to only aspirin", as this condition can also be triggered by other NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1, and is not restricted to just aspirin alone.

Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma. It consists of:

• Nasal polyposis
• Bronchial asthma
• Aspirin intolerance

A patient with Samter's triad experiences severe asthma and nasal polyposis triggered by aspirin or other COX-1 inhibitors. This condition involves nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, anosmia, and recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis, with acute asthma attacks often occurring a few hours after ingestion of these medications.

These patients overproduce leukotrienes due to COX-1 inhibition and decreased prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) levels. Therefore, they should avoid COX-1 inhibitors like aspirin and most NSAIDs but can generally tolerate COX-2 inhibitors and acetaminophen.

Treatment typically includes leukotriene modifiers, and in some cases, aspirin desensitization may be used to manage symptoms and allow the use of aspirin or NSAIDs if necessary for other conditions. Recent advances in treatment include biologics such as Dupilumab and IL-5 inhibitors, which are increasingly effective in managing aspirin-induced asthma and may replace aspirin desensitization except when ongoing aspirin or NSAID therapy is required.

Other options:

Option A: The reaction in aspirin-induced asthma is not due to an allergic sensitization but rather due to the inhibition of COX-1 and subsequent overproduction of leukotrienes.

Option B: Montelukast, a leukotriene receptor antagonist, is effective in managing symptoms of aspirin-induced asthma by counteracting the elevated levels of leukotrienes that contribute to inflammation and respiratory issues.

Option D: It occurs with exposure to other NSAIDs too, that block COX-1. Patients with aspirin-induced asthma can react to other NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1, not just aspirin.
questions.learning: Occur on exposure to only aspirin — The diagnosis for this patient with breathing difficulty and nasal polyposis, triggered by aspirin, a COX-1 inhibitor is aspirin-induced asthma, also known as Samter's triad.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Beta 2 receptor action leading to hyperglycemia/ hypoglycemia is mediated by which of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Adenylyl cyclase

Beta 2 receptor action leading to hypoglycemia/ hyperglycemia is mediated by adenylyl cyclase. Catecholamines act through beta 2 receptors and they use adenylyl cyclase - cAMP second messenger system to stimulate the target tissues.

Other hormones that use adenylyl cyclase - cAMP second messenger system are :

• Adrenocorticotropic hormone
• Angiotensin II
• Corticotropin-releasing hormone
• Calcitonin
• Follicle-stimulating hormone
• Glucagon
• Growth hormone-releasing hormone
• Human chorionic gonadotropin
• Luteinizing hormone
• Parathyroid hormone
• Secretin
• Somatostatin
• Thyroid-stimulating hormone
• Vasopressin

Hormones exert their actions by stimulating cAMP production within the cells. When the hormone binds to the membrane receptor, the receptor is coupled to the G protein. This G protein can either stimulate (Gs protein) or inhibit (Gi protein) adenylyl cyclase that controls the conversion of cytoplasmic adenosine triphosphate to adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). The protein kinases dependent on cAMP are thus activated. This leads to a series of biochemical reactions enabling the hormone to exert its actions.

Guanylyl cyclase is the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of cGMP.
questions.learning: Adenylyl cyclase Beta 2 receptor action leading to hypoglycemia/ hyperglycemia is mediated by adenylyl cyclase. Catecholamines act through beta 2 receptors and they use adenylyl cyclase - cAMP second messenger system to stimulate the target tissues.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following images accurately represents the medical condition described in the given scenario?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a neonate with "respiratory distress" and a "scaphoid (sunken) abdomen" is highly characteristic of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH). The X-ray image confirms this by showing "bowel loops within the thoracic cavity," usually on the left side, which displace the heart and lungs. This occurs due to a failure in the development of the pleuroperitoneal membrane, most commonly through the Bochdalek foramen. Intestinal obstruction (Option B) would show dilated loops within the abdomen and typically presents with abdominal distension, not a scaphoid abdomen. Pleural effusion (Option C) and pneumonia (Option D) present with fluid or consolidation in the chest, but they do not involve the migration of abdominal organs into the thorax. CDH is a neonatal emergency because the herniated organs cause pulmonary hypoplasia, leading to severe respiratory failure. Management involves immediate stabilization with intubation and a nasogastric tube to decompress the bowel, followed by surgical repair once the neonate is hemodynamically stable
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a neonate with "respiratory distress" and a "scaphoid (sunken) abdomen" is highly characteristic of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient is planned to undergo hysteroscopic polypectomy using bipolar electrocautery. What is the ideal agent for distention?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Normal saline

Normal saline is the ideal fluid media used for bipolar electrocautery as it can function regardless of the fluid electrolyte content.

Normal saline and lactated Ringer solutions are commonly used isotonic, electrolyte-containing fluids in operating rooms for diagnostic hysteroscopy procedures. These solutions can cause volume overload and, if rapidly absorbed in large volumes, may lead to pulmonary edema.

Isotonic, electrolyte-containing fluids are contraindicated for use with monopolar electrosurgical devices because they conduct electrical current, dissipate instrument energy and render the instrument ineffective. Low-viscosity, electrolyte-poor fluids such as 1.5-percent glycine, 3-percent sorbitol, and 5-percent mannitol are preferred as they are non-conductive and can be safely used with monopolar electrosurgical energy devices.

The primary risk of using hypotonic, hypoosmolar solutions is the intravascular absorption of these fluids, which can lead to acute hyponatremia and hypo osmolality.

The criteria for terminating the procedure for electrolyte-deficient fluid is a deficit of 1 L and electrolyte-rich fluid is a deficit of 2.5 L.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old female with a history of chest pain and upper respiratory tract infection, seven days ago, presents with shortness of breath. She has BP of 100/60 mm Hg and a pulse rate of 110/min. Chest x-ray reviews an enlarged heart, which appears like a water bottle. Which of the following is incorrect?
options: Loud S1 is a common finding
Echo will show diastolic RA/RV collapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Loud S1 is a common finding

The water-bottle shaped heart on chest X-ray strongly suggests:

Pericardial Effusion → Cardiac Tamponade

Supporting clues:

| Finding | Explanation

| ------- | -----------

| Tachycardia | Compensatory response

| Hypotension | Reduced cardiac output

| Dyspnea | Reduced ventricular filling

In cardiac tamponade, muffled heart sounds are a key finding, not a loud S1.

The definitive treatment is: Pericardiocentesis

A needle is inserted into the pericardial space to remove fluid and relieve pressure.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 30 year old woman came to OPD with a twin pregnancy at 10 weeks of gestation. She has a 3 year old female child who was born at term and had 2 first trimester abortions previously. Which of the following is the correct representation of her obstetric score/formula. G=gravid, P= para:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. G4P1 A2 L1

The obstetric score is G4P1A2L1.

Gravida and para refer to pregnancies and not to babies.
Gravida: Total number of pregnancies including the present one.
Para: Total number of pregnancies crossing the period of viability, which is 28 weeks in India.

As such, a woman who delivers twins in the first pregnancy is still a gravida 1 and para 1. A pregnant woman with a previous history of 2 abortions and 1 term delivery can be expressed as 4th Gravida but primipara.

It is customary in clinical practice to summarise the past obstetric history by 2 digits

First digit: Number of viable births
Second digit: Number of abortions
Both digits connected with a “+” sign affixing the letter P.
Thus, P1+2 denotes patient had 1 viable birth and 2 abortions.

In some centres, it is expressed by 4digits connected by dashes, P(A-B-C-D)
A: Number of term pregnancies (37-42 weeks)
B: Number of preterm pregnancies (28 to less than 37 weeks)
C: Number of miscarriages (less than 28 weeks)
D: Number of children alive at present.
questions.learning: G4P1 A2 L1 — The obstetric score is G4P1A2L1. Gravida and para refer to pregnancies and not to babies.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Among the extra intestinal manifestations of Crohn’s disease, which one of the following is related to the disease activity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eye complications (Iritis/Uveitis)

• Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) occur in 25–40% of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Some manifestations parallel intestinal disease activity, while others occur independently.
• Eye manifestations (episcleritis, iritis, uveitis) are commonly associated with active Crohn’s disease and may improve with treatment of the intestinal inflammation.

Why not other options?

• B. Renal calculi

• Not related to disease activity.
• Occur due to hyperoxaluria from ileal disease or resection.

• C. Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)

• Usually independent of bowel disease activity.
• More commonly associated with ulcerative colitis than Crohn’s disease.

• D. Chronic active hepatitis:

• Not directly related to Crohn’s disease activity.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 31-year-old lady with diabetes mellitus delivers a term neonate. Which of the following problems is associated with a baby born to this lady?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglycemia

The condition associated with an infant born to a mother with diabetes mellitus is hypoglycemia.

In pregestational diabetes and gestational diabetes mellitus, maternal hyperglycemia causes a higher amount of blood glucose to pass through the placenta into the fetal circulation. It results in fetal hyperglycemia leading to fetal hyperinsulinism. These increased insulin levels continue to persist after delivery which leads to hypoglycemia. Extra glucose in the fetus is stored as body fat causing macrosomia. These newborns are at risk of developing various complications due to fetal hyperglycemia. They are:

* Gastrointestinal: These infants may demonstrate abdominal distention caused by a transient delay in the development of the left side of the colon due to fluctuations in maternal and fetal glucose resulting in small left colon syndrome.

* Metabolic: Hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia

* Neural: Neural tube defects like caudal regression syndrome, encephalocele, anencephaly

* Respiratory: Respiratory distress syndrome, transient tachypnea of newborn, persistent pulmonary hypertension

* Cardiac: Cardiomegaly, cardiac malformations like a ventricular or atrial septal defect, transposition of the great vessels(most specific), truncus arteriosus, double-outlet right ventricle, tricuspid atresia, coarctation of the aorta

* Haematological: Polycythemia, renal vein thrombosis

* Others: Hyperbilirubinemia, insulin resistance, diabetes, sudden intrauterine death

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the treatment of choice for a woman with atrophic vaginitis with complaints of itching?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Topical estrogen

Atrophic vaginitis is treated with topical estrogen vaginal cream.

Atrophic vaginitis (senile vaginitis) is seen in postmenopausal women due to the thinning of vaginal mucosa (lack of estrogen). They present as discomfort (itching) and dryness in the vulva with dyspareunia. Occasionally, they may also complain of yellowish or blood-stained vaginal discharge.

The possibility of a coexisting carcinoma of the body or the cervix has to be excluded before treating it with estrogen supplements. Though topical application is the initial treatment, systemic estrogens (hormone replacement therapy) can be considered based on the patient's profile and the severity of the symptoms.

Other options:

Option A: Steroids are not indicated in the management of atrophic vaginitis as the inflammation is due to a lack of estrogen. Furthermore, they may predispose the patient to vaginal infections.

Option C: Antihistamines antagonize histamine receptors and prevent the allergic response. Since atrophic vaginitis is not an allergy response, they are not indicated in the treatment.
questions.learning: Topical estrogen Atrophic vaginitis is treated with topical estrogen vaginal cream. Atrophic vaginitis (senile vaginitis) is seen in postmenopausal women due to the thinning of vaginal mucosa (lack of estrogen).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of breech presentation in pregnancy? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prematurity

Breech presentation is more common in preterm pregnancies because the fetus is smaller and has greater mobility within the uterine cavity.

As pregnancy advances:

• Most fetuses spontaneously rotate to a cephalic presentation by term
• Premature fetuses may not yet have undergone this rotation

Thus, prematurity is the most common cause of breech presentation.

Other causes/risk factors for breech presentation:

• Uterine anomalies
• Placenta previa
• Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios
• Multiple gestation
• Fetal anomalies (eg, hydrocephalus)
questions.learning: Prematurity Breech presentation is more common in preterm pregnancies because the fetus is smaller and has greater mobility within the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The medical condition shown below in the image of a pregnant woman is called as?
questions.explanation: The provided anatomical diagram of a pregnant uterus illustrates the placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment, directly overlying the internal cervical os. This condition is called placenta previa (Option B). It is a leading cause of painless vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy. Vasa previa (Option A) occurs when fetal blood vessels from the cord or placenta cross the internal os ahead of the fetus. Placenta accreta (Option C) is a more serious condition where the placenta grows too deeply into the uterine wall, making it difficult to detach after birth. Abruptio placenta (Option D) is the premature separation of a normally implanted placenta, which usually presents with painful bleeding and a tense abdomen. Based on the specific anatomical position shown in the image—where the placenta is simply "in the way" of the birth canal—placenta previa is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The provided anatomical diagram of a pregnant uterus illustrates the placenta implanted in the lower uterine segment, directly overlying the internal cervical os.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When a dataset shows wide variation, skewness, or contains outliers, which measure of central tendency is most appropriate to use?
questions.explanation: The choice of central tendency depends on the distribution of the data. The Mean (Option A) is the most common measure but is highly sensitive to outliers and skewed data; even a single extreme value can significantly pull the mean away from the center of the majority of the data. The Median is the "middle" value when data is ordered. It is not affected by extreme outliers or skewness, making it the most robust and preferred measure of central tendency for non-normally distributed data. The Mode (Option B) is the most frequently occurring value and is useful for categorical data but less helpful for interpreting the "center" of continuous numerical data. Standard deviation (Option D) is a measure of dispersion, not central tendency. Therefore, for skewed medical or demographic data, the median provides the most accurate representative "center."

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · Basics Of Cell Cytoskeleton
questions.text: Which of the following are present in the intercalated disc of cardiac muscle? 1. Fascia adherens 2. Desmosome (Macula adherens) 3. Gap junction 4. Tight junction (Zonula occludens)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, 3

Intercalated discs are specialized junctions that connect adjacent cardiac muscle cells, providing both mechanical strength and electrical coupling required for synchronized cardiac contraction. They contain–

• Fascia adherens: anchors actin filaments and transmits contractile force.
• Desmosomes (macula adherens): provide strong mechanical attachment, preventing separation of cardiomyocytes during contraction.
• Gap junctions: allow rapid passage of ions between cells, enabling electrical coupling and synchronized depolarization.

Why not the other options?

• B. Gap junction only: Ignores the mechanical junctions essential for maintaining tissue integrity.
• C. Tight junction included: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) are absent in cardiac intercalated discs.
• D. Includes tight junctions: Incorrect because tight junctions are characteristic of epithelial cells, not cardiac muscle.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 Intercalated discs are specialized junctions that connect adjacent cardiac muscle cells, providing both mechanical strength and electrical coupling required for synchronized cardiac contraction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 54-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever, abdominal pain, and altered sensorium. Ascitic fluid analysis shows: Total leukocyte count: 800 cells/mm³ Neutrophils: 320 cells/mm³ Protein: low Culture: pending What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an identifiable intra-abdominal source, most commonly seen in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

Diagnostic criterion: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count ≥250 cells/mm³

Typical findings:

• Low ascitic fluid protein
• Fever, abdominal pain, altered mental status
• Culture may be positive (commonly E. coli, Klebsiella, Streptococcus) but treatment should start even if culture results are pending.

Management:

• Empiric third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., cefotaxime)
• Albumin infusion to reduce risk of hepatorenal syndrome.
questions.learning: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is a bacterial infection of ascitic fluid without an identifiable intra-abdominal source, most commonly seen in patients with cirrhosis and ascites.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is not true regarding the procedure done using the instrument given in the image below?
options: Procedure can be done in both lateral & prone position
Diagnosing an infiltrative or granulomatous disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Contraindicated if platelet count <40,000

The image shows a bone marrow biopsy needle. Thrombocytopenia is not in itself a contraindication for bone marrow biopsy. However, a platelet count >20,000 is ensured for safety purposes.

Indications of bone marrow biopsy:

• Evaluation of unexplained anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia
• Evaluation of polycythemia, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis
• Diagnosis and staging of lymphoma or solid tumors
• Diagnosis and evaluation of plasma cell disorders and leukemias
• Evaluation of suspected infiltrative and storage diseases
• Evaluation of fever of unknown origin, suspected mycobacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections, or granulomatous diseases

Contraindications of bone marrow biopsy:

• Severe hemophilia
• Severe disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
• Severe bleeding disorders

Procedure for bone marrow biopsy:

Prone or lateral position is chosen for the procedure. Posterior superior iliac spine is identified. After disinfection and local anaesthesia, the patient is asked to inhale slowly through the nose and exhale slowly through the mouth to relieve anxiety .The needle is inserted and rotated on its axis.

On reaching the desired depth, the stylet is removed and needle is advanced. The needle is rotated in the opposite direction to loosen the specimen. It is then withdrawn using the same rotational movement.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The perinatal transmission of infection shows the spectrum of anemia, possibly myocarditis, high output cardiac failure, and ascites. Identify the causative agent.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Parvovirus B19

The given clinical vignette with anemia, myocarditis, high output cardiac failure, ascites and the image showing hydrops fetalis point to a diagnosis of erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease) caused by parvovirus B19.

Parvovirus B19 infects fetal erythroid progenitor cells and causes anemia. Severe anemia leads to high-output cardiac failure and hydrops fetalis. In addition to bone marrow, the liver is also affected causing ascites, because it is involved in erythropoiesis in the early fetal life.

Erythema infectiosum presents as a prodrome of low-grade fever, headache, and a mild upper respiratory tract infection after an incubation period of 4-28 days. A characteristic rash occurs in 3 stages:

• Erythematous facial flushing causing a slapped cheek appearance in the 1st stage
• Diffuse macular erythema spreads to the trunk and proximal extremities in the 2nd stage.
• Central clearing of the macular lesions, giving the rash a lacy, reticulated appearance in the 3rd stage.

The rash is more prominent on extensor surfaces and spares the palms and soles. At this stage, affected children are afebrile and do not appear ill.  Children with erythema infectiosum are not likely to be infectious at presentation.

Complications of the disease include:

• Arthralgias or arthritis
• Transient Aplastic Crisis: A transient arrest of erythropoiesis and absolute reticulocytopenia in serum hemoglobin in individuals with chronic hemolytic conditions like sickle cell anemia
• Thrombocytopenic purpura
• Myocarditis
• A papular-purpuric “gloves-and-socks” syndrome
• Neurological: Aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and peripheral neuropathy, stroke in children with sickle cell disease
• Infection-associated hemophagocytic syndrome in immunocompromised patients
• Maternal infection is associated with nonimmune fetal hydrops and intrauterine fetal demise

There is no data to support the use of IVIG for postexposure prophylaxis, however, it has been used with some success to treat B19-related episodes of anemia and bone marrow failure in immunocompromised children. There is no specific antiviral therapy for B19 infection.
questions.learning: Parvovirus B19 — The given clinical vignette with anemia, myocarditis, high output cardiac failure, ascites and the image showing hydrops fetalis point to a diagnosis of erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease) caused by parvovirus B19.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following structures do not pass through both greater and lesser sciatic foramens?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tendon of obturator internus

The anatomical pathways of structures traversing the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, a classic integration of pelvic anatomy + clinical procedures (e.g., pudendal nerve block).

• Structures that pass through both greater AND lesser sciatic foramina (via a loop around the sacrospinous ligament):

• Pudendal nerve
• Internal pudendal vessels
• Nerve to obturator internus

Pathway:

• Exit pelvis via greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis)
• Hook around ischial spine / sacrospinous ligament
• Enter perineum via lesser sciatic foramen
• Exception (Correct answer): Tendon of obturator internus

• Originates inside pelvis
• Exits only through lesser sciatic foramen
• Does NOT pass through greater sciatic foramen

Pudendal nerve block is given near the ischial spine

• Injury/compression here can affect:

• Perineal sensation
• External anal & urethral sphincters

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with heart disease has breathlessness on going to the bathroom. What grade does he belong to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. NYHA 3

This patient with heart disease with dyspnea on going to the bathroom, which is an activity of daily living/ ordinary activity, may be classified as NYHA class 3.

The New York Heart Association (NYHA) has outlined criteria that may be used to classify patients with heart disease based on their functional disability.

NYHA Classification of Heart Failure:

NYHA class
Description

I

• No limitation of physical activity
• Ordinary physical activity does not cause symptoms

II

• Slight limitation of physical activity
• Comfortable at rest, but ordinary physical activity causes symptoms

III

• Marked limitation of physical activity
• Comfortable at rest, but less than ordinary physical activity causes symptoms

IV

• Unable to carry out any physical activity without symptoms or symptoms at rest

The Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale is used to classify the severity of symptoms in respiratory diseases, specifically COPD.

Modified MRC (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale:

• 0- Breathless only with strenuous exercise
• 1- Breathless when hurrying on a level or walking up a hill
• 2- Walks slower than peers or has to stop for breath when walking on level
• 3- Stops for breath after walking about 100m or for a few minutes
• 4- Breathless at rest
questions.learning: NYHA 3 — This patient with heart disease with dyspnea on going to the bathroom, which is an activity of daily living/ ordinary activity, may be classified as NYHA class 3.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 20-year-old lady presents with sudden palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, and a feeling like she is being choked. She had a history of a COVID-19 infection 1 year ago and fears she might die because she was positive for COVID-19. Physical examination, ECG, and laboratory workup were unremarkable. This is the first time she is experiencing an episode like this which lasts normally for around 20 minutes. What is the most likely diagnosis ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Panic attack

This clinical vignette describes a classic panic attack as she has symptoms of palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, feelings of choking and fear of dying although her examination and lab findings are normal.

A panic attack is characterized by a sudden onset of overwhelming fear or severe discomfort, which can persist for several minutes to hours. Recurrent panic attacks are termed panic disorders.

Panic attacks can occur in other disorders, particularly in specific phobias, social phobias, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unexpected panic attacks occur at any time and are not associated with any identifiable situational trigger. Attacks in patients with social and specific phobias are usually expected in response to a specific stimulus.

Some panic attacks do not fit into unexpected or expected attacks, and these attacks are referred to as situationally predisposed panic attacks. They may or may not occur on exposure to a specific trigger, or may occur immediately after exposure or after a considerable period of time.

Four or more of the following should be present to label it a panic attack:

* Racing or pounding heart, palpitations

* Involuntary shaking/trembling

* Chills or hot flashes

* Shortness of breath or smothering sensation

* Upset stomach or nausea

* Choking sensation

* Pain or discomfort in the chest region

* Overwhelming fear of death

* Sensation of light-headedness/dizziness/ faintness

* Depersonalization (disconnected from oneself) or derealization (detached from reality)

* Sense of losing control over oneself  or “going crazy”

* Tingling or numbness (paresthesias)

Pearl PF1276: Anxiety disorders

• Dyspnea
• Tachypnea
• Palpitations
• Sweating
• Dizziness
• Chest pain
• Tightness
• Paresthesias
• Emotional and cognitive
symptoms
• Feeling that something catastrophic is
about to happen.

Occur spontaneously without overt precipitants.

They often avoid situations/ places in which panic attacks have occurred.

Treatment is with benzodiazepines or SSRI/ SNRI and cognitive behavioural therapy

a variety of topics (job, health, finances, etc.) > 6 months.

3 or more of the following symptoms:

• Restlessness
• Fatigue
• Difficulty concentrating
• Irritability
• Muscle tension
• Sleep disturbance

Treatment:

First line: CBT, SSRIs or SNRIs

Second-line: Benzodiazepines, Buspirone
questions.learning: Panic attack — This clinical vignette describes a classic panic attack as she has symptoms of palpitations, sweating, breathlessness, feelings of choking and fear of dying although her examination and lab findings are normal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statistical terms is incorrectly matched with its associated concept?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mean, Median – Dispersion

Mean and median are measures of central tendency, not dispersion.

Standard error reflects variability of a sample statistic.

Correlation coefficient measures relationship between variables.

Moments are numerical measures that describe the shape of a distribution about a reference point (usually the mean). They help in understanding not just where the data is centered, but how the data is distributed around that centre.

• First moment (about the mean) → Mean (measure of central tendency)
• Second central moment → Variance (measure of dispersion)
• Third central moment → Skewness (measure of asymmetry of the distribution)
• Fourth central moment → Kurtosis (measure of peak / tail heaviness of the distribution)

Hence, the incorrect match is Mean, Median – Dispersion.
questions.learning: Mean, Median – Dispersion Mean and median are measures of central tendency, not dispersion. Standard error reflects variability of a sample statistic.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. He has a past history of peptic ulcer disease. Physical examination reveals rigidity. X-ray abdomen is as shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urgent surgical exploration

The clinical vignette with physical examination findings of rigidity, x-ray findings showing free air under the diaphragm with an underlying history of peptic ulcer disease is indicative of peptic ulcer perforation. The next best step in the management of this patient is urgent surgical exploration.

GI tract perforation:

Common causes include surgery, blunt or penetrating injury, bowel obstruction, peptic ulcer disease, corrosive agents, or particular medications.

Patients may present with acute pain, abdominal/pelvic mass due to an abscess or phlegmon formation, fistula formation(such as in Crohn's disease), sepsis

Physical examination shows subcutaneous gas (mediastinal gas might be heard as a systolic "crunch" - Hamman's sign). When free intraperitoneal perforation has occurred, signs of peritonitis are present.

Diagnosis may be made based on clinical exam findings of peritonitis and history. However, confirmation is obtained by demonstrating pneumoperitoneum. X-ray, USG, or CT scan may be used to quickly identify free air. Erect X-ray is commonly used and it shows the presence of free air under the diaphragm(shown in the image below)

Management - Initial management includes intravenous (IV) fluid therapy, cessation of oral intake, and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Indications for immediate bowel exploration are

* Sepsis/diffuse peritonitis(as in this patient)

* Bowel ischemia

* Complete or closed-loop bowel obstruction
questions.learning: Urgent surgical exploration — The clinical vignette with physical examination findings of rigidity, x-ray findings showing free air under the diaphragm with an underlying history of peptic ulcer disease is indicative of peptic ulcer perforation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the underlying factor responsible for the occurrence of LH surge?
questions.explanation: The LH (Luteinizing Hormone) surge is the critical event that triggers ovulation. It is caused by a unique "positive feedback" mechanism. During the late follicular phase of the menstrual cycle, the dominant follicle produces increasingly high levels of estradiol. When estradiol levels remain above a certain threshold (typically pg/mL) for approximately 48 hours, the normal negative feedback on the pituitary switches to positive feedback. This triggers a massive, rapid release of LH from the anterior pituitary gland. FSH (Option A) also rises slightly during this time, but it is not the primary driver of the surge. Progesterone (Option C) levels are low during the follicular phase and only rise after ovulation occurs. LH (Option D) is the result of the surge, not its underlying cause. Therefore, the peak in estradiol is the definitive physiological trigger for the LH surge
questions.learning: The LH (Luteinizing Hormone) surge is the critical event that triggers ovulation. It is caused by a unique "positive feedback" mechanism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with multiple colonic polyps and is diagnosed with colorectal carcinoma. There is a strong family history suggestive of Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC). Which DNA repair mechanism is most likely defective in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Mismatch repair

Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also called Lynch syndrome, is caused by defects in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) system. This repair mechanism normally corrects base–base mismatches and small insertion/deletion errors that occur during DNA replication.

Common genes involved:

• MLH1
• MSH2
• MSH6
• PMS2

Why other options are incorrect:

• Nucleotide excision repair: Repairs bulky DNA lesions such as thymine dimers caused by UV radiation (defective in xeroderma pigmentosum).
• Base excision repair: Corrects small base modifications such as deamination or oxidation.
• Double-strand break repair: Repairs DNA breaks through homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining.
questions.learning: Mismatch repair Hereditary Non-Polyposis Colorectal Cancer (HNPCC), also called Lynch syndrome, is caused by defects in the DNA mismatch repair (MMR) system.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The blood pressure of a population was tracked from childhood to adulthood. It was observed that those who had lower BP in childhood had low BP in adulthood, while those who had higher BP in childhood had high BP in adulthood. This can be best described as____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tracking of blood pressure

The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure.

In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood. The BP in individuals with low BP levels tend to remain low, and in those with high BP levels, they tend to remain high. This phenomenon of persistence of rank order of blood pressure has been described as "tracking".

Other options:

Option A: The rule of halves depicts the disease burden of hypertension in the community. It states that only about half of the hypertensive subjects in the general population are aware of the condition. Only half of those aware are being treated and only half of those being treated are considered to be adequately treated.

A pictorial representation of the rule of halves in hypertension is shown below:

Option B: The WHO STEPwise approach to non-communicable disease (NCD) risk factor surveillance (STEPS) is a simple, standardized method for collecting, analyzing, and disseminating data on key NCD risk factors such as tobacco use, alcohol use, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, overweight and obesity, raised blood pressure, raised blood glucose, and abnormal blood lipids.
questions.learning: Tracking of blood pressure — The above phenomenon is best described as the "tracking" of blood pressure. In this phenomenon, the blood pressure of individuals is followed up from early childhood into adulthood.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 20-year-old pregnant female presents with conductive hearing loss of 54db, not associated with tinnitus. Pure tone audiometry shows a notch at 2000 Hz. Which of the following is correct regarding the pathophysiology of the disease?
options: Ossicular fixation with intact tympanic membrane
Ossicular fixation with perforated tympanic membrane
Erosion of stapes footplate with perforated tympanic membrane
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ossicular fixation with intact tympanic membrane

The given clinical scenario of a young pregnant female with bilateral conducting hearing loss and notch at 2000Hz (Carhart's notch) is suggestive of otosclerosis where there is an ossicular fixation with the intact tympanic membrane.

Otosclerosis is the disease of the bony labyrinth in which a normally dense endochondral layer of the bony otic capsule is replaced by irregularly laid spongy bone. It has a positive family history with an autosomal dominant trait. It is more commonly seen in females between 20-30 years of age and the hearing loss is aggravated during pregnancy and menopause. It may be associated with osteogenesis imperfecta and a viral infection like measles.

Stapedial otosclerosis is the most common type of otosclerosis. Here the lesion starts just in front of the oval window in an area called fissula ante fenestram. There is fixation of stapes footplate.

Patients present with a bilateral conductive type of hearing loss, tinnitus (commonly in cochlear type and active stage), paracusis willisii (better hearing in noisy surroundings than in a quiet place), vertigo, and a monotonous, well-modulated soft speech.

The tympanic membrane is quite normal and mobile. Eustachian tube function is also normal. Pure tone audiometry shows a dip at 2000 Hz in the bone conduction curve known as the Carhart's notch. Tympanometry shows an As type of tympanogram in which there is reduced compliance at or near the ambient air pressure.

On examination, Schwartz sign/flamingo flush showing a red blush of the tympanic membrane due to vascularity can be seen.

Treatment includes medical, surgical management, and hearing aids. Medical management with sodium fluoride is used in the active stage to speed up the maturity of the active focus and halt further cochlear loss. The treatment of choice is surgical management which includes stapedotomy/stapedectomy with the placement of a prosthesis. Hearing aids are used in patients who refuse or are unfit for the surgery.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A neonate is diagnosed with gastroschisis. What is the most appropriate management approach for this condition?
questions.explanation: Gastroschisis is a neonatal emergency characterized by an abdominal wall defect (usually to the right of the umbilicus) through which the bowel herniates without a protective sac. The most appropriate management strategy is prompt surgical wall repair. Because the bowel is exposed directly to the air and amniotic fluid, the neonate is at high risk for fluid loss, hypothermia, and infection. Immediate care involves placing the lower half of the baby in a sterile "bowel bag" to minimize losses. The repair may be a "primary closure" if the abdominal cavity can accommodate the bowel, or a "staged closure" using a preformed silo (Option C, "slowly putting it inside," describes the process of staged closure, but the overall strategy is the surgical repair). Wait and watch (Option B) is fatal. Surgical excision (Option D) is incorrect as the bowel must be preserved. Unlike omphalocele, gastroschisis is rarely associated with other genetic syndromes but often involves significant bowel dysmotility post-repair
questions.learning: Gastroschisis is a neonatal emergency characterized by an abdominal wall defect (usually to the right of the umbilicus) through which the bowel herniates without a protective sac.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old male patient, a known case of left inguinal hernia presents to the emergency with an acute onset of pain abdomen associated with nausea, vomiting and abdominal distension. His pulse rate is 102/min, BP is 100/70 mmHg and respiratory rate is 24/min. On local examination, the skin overlying the swelling is tense and erythematous. There is localized tenderness over the swelling; the swelling is irreducible with absence of cough impulse. The most probable clinical diagnosis in this patient is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Strangulated hernia

A strangulated hernia occurs when the blood supply to the herniated bowel is compromised, leading to ischemia. It presents with features of intestinal obstruction along with local signs of inflammation. Features include pain, irreducibility, absent cough impulse, localized tenderness, tense erythematous skin, and signs of intestinal obstruction.

Why not the other options?

• A. Obstructed hernia: Causes intestinal obstruction but blood supply is intact; skin is usually not erythematous or tense.
• C. Incarcerated hernia: Irreducible but without obstruction or vascular compromise.
• D. Irreducible hernia: Simply cannot be reduced; no features of obstruction or strangulation.
questions.learning: Strangulated hernia — A strangulated hernia occurs when the blood supply to the herniated bowel is compromised, leading to ischemia. It presents with features of intestinal obstruction along with local signs of inflammation.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 38-year-old person with a history of intravenous drug abuse presents with malaise, fatigue, rigors, and a pan-systolic murmur best heard at the left sternal border. Based on these clinical features and risk factors, which organism is most likely to be isolated on blood culture?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of infective endocarditis (IE), specifically right-sided involvement as indicated by the pan-systolic murmur at the left sternal border (tricuspid regurgitation). Intravenous drug users (IVDU) have a high risk of developing IE, and Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism in this population, accounting for over 50% of cases. It typically results in an acute, destructive form of the disease. Streptococcus sanguis (Option A) is a common cause of subacute IE but is usually associated with dental procedures. Enterococcus (Option B) is often linked to genitourinary manipulations. Coxiella burnetii (Option C) is the cause of Q fever endocarditis, which is much rarer. Given the specific lifestyle risk factor and the acute presentation (rigors), Staphylococcus aureus is the statistically and clinically most probable pathogen
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of infective endocarditis (IE), specifically right-sided involvement as indicated by the pan-systolic murmur at the left sternal border (tricuspid regurgitation).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40 year old with high myopia wearing thick glasses from childhood came with complaints of sudden onset of flashes of light in left eye. What could be the likely cause ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retinal detachment

The given scenario of patient with severe myopia presenting sudden onset of flashes of light is likely retinal detachment.

Retinal detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

Risk factors include myopia, previous intraocular surgery such as aphakia or pseudophakia, a family history of retinal detachment, and trauma.

Clinical features include sudden painless loss of vision, flashes of light or photopsia, floaters in the eye, and curtains in the field of vision.

Examination findings will reveal:

• Normal or slightly low intraocular pressure
• Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect)
• Altered red reflex on the distant direct ophthalmoscope
• Indirect ophthalmoscopy may show grey reflex of the freshly detached retina or breaks in the retina
• Vitreous pigments on the anterior vitreous (Shaffer sign)
• Shifting fluid sign- Change in the position of the detached area with a change in gravity is the hallmark of exudative retinal detachment.
Management of rhegmatogenous retinal detachment includes sealing of retinal breaks, reducing the vitreous traction on the retina, and flattening of the retina by draining the subretinal fluid. Scleral buckling, pneumatic retinopexy, and pars plana vitrectomy can help in maintaining the chorioretinal apposition.

Treating the cause helps in exudative retinal detachment. Enucleation can be done if intranuclear tumors are present.
questions.learning: Retinal detachment — The given scenario of patient with severe myopia presenting sudden onset of flashes of light is likely retinal detachment. Retinal detachment is the separation of the neurosensory retina and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia developed muscular dystonia, which was treated. The patient currently complains of dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension. What drug is most likely responsible for these side effects?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Benztropine

The given scenario of dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension is a result of benztropine, which is used to treat antipsychotic-induced dystonia.

Adverse effects may include dry mouth, decreased thirst, mydriasis, blurred vision, palpitations, urinary retention, restlessness, hallucinations, xerostomia, photophobia, tachycardia, flushing, warm, dry skin, constipation, anhidrosis, delirium, and coma.

Acute muscular dystonia:

This is an extrapyramidal symptom (EPS) that occurs due to the antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors. Acute dystonia is more commonly associated with high-potency typical antipsychotics like haloperidol and occurs within 1 to 5 days of initiation of therapy. It occurs most commonly among younger patients and is characterised by muscle spasms involving linguofacial muscles, causing torticollis, locked jaw or trismus, grimacing, tongue thrusting, and oculogyric crisis in severe form.

Treatment:

* Anticholinergic agents like benztropine or diphenhydramine, by blocking striatal cholinergic receptors, balance the dopaminergic activity and are given as first-line treatment for dystonia.

* Benzodiazepines (diazepam) antagonise the excitatory dopaminergic neurons by their GABA agonist action and are used in refractory cases or when anticholinergic use is contraindicated.

Other options:

Option B: Quetiapine is another atypical antipsychotic with a favourable extrapyramidal side effects profile.

Option C: Haloperidol has a high risk of developing extrapyramidal side effects (EPS) such as akathisia, dystonia, and tardive dyskinesia.

Option D: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic that has low affinity to D2 receptors & high affinity to D4 receptors. This causes the least extrapyramidal side effects.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: After the parotidectomy operation, a patient presents with excessive sweating and redness over the parotid region. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Frey's Syndrome (gustatory sweating) is a frequent complication following parotid surgery. It occurs due to aberrant regeneration of the auriculotemporal nerve. Normally, this nerve carries parasympathetic fibers to the parotid for salivation and sympathetic fibers to sweat glands. After injury, the regrowing parasympathetic fibers mistakenly connect to the sweat glands of the overlying skin. Consequently, whenever the patient eats and stimulates salivation, they also experience localized sweating and redness. Horner's syndrome (Option B) presents with a triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis (decreased sweating). Bell's palsy (Option C) is an idiopathic facial nerve paralysis causing weakness but not gustatory sweating. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia (Option D) involves severe paroxysmal pain in the throat or ear. Given the specific post-operative presentation of sweating triggered by eating, Frey's syndrome is the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: Frey's Syndrome (gustatory sweating) is a frequent complication following parotid surgery. It occurs due to aberrant regeneration of the auriculotemporal nerve.
