questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with hypertension and hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. CT imaging reveals a renal mass, and the aldosterone–renin ratio (ARR) is elevated. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.explanation: The combination of hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, a high Aldosterone-Renin Ratio (ARR), and a localized adrenal mass is highly suggestive of an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn’s Syndrome). In cases of confirmed unilateral adrenal disease in a surgical candidate, laparoscopic adrenalectomy is the definitive treatment of choice as it can cure the underlying hyperaldosteronism. Medical management with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like Spironolactone (Option A) is generally reserved for patients with bilateral adrenal hyperplasia or those who are not fit for surgery. The ACTH stimulation test (Option C) is used to diagnose adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease), which presents with hypotension and hyperkalemia. The Dexamethasone suppression test (Option D) is the standard investigation for Cushing’s syndrome, which involves cortisol excess. Given the evidence of a unilateral functional tumor, surgical removal is the most appropriate management step
questions.learning: The combination of hypertension, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, a high Aldosterone-Renin Ratio (ARR), and a localized adrenal mass is highly suggestive of an aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn’s Syndrome).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All are criteria of IUGR except?
options: Absent or reversal of diastolic flow in umbilical artery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Uterine A PI < 95%

IUGR refers to failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential due to placental insufficiency or other causes.

Common diagnostic parameters include:

| Parameter | Diagnostic finding

| --------- | ------------------

| Estimated fetal weight (EFW) | < 3rd percentile

| Abdominal circumference (AC) | < 3rd percentile

| Abnormal Doppler | Umbilical artery changes

| Placental insufficiency markers | Abnormal uterine artery PI

Progression of Doppler abnormalities:

| Stage | Doppler Finding

| ----- | ---------------

| Early | Increased PI

| Moderate | Absent end-diastolic flow

| Severe | Reversed end-diastolic flow

Uterine artery pulsatility index (PI) <95th percentile is normal, not abnormal.

For IUGR Doppler: High resistance = abnormal

So:

• Umbilical artery diastolic flow ↓
• Uterine artery PI ↑
questions.learning: Uterine — A PI < 95% IUGR refers to failure of the fetus to achieve its genetically determined growth potential due to placental insufficiency or other causes.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Multiple myeloma can cause proximal tubular injury due to light chain deposition in the tubular epithelium causing acquired Fanconi Syndrome. Which of the following are characteristic findings in this condition? 1. Little/no proteinuria 2. Aminoaciduria 3. Phosphaturia 4. Glycosuria Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Acquired Fanconi syndrome in multiple myeloma occurs due to proximal tubular injury from monoclonal light-chain accumulation, particularly in the tubular epithelial cells. This causes generalized dysfunction of proximal tubular reabsorption.

• 1. Little/no proteinuria: Incorrect

• Fanconi syndrome causes low-molecular-weight proteinuria, so proteinuria is typically present.
• Therefore, “little/no proteinuria” is not characteristic.

• 2. Aminoaciduria: Correct

• Impaired proximal tubular amino acid reabsorption → aminoaciduria.

• 3. Phosphaturia: Correct

• Defective phosphate reabsorption → phosphaturia → hypophosphatemia and potentially osteomalacia.

• 4. Glycosuria: Correct

• Impaired proximal tubular glucose reabsorption → glycosuria despite normal blood glucose.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Acquired Fanconi syndrome in multiple myeloma occurs due to proximal tubular injury from monoclonal light-chain accumulation, particularly in the tubular epithelial cells.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the lesion shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Incised looking laceration

The image depicts a wound with linear splitting of the tissue, sharp margins, and crushed hair follicles, which is suggestive of an incised-looking lacerated wound.

Incised-looking lacerated wounds are seen at sites where the skin overlies an area of the bone where there is scanty underlying subcutaneous tissue. A blunt force causes linear splitting of the tissue which results in the laceration resembling an incised wound. There will be extensive tissue crushing but the margins will be clear and delineable.

Common areas are Scalp, Forehead, Eyebrows, Zygoma, Lower jaw, Perineum, Shin, and Iliac crest.

Laceration (Option-A)

A laceration is a tear or a split in the skin, mucous membrane, muscle, or any internal organ produced by blunt force. The full thickness of the skin is penetrated.

Features of laceration:

• Margins are irregular with pieces of tissue attached in between called tissue tags or bridges. Tears that are seen at the ends, diverging away from the main laceration are called swallow tails.
• Bruising is seen around the margins.
• Deeper tissues are unevenly divided with tissue tags.
• Hair bulbs are crushed.
• Depth of the wound contains abundant foreign material such as dust particles, paint material of the vehicle involved, etc
• In skin lacerations, usually one of the margins overhangs the other. This helps in assessing the direction of the force.
• A laceration, on healing, produces a permanent scar.

Classification of a laceration:

• Split laceration (incised - like laceration)

• This occurs when the skin is crushed between two hard objects
• For example, during a fall, the scalp gets crushed between the skull from inside and hard ground outside. This results in a wound, which usually mimics an incised one unless examined closely.

• Stretch laceration

• As the name implies, it occurs due to the over-stretching of the skin, beyond its elasticity.
• This typically occurs in the setting of a fracture, where the fracture fragment may stretch and pierce the skin to project out

• Avulsed laceration

• An avulsion is a lesion where the skin separates or peels off by tearing from the underlying tissues. It may overhang the wound.
• This is common in road traffic accidents.

• Tears - Tearing of skin and subcutaneous tissue can occur from localized impact
• Cuts - Injury leads to a deep and wide injury leading to a cut

Incised wound (Option-B)

An incised wound is a clean-cut wound made with a sharp-edged instrument, through the skin and subcutaneous tissues, including blood vessels. It is more in length than depth. The edges are well-defined and usually everted, free from contusions and abrasions. It is generally spindle-shaped. The depth is more at the commencement and progressively becomes shallower, known as tailing. Tailing determines the direction of the force applied when creating the wound.

The image below shows two spindle-shaped incisions.

Laceration-looking incised wounds (Option C)

In areas of the body where a loose layer of muscle fibres is attached to the skin, the edges of the incision may become inverted, adherent, and wrinkled leading to it simulating a lacerated wound. Such wounds are called lacerated-looking incised wounds. These are commonly seen in Scrotum and Axilla.
questions.learning: Incised looking laceration — The image depicts a wound with linear splitting of the tissue, sharp margins, and crushed hair follicles, which is suggestive of an incised-looking lacerated wound.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient with visual disturbances has a past history of cataract surgery. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) findings are shown. Which syndrome is most likely associated with these findings?
questions.explanation: Irvine-Gass Syndrome is a specific form of cystoid macular edema (CME) that occurs as a complication following cataract surgery. The Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) finding characteristically shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and a loss of the normal foveal depression due to fluid accumulation. Posner-Schlossman Syndrome (Option A) involves recurrent episodes of high intraocular pressure and mild uveitis but is not associated with this pattern of macular edema. Central Serous Retinopathy (Option C) presents with neurosensory retinal detachment, often showing an "ink-blot" pattern on angiography, rather than the intraretinal cysts seen in CME. Elschnig Pearls (Option D) are clusters of epithelial cells on the posterior lens capsule that cause opacification, not retinal edema. Treatment for Irvine-Gass Syndrome often involves topical NSAIDs or steroids to reduce inflammation and promote fluid absorption. Most cases resolve within several months, but some require more aggressive intravitreal therapy
questions.learning: Irvine-Gass Syndrome is a specific form of cystoid macular edema (CME) that occurs as a complication following cataract surgery. The Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) finding characteristically shows intraretinal cystoid spaces and a loss of the normal…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: For ectopic pregnancy, how often should hCG levels be repeated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 48 hours

In ectopic pregnancy, hCG levels should be repeated every 48 hours, as the normal doubling time of hCG in a viable intrauterine pregnancy is 48 hours.

Serum β hCG can be used to differentiate tubal ectopic pregnancy from missed abortion and early intrauterine pregnancy. If the level is ≥2000 IU/L, ectopic pregnancy is suspected. If the level is <1500 IU/L, a repeat serum β hCG is taken after 48 hours. If the levels are:

* Doubled - early intrauterine pregnancy

* Decreased - abortion

* Increased but less than doubled value - ectopic pregnancy

Investigations for ectopic pregnancy:

* Serum β hCG - lower levels compared to normal pregnancy, prolonged doubling time

* Transvaginal ultrasound - empty uterine cavity, fluid in pouch of Douglas, adnexal mass

* Colour Doppler - ring of fire pattern

* Diagnostic laparoscopy may be done when the diagnosis is still uncertain after serial β-hCG monitoring and repeat ultrasonography.

* Dilatation and curettage - decidua identified without villi

* Serum progesterone

* Culdocentesis

Pearl PF2195: Beta hCG in pregnancy

The pattern of beta hCG :

First detectable in plasma 7 to 9 days post-LH surge

⇓

Doubles every 2 days

⇓

Peaks at 8 to 10 weeks of gestation(~100 IU/mL)

⇓

Begins to decline at 10 to 12 weeks

⇓

Plateau at 16 weeks till term

* Higher maternal plasma hCG levels- Multifetal pregnancy, erythroblastosis fetalis, gestational trophoblastic disease, Down syndrome.

* Lower hCG plasma levels -early pregnancy wastage and ectopic pregnancy.
questions.learning: 48 hours In ectopic pregnancy, hCG levels should be repeated every 48 hours, as the normal doubling time of hCG in a viable intrauterine pregnancy is 48 hours.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An elderly lady presents with abdominal pain and distension. She has a history of scoliosis. Given below is the erect X-ray abdomen radiograph of the lady. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus
Large bowel obstruction due to fecolith
Small bowel obstruction due to bowel perforation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus

The given clinical scenario with an old woman and the radiograph showing characteristic coffee bean appearance are highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus causing a large bowel obstruction.

Sigmoid volvulus is a cause of large bowel obstruction and occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon. Symptoms include constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea, and/or vomiting. The onset may be acute or chronic. It occurs more commonly in patients with a history of mental illness and chronic constipation.

X-ray abdomen shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign, Frimann-Dahl sign (three dense lines converge towards the site of obstruction), and the absence of rectal gas. CT may reveal a large gas-filled loop without haustral markings, forming a closed-loop obstruction.

Here are some pointers that help in differentiating the two volulus:

Sigmoid volvulus
Cecal volvulus

More common incidence
Less common incidence

Coffee bean sign is typical.
Coffee bean sign is occassionally seen

Seen in old age, psychiatric patients
Usually seen in those aged 30-60 years old

The top of the sigmoid volvulus usually lies very high in the abdomen with its apex on the left side.

• In half the patients, the caecum twists and inverts so that the pole of the caecum and the appendix occupy the left upper quadrant.
•

In other patients, the twist occurs in an axial plane without inversion and the caecum still occupies the right half of the abdomen.

Haustra aren't usually seen
Haustra usually seen

Multiple air-fluid level seen
One air-fluid level seen

Attached air-filled appendix can be seen

Other options:

Option B: In large bowel obstruction due to fecolith, the presence of haustrations is a feature. Haustral folds are irregular and do not cross the entire diameter of the bowel. These are absent in the cecum. The given image shows haustrations in large bowel obstruction.

The following image shows an x-ray radiograph of large bowel obstruction:

Option C: Cecal volvulus shows characteristic radiological findings like cecal dilatation, single air-fluid level that may extend into the left upper quadrant, and absence of gas in the distal colon. The colonic haustrations are well maintained.

The following image shows an x-ray radiograph of cecal volvulus:

Option D: In small bowel obstructions, the obstructed bowel loops are central in location and lie transversely. The jejunal obstruction shows valvulae conniventes (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel) giving it a ladder effect. The distended cecum may show the presence of gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

Common causes of small bowel obstruction are adhesions (~60%), neoplasms (~20%), hernias (~10%), Crohn's disease (~5%) and other miscellaneous conditions (~5%).

The following image shows an x-ray radiograph of small bowel obstruction:

Cases of bowel perforation have an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus.

The below radiograph image shows a hollow viscus perforation:
questions.learning: Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus — The given clinical scenario with an old woman and the radiograph showing characteristic coffee bean appearance are highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus causing a large bowel obstruction.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Pick from the following the usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy:
options: Rough handling of thyroid during surgery
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inadequate patient preparation

The usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy is inadequate patient preparation before surgery. Patient preparation pre-operatively involves ensuring a euthyroid state.

Rough handling of the thyroid in thyroidectomy does not cause a thyroid storm. Though a significant amount of thyroglobulin is stored in the acinar cells, they are inactive unless converted to thyroxine (T3 and T4).
questions.learning: Inadequate patient preparation — The usual cause of thyroid storm in thyroidectomy is inadequate patient preparation before surgery. Patient preparation pre-operatively involves ensuring a euthyroid state.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: True statement about teduglutide is :
options: It is recommended for patients with colorectal cancer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. It is a GLP- 2 analogue

Teduglutide is a GLP-2 analogue.

It has been recently approved for the treatment of short bowel syndrome. Teduglutide binds to enteric neurons and endocrine cells, stimulating the release of a number of hormones such as insulin-like growth factor, this stimulates mucosal epithelial growth and enhances fluid absorption.

The drug has a t1/2 of 1–2 hours and is administered subcutaneously once daily. It can potentially cause bowel cancer, therefore it is not recommended for patients with active malignancies.

Note: GLP-1 analogs are used for the treatment of Type II diabetes mellitus.
questions.learning: It is a GLP- 2 analogue Teduglutide is a GLP-2 analogue. It has been recently approved for the treatment of short bowel syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient comes to the outpatient clinic with dilated tortuous veins in his lower limb. Varicose veins is suspected. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Duplex scan

Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice for varicose veins.

Varicose veins refer to subcutaneous dilated veins of more than 3 mm in diameter.

Investigations :

* Clinical examination

* Venous duplex ultrasound which tells about:

* The site of reflux

* Size of vein

* Location of perforators

* Presence of obstruction in the deep venous system

* Indication of pelvic source of reflux or obstruction

* MR venography

* Invasive procedures such as contrast venography or intravenous ultrasound.

Management of varicose veins

Incompetence
Management

Great saphenous vein (GSV) and saphenofemoral (SFJ)

• Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

• Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

Short saphenous vein (SSJ) and saphenopopliteal (SPJ)

• Flush ligation of SPJ (Stripping is not done to prevent sural nerve injury)
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

Perforator

• Dodd and Crockett surgery - Multiple subfascial ligations
• Subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS) - smaller incision, so cosmetically better
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

New treatment modalities:

* Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4.

* Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive

* TriVex - Transilluminated powered phlebectomy

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient scheduled for elective hip surgery in 5 days is taking aspirin, a multivitamin, enalapril, and metoprolol. What is the appropriate perioperative management for this patient?
options: Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output
Increase aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Stop enalapril

In the given clinical scenario, where a patient is scheduled for elective hip surgery in 5 days and is taking aspirin, a multivitamin, enalapril, and metoprolol, the recommended perioperative management includes discontinuing enalapril, as it is an ACE inhibitor.

ACE inhibitors are discontinued 24 hours before surgery due to the risk of hemodynamic instability. ACE inhibitors block the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), leading to vasodilation and reduced blood pressure. During anaesthesia, there is already vasodilation and decreased sympathetic tone → combining this with ACE inhibitors can cause severe hypotension that is resistant to fluids.
Aspirin can be maintained unless the patient is scheduled for neurosurgery or retinal surgery, provided the dosage remains unchanged. Metoprolol, being a beta-blocker, should always be continued.

Pearl PF1221: Drugs that should be discontinued prior to surgery

Drugs that should be discontinued prior to surgery

* Topical medications - discontinue on the day of surgery

* Diuretics except thiazides - discontinue on the day of surgery

* Oral hypoglycemic agents - discontinue on the day of surgery

* Sildenafil - Discontinue 24 hours before the day of surgery

* NSAIDs - Discontinue 48 hours before the day of surgery

* Warfarin - Discontinue 4 days before surgery, except for patients having cataract surgery without a bulbar block.

* Short-acting Insulins except when given by a continuous pump

* Thienopyridines (e.g., clopidogrel, ticlopidine) except in cataract surgery, patients with metallic/drug-eluting stents

* Aspirin should be discontinued 3 days before the surgery, in selected cases where reversal of platelet inhibition is necessary

* MAO Inhibitors - 2 weeks prior (MAO Inhibitors are usually continued.They should be discontinued if the patient and anesthesiologist factors are not favourable to continue them)

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 12-year-old boy presented to a health centre in Telangana along with his parents, with complaints of recurrent diarrhoea and skin changes on areas of the body exposed to sunlight. There is a history of progressive disorientation and increasing irritability. The child and his family ate sorghum cereal, there was very little consumption of milk and no consumption of foods of animal origin like meat, though the family is not strictly vegetarian by food habit. Consider the following plans of action: 1. Absolute avoidance of milk in the child’s diet 2. Encouraging shift of cereal consumption from sorghum to maize 3. Encouraging consumption of meat in the child’s diet, if the family can afford 4. Supplementation with nicotinic acid or nicotinamide Which of the plans of action given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3 and 4 only

The child has the classic 3 Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis — photosensitive skin lesions
• Dementia — irritability, disorientation and neuropsychiatric changes

Why sorghum (jowar) causes pellagra:

Sorghum-based diets (common in parts of the Deccan plateau, including Telangana) are strongly associated with pellagra due to the "leucine excess theory" — sorghum is unusually rich in the amino acid leucine, which interferes with the enzymes involved in the tryptophan → niacin conversion pathway, precipitating niacin deficiency even when dietary intake isn't grossly inadequate. Lack of milk and animal-source foods (both good tryptophan/niacin sources) compounds the deficiency.

Evaluating the options:

1. Absolute avoidance of milk — Incorrect. Milk is actually a good source of tryptophan and should be encouraged, not avoided. Avoiding it would worsen the deficiency.
2. Shift from sorghum to maize — Incorrect. This is a classic distractor. Maize is equally, if not more strongly, associated with pellagra — its niacin is present in a biologically unavailable bound form (niacytin), and it too is deficient in tryptophan. Shifting from sorghum to maize does not solve the problem and may worsen it.
3. Encouraging meat consumption — Correct. Meat is rich in both tryptophan and preformed niacin, directly addressing the deficiency.
4. Supplementation with nicotinic acid/nicotinamide — Correct. This is the definitive treatment for established pellagra.

Exam pearl: Both sorghum and maize are classically linked to pellagra (via different mechanisms — leucine excess in sorghum vs. bound/unavailable niacin in maize) — so "switching cereals" is never the fix; the fix is adding tryptophan/niacin-rich foods (milk, eggs, meat, groundnuts) and direct niacin supplementation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following should not be included in the school health service?
questions.explanation: According to established public health guidelines for school health programs, it is not mandatory or standard practice to have a Doctor on the premises (Option B) at all times in every school. Instead, medical care is typically provided through periodic visits by mobile health teams or through a designated referral system to a nearby Primary Health Centre (PHC). The essential components that should be included are: the education and rehabilitation of handicapped children (Option A) to ensure inclusive learning; regular dental and eye health services (Option C) to detect vision and hearing problems early; and the maintenance of comprehensive School health records (Option D) for every student to track their growth and immunization status. Other key components include nutrition (Mid-Day Meal), environmental sanitation, and health education. While a nurse or first-aid provider may be present, the structural leadership of the school health service is community-based and integrated with the broader primary health care system rather than requiring an on-site full-time physician
questions.learning: According to established public health guidelines for school health programs, it is not mandatory or standard practice to have a Doctor on the premises (Option B) at all times in every school.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: An 11-year-old girl was found to be quiet and shy in her classroom with intermittent crying, for the past few days. It was discovered that her uncle was touching her genitalia inappropriately. The duty of the principal is to report this to?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Police

The principal has to report this case to the police.

The POCSO Act, 2012 is a comprehensive law for the protection of children from the offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography. This is done while safeguarding the interests of the child at every stage of the judicial process by incorporating child-friendly mechanisms for reporting, recording of evidence, investigation, and speedy trial of the offence through designated special courts.

Section 21(1) of the POCSO Act, 2012 requires mandatory reporting of cases of child sexual abuse to the law enforcement authorities and applies to everyone including parents, doctors, and school personnel. Failure to report a suspicion of child abuse is an offence under the Act.
questions.learning: Police — The principal has to report this case to the police. The POCSO Act, 2012 is a comprehensive law for the protection of children from the offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and pornography.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Tube shown below causes resistance which is primarily because of
questions.explanation: The image shows an endotracheal tube (ETT), which is used to maintain airway patency during anesthesia or critical care. According to Poiseuille's Law, the resistance to gas flow through a tube is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (diameter). This means that even a small reduction in the internal diameter (Option D) of the ETT results in a massive increase in work of breathing and airway resistance. While the length of the tube (Option C) also contributes to resistance linearly, its impact is much less significant compared to the diameter. Curvature (Option A) and circumference (Option B) are not the primary physical determinants of resistance in clinical gas flow models. Therefore, choosing the largest appropriate diameter ETT is crucial in clinical practice to minimize flow resistance. This physical principle explains why even a layer of secretions narrowing the internal diameter of the tube can significantly increase a patient's respiratory distress

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A female body was brought in for autopsy. The body was discovered in a closed room with a heat stove running during the dead body recovery, with cherry red discolouration on the skin and mucosal regions. What is the most probable cause of her death?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CO poisoning

In the given case of a female found dead in a closed room with smoke from a heat stove, with cherry red discolouration on the skin and mucosal regions, the most probable cause of her death is carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, which can occur from smoke in an enclosed space.

The colour of postmortem staining in CO poisoning is cherry red. Carbon monoxide is a byproduct of incomplete combustion of organic materials, such as wood. When inhaled, CO binds to haemoglobin in the blood with an affinity approximately 240 times greater than that of oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb). This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, leading to tissue hypoxia.

The cherry red discolouration is a hallmark of CO poisoning. This occurs because COHb imparts a bright red colour, distinct from the darker hue associated with deoxygenated haemoglobin.

Postmortem hypostasis/postmortem staining/postmortem lividity/livor mortis/suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discolouration of the superficial layers of the skin due to the collection of blood in toneless capillaries.

It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to engorged vessels showing through the skin seen on the dependent parts due to the pooling of blood under the effect of gravity.

This staining starts as mottled patches 1-3 hours following death and develops to a uniform area of staining in 3-6 hours. Full development and fixation of hypostasis occur within 6–12 hours. This finding usually develops within 4 hours and persists until putrefaction. Fixation of hypostasis occurs earlier in the summer. It is delayed in asphyxial deaths and in intracranial lesions.

Pearl PF1096: Color of Postmortem Hypostasis in Various Conditions

Poisoning/Condition
Postmortem staining

Carbon monoxide

Cherry red

Cyanides

Brick red/dark pink

Potassium chlorate

Chocolate brown

Phosphorous
Dark brown

Nitrites

Red brown

Hydrogen sulphide

Bluish green

Opium
Grayish/black

Asphyxia
Dark purple

Hypothermia
Bright pink

Septic abortion (Cl. Welchii infection)
Brown/pale bronze

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is an indication of high tracheostomy?
options: Suspicion of Laryngeal carcinoma planned for surgery later
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Suspicion of Laryngeal carcinoma planned for surgery later

Laryngeal carcinoma is an indication of high tracheostomy. It is done at the level of the 1st tracheal ring and an opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland.

The disadvantage of a high tracheostomy is subglottic stenosis at the level of the cricoid and perichondritis of the cricoid. However, in laryngeal carcinoma this would be a temporary measure as the definitive management is total laryngectomy.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

1. Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.
2. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance
3. Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood
4. Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.
5. Allows positive pressure respiration
6. Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

1. Respiratory obstruction due to

1. Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis)
2. Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures
3. Neoplasms
4. Foreign bodies or edema
5. Bilateral abductor paralysis
6. Congenital anomalies

2. Retained secretions

1. Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles
2. Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions
3. Painful cough

3. Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis
questions.learning: Suspicion of Laryngeal carcinoma planned for surgery later Laryngeal carcinoma is an indication of high tracheostomy. It is done at the level of the 1st tracheal ring and an opening is made above the isthmus of the thyroid gland.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presented with recurrent episodes of fever with chills. MRCP image is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Primary sclerosing cholangitis

The presence of fever and chills, along with the MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic beading is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Option B: Caroli's disease is a rare congenital condition characterized by irregular dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal extrahepatic duct system. It is common in both sexes and mostly presents before the age of 30 years with abdominal pain, cholangitis, or end-stage liver disease. MRCP shows irregular, cystic dilation of the large proximal intrahepatic bile ducts with a normal common bile duct.

Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is an autoimmune condition characterized by inflammatory strictures involving the intra and extra-hepatic biliary tree. It is a progressive condition that leads to secondary biliary cirrhosis.

MRCP or ERCP will show demonstrate multifocal, diffuse dilatation and strictures of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic biliary trees, this pattern is a beading or chain of lakes appearance. Pseudodiverticula of extrahepatic bile ducts are pathognomic of PSC. MRCP is useful in diagnosis and surveillance, while ERCP is reserved for the treatment of dominant strictures and to exclude malignancy.

The below image shows a cholangiogram of primary sclerosing cholangitis:

The common age group of primary sclerosing cholangitis is 30-45 years. Men are affected twice as commonly as women. Two-thirds of these cases are associated with ulcerative colitis. It is also associated with Riedel’s thyroiditis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. 10–20% of patients develop cholangiocarcinoma.

Clinical features of a patient with PSC include pruritis, fever, chills, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice, and weight loss.

Liver function tests show a cholestatic pattern with an elevation of ALP and GGT and smaller rises in the aminotransferases. Bilirubin values may be variable.

Liver biopsy excludes other causes of cholestatic liver disease and defines the stage of PSC. It shows onion skin concentric periductal fibrosis. With disease progression, periportal fibrosis occurs, progressing to bridging necrosis, and eventually biliary cirrhosis.

Currently, there is no known effective medical therapy. Surgical management involving resection of extrahepatic biliary tree and hepaticojejunostomy has shown reasonable effects. For patients with advanced liver disease, liver transplantation is the only available option.

Other options:

Option C: Oriental cholangitis, also known as recurrent pyogenic cholangitis is characterized by recurrent attacks of cholangitis due to bile stasis and stone formation. Patients between 30-40 years and both sexes are equally affected. It is caused due to infections (liver flukes, E.coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Proteus). Patients present with Charcot's triad (intermittent fever, pain, and jaundice). MRCP shows intra or extrahepatic calculi, dilatation of ducts, and strictures.

Option D: Biliary carcinoma  (cholangiocarcinoma) most commonly affects patients >60 years and presents with fever, abdominal pain, weight loss, and features of obstructive jaundice. MRCP shows irregular narrowing of the bile duct involved by the tumor, with asymmetric upstream dilatation of the intrahepatic ducts.
questions.learning: Primary sclerosing cholangitis — The presence of fever and chills, along with the MRCP showing multiple areas of intrahepatic beading is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis.

questions.text: Which of these is not included in the TNM stage T4b of breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Skin erythema involving > 1/3rd surface

T4b breast cancer includes:

• Peau d’orange (skin edema)
• Ulceration of skin
• Ipsilateral satellite skin nodules

These are features of direct skin involvement by breast carcinoma.

“Skin erythema involving >1/3 of breast surface” is a criterion for: Inflammatory breast cancer which is classified as T4d, not T4b.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with periorbital ecchymosis (“raccoon eyes”), a classic clinical sign suggestive of a basilar skull fracture. This finding points toward injury involving a specific region of the cranial fossa. Which part of the cranial fossa is most likely affected in such a case?
questions.explanation: "Raccoon eyes" (bilateral periorbital ecchymosis) is a clinical sign of a basal skull fracture, specifically involving the anterior cranial fossa. The fracture of the orbital roof or the cribriform plate allows blood to track from the site of injury and accumulate in the loose areolar tissue around the orbits. Fractures of the middle cranial fossa (Option B) are classically associated with Battle's sign (ecchymosis over the mastoid process) and CSF otorrhea. Posterior cranial fossa (Option C) fractures are rarer and present with different signs. The "bone aponeurotic layer" (Option D) is a component of the scalp, not a cranial fossa. The appearance of raccoon eyes may be delayed for 1–3 days following the injury. It is a critical physical exam finding that alerts the clinician to the high risk of serious underlying intracranial injury and potential complications like CSF rhinorrhea and meningitis

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with a known history of peptic ulcer disease presents with arthritis and subsequently develops carditis. Which anti-inflammatory drug would be the most appropriate choice in this situation?
questions.explanation: In patients requiring anti-inflammatory therapy who have a history of Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD), standard non-selective NSAIDs pose a high risk of causing gastrointestinal bleeding. Celecoxib is a COX-2 selective inhibitor. It effectively reduces inflammation while sparing the COX-1 enzyme, which is responsible for producing the prostaglandins that protect the gastric mucosa. This makes it the preferred anti-inflammatory choice for patients with high GI risk. Ibuprofen (Option A) and Diclofenac (Option B) are non-selective inhibitors that block both COX-1 and COX-2, significantly increasing the likelihood of gastric injury and ulcer recurrence in susceptible individuals. Naloxone (Option C) is an opioid antagonist used for reversing drug overdoses and has no anti-inflammatory properties. Therefore, celecoxib provides the safest profile for managing this patient's symptoms without exacerbating their pre-existing gastric issues
questions.learning: In patients requiring anti-inflammatory therapy who have a history of Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD), standard non-selective NSAIDs pose a high risk of causing gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text:
Choose the true statements:

i. The most commonly fractured carpal bone is the lunate

ii. The scaphoid is most commonly fractured at the waist

iii. The cast for scaphoid fracture is set in a glass-holding position

iv. Kienböck's disease is due to osteonecrosis of the lunate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ii, iii and iv only

Statements ii, iii, and iv are true, and statement i is incorrect.

Statement i: The most commonly fractured carpal bone is the lunate is a false statement. The most common fractured bone is the scaphoid.

Statement ii: The scaphoid is most commonly fractured at the waist is a true statement. A scaphoid fracture is more common in young adults. Commonly, the fracture occurs through the waist of the scaphoid.

Statement iii: The cast for scaphoid fracture is set in a glass holding position is a true statement. The affected hand is immobilized in a scaphoid cast for 3-4 months. The scaphoid cast extends from below the elbow to the metacarpal heads including the thumb up to the inter-phalangeal joint. The wrist is maintained in a little dorsiflexion and radial deviation (glass holding position).

Statement iv: Kienböck's disease is due to osteonecrosis of the lunate is a true statement. Kienböck's disease is usually seen in young adults, who present with pain and stiffness in the wrist. A history of trauma may be present. On examination, localized tenderness can be appreciated over the lunate, and a reduction in grip strength can be noted. Limited and painful wrist movements are noted in the later stages of the disease.
questions.learning: ii, iii and iv only Statements ii, iii, and iv are true, and statement i is incorrect. Statement i: The most commonly fractured carpal bone is the lunate is a false statement.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the early sign of pregnancy on TVS?
questions.explanation: The gestational sac (G sac) is the first sonographic evidence of pregnancy visible on Transvaginal Sonography (TVS). It typically appears between 4 and 5 weeks of gestation. Identifying the G sac is the earliest method to confirm the location of the pregnancy and establish gestational age. The yolk sac (Option B) appears slightly later, at approximately 5.5 weeks. Fetal pole and cardiac activity (Options C and D) are usually detectable between 5.5 and 6 weeks of gestation. Key indicators of a healthy intrauterine pregnancy include the "intradecidual sign" (an anechoic center with an echogenic rim) and the "double decidual sign" (two concentric rings around the sac). TVS is significantly more sensitive than transabdominal sonography for these early findings, allowing for the timely detection of ectopic pregnancies or early failure
questions.learning: The gestational sac (G sac) is the first sonographic evidence of pregnancy visible on Transvaginal Sonography (TVS). It typically appears between 4 and 5 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The antiviral drug having dual antiviral activity against HIV and HBV is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emtricitabine

Antiviral drug having dual antiviral activity against HIV and HBV is emtricitabine.

It is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor similar to lamivudine. It has activity against HIV-1, HIV-2, and HBV.
questions.learning: Emtricitabine Antiviral drug having dual antiviral activity against HIV and HBV is emtricitabine. It is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor similar to lamivudine.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a history of diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers in the intestine. Microscopic findings reveal quadrinucleated cysts. Which of the following can be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Metronidazole + Paromomycin

This patient's clinical features of diarrhea and flask-shaped ulcers with quadrinucleate cysts are suggestive of amoebiasis caused by Entamoeba histolytica. The most appropriate treatment for this patient is metronidazole (or tinidazole) + a luminal amoebicide like paromomycin, diloxanide furoate, or iodoquinone.

As metronidazole is so well absorbed in the gut, the levels may not be therapeutic in the colonic lumen. The drug is also less effective against cysts. Therefore, patients with amoebic colitis or amoebic liver abscess should receive a luminal agent in addition.

Clinically, infection with entamoeba histolytica may present as,

* Amoebic colitis- Patients with amoebic colitis typically present with colicky abdominal pains and diarrhoea. There is associated tenesmus and heme-positive stool. In amoebiasis, the organisms attach to the colonic epithelium, invade the crypts and burrow laterally to create a flask-shaped ulcer. Tissue damage results in inflammation.

* Amoebic liver abscess- Patients usually present with fever, abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and enlargement and tenderness of the liver. A characteristic "anchovy sauce-like" pus may be seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: GI Hepatobiliary System · Integrated Gi Hpb
questions.text: The serologic marker detectable during the ‘window’ period of hepatitis B infection is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Anti-HBc IgM

The window period of hepatitis B infection is the interval when HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. During this period, the only reliable serological marker is anti-HBc IgM.

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-HBsAb: Appears after the window period, indicating recovery or vaccination.
• B. Anti-HBc IgG: Appears later and persists lifelong; not the marker of the window period.
• D. HBeAg: Marker of active viral replication and high infectivity, not specific for the window period.
questions.learning: Anti-HBc IgM — The window period of hepatitis B infection is the interval when HBsAg has disappeared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared. During this period, the only reliable serological marker is anti-HBc IgM.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a suicide inhibitor? 1. Nor-ethindrone 2. Ritonavir 3. Spironolactone 4. Benzbromarone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3

Enzyme + drug (looks like substrate)

↓

Drug gets activated inside enzyme

↓

Forms covalent bond

↓

Enzyme permanently inactivated

A suicide inhibitor irreversibly inactivates its target enzyme during metabolism. Norethindrone and spironolactone form reactive intermediates that permanently inhibit steroid-metabolizing CYP enzymes. Ritonavir is a potent but reversible CYP inhibitor, and benzbromarone acts mainly as a uricosuric drug. Hence only 1 and 3 are classic mechanism-based inhibitors.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old primigravida at 41+3 weeks gestation is brought to the emergency department after prolonged labor (18 hours) at home. She is dehydrated, with pulse 126/min, BP 90/58 mmHg, and temperature 100°F. On examination, the uterus is tense and contracted, and a transverse ridge is seen and felt across the lower abdomen. Fetal heart rate is 100 bpm with late decelerations. What is the transverse band seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Retraction ring

Retraction Ring (Bandl's Ring) is a visible transverse ridge between the upper and lower uterine segments. It occurs in prolonged obstructed labor when:

• Upper uterine segment contracts strongly
• Lower uterine segment becomes thin and overstretched

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles are ectoderm-derived?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ciliaris

Why Ciliaris?

The ciliaris muscle is derived from neural crest cells. It is an intraocular smooth muscle that controls lens accommodation.

Why the Others Are Wrong

| Option | Embryological Origin | Why Wrong

| ------ | -------------------- | ---------

| A — Cardiac muscle | Mesoderm (splanchnic/lateral plate) | Completely mesodermal

| B — Smooth muscle of gut | Mesoderm (splanchnic lateral plate) | Not ectoderm

| C — Erector pili | Mesoderm | Common trap — it's a skin muscle but still mesodermal

| D — Ciliaris | Neural crest | Correct

The two key ones to remember:

• Ciliaris — accommodation (Neural crest)
• Sphincter and dilator pupillae — neuroectoderm

Erector pili is the classic distractor — students assume "skin = ectoderm," but the smooth muscle itself comes from mesoderm (specifically, mesenchyme).
questions.learning: The ciliaris muscle is derived from neural crest cells. It is an intraocular smooth muscle that controls lens accommodation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a function of secondary messengers?
options: They transmit signals from cell surface receptors to intracellular receptors.
Regulation of cellular processes such as metabolism and gene expression
Integration of multiple signaling pathways within the cell
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Direct activation of DNA replication

Direct activation of DNA replication is not a function of secondary messengers.

Secondary messengers are intracellular molecules that relay and amplify signals from extracellular stimuli, such as hormones, neurotransmitters, or growth factors. They act as intermediaries between cell surface receptors and the internal signalling pathways that execute the cellular response. Secondary messengers are crucial for translating external signals into appropriate cellular actions.

They carry the message from the cell surface receptor to other parts of the cell, initiating a series of actions that lead to a response and help control different cellular activities, including metabolism, growth, and how cells respond to external signals.

Types of Secondary Messengers:

* Cyclic AMP (cAMP): Increases activity in the cell by activating other proteins.

* Cyclic GMP (cGMP): Similar to cAMP, it activates proteins and affects various functions like muscle relaxation.

* Inositol Triphosphate (IP3): Helps release calcium from inside the cell, which can influence many cellular activities.

* Diacylglycerol (DAG): Works with IP3 to activate other proteins that affect cell functions.

* Calcium Ions (Ca²⁺): Act as a messenger to control various processes such as muscle contractions and neurotransmitter release.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After three months, blood pressure readings are compared between two groups of hypertensive patients: one group of 100 patients received medical treatment, while the other group of 100 patients was advised lifestyle modifications. Which statistical test should be used to assess the significance of the difference in blood pressure between these two groups?
questions.explanation: In this scenario, researchers are comparing the mean values of a continuous variable (blood pressure) between two independent groups (medical advice group vs. lifestyle change group). The un-paired t-test (also known as the independent samples t-test) is the correct statistical method for this comparison. ANOVA (Option A) is used when comparing the means of three or more groups. The Chi-square test (Option C) is used for categorical data, such as comparing proportions of patients who reached a goal rather than the actual blood pressure values. McNemar's test (Option D) is used for paired categorical data, such as comparing results in the same group before and after an intervention. Because the study involves two distinct groups of 100 patients each and evaluates a quantitative variable, the un-paired t-test is the gold standard for determining if the observed difference between the interventions is statistically significant
questions.learning: In this scenario, researchers are comparing the mean values of a continuous variable (blood pressure) between two independent groups (medical advice group vs. lifestyle change group).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which post-translational modification is common to collagen, hemoglobin, and immunoglobulins?
questions.explanation: Hydroxylation is a post-translational modification involving the addition of –OH groups to specific amino acids, and it is considered common across collagen, hemoglobin, and immunoglobulins. 1. In collagen, hydroxylation of proline and lysine is essential for triple-helix stability and tensile strength. 2. In hemoglobin, hydroxylation of certain residues (e.g., histidine) is described in exam contexts as influencing oxygen binding properties. 3. In immunoglobulins, hydroxylation contributes indirectly to proper folding, glycosylation, and structural stability. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Subunit aggregation: Seen in hemoglobin and immunoglobulins, but collagen primarily depends on hydroxylation for stability, not just aggregation. (B) Splicing: A post-transcriptional RNA process, not post-translational. (C) Poly A tail addition: Also a post-transcriptional modification of mRNA. Hence, the best common post-translational modification is hydroxylation
questions.learning: Hydroxylation is a post-translational modification involving the addition of –OH groups to specific amino acids, and it is considered common across collagen, hemoglobin, and immunoglobulins.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a middle-aged man who presents to the psychiatry OPD with a 7-month history of auditory hallucinations, believing that aliens are commanding him to harm his family?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with core psychotic symptoms: auditory hallucinations ("hearing voices from aliens") and command-type instructions with potential delusional content. According to ICD-10 and DSM-5 criteria, a diagnosis of Schizophrenia (Option C) requires the presence of these symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, or disorganized speech) for a significant duration, typically at least one to six months. This patient’s symptoms have persisted for seven months, fulfilling the chronic duration criteria. Mania (Option A) is characterized by elevated mood, racing thoughts, and decreased need for sleep, which are not described here. Delusional disorder (Option B) involves non-bizarre delusions without prominent hallucinations like hearing alien voices. Brief psychotic disorder (Option D) is limited to symptoms lasting less than one month. Given the specific nature of the bizarre hallucinations and the seven-month duration, Schizophrenia is the most accurate psychiatric diagnosis. Management involves antipsychotic medication and psychosocial support
questions.learning: The patient is presenting with core psychotic symptoms: auditory hallucinations ("hearing voices from aliens") and command-type instructions with potential delusional content.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The active site of enzyme is complimentary to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Substrate

The active site of an enzyme is a specific region where the substrate binds to form the enzyme–substrate complex. The shape and chemical properties of the active site are complementary to the substrate, allowing specific recognition and binding, which enables the enzyme to catalyze the reaction efficiently.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Transition state: The enzyme stabilizes the transition state during catalysis, but the active site is primarily designed to bind the substrate initially.
• Allosteric activator: These molecules bind to allosteric sites, not the active site.
• Product: Products are formed after the reaction and typically have lower affinity for the active site, allowing their release.
questions.learning: Substrate — The active site of an enzyme is a specific region where the substrate binds to form the enzyme–substrate complex. The shape and chemical properties of the active site are complementary to the substrate, allowing specific recognition and…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient from a Mediterranean country visits Africa, where he develops malaria. He is treated with primaquine and later develops hemolytic anemia. Deficiency of an enzyme involved in which of the following pathways could be the cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway

The deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme, which is involved in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway, could be the cause behind this presentation.

G6PD is an enzyme that plays a critical role in redox reactions that occur in all aerobic cells. It is the only source of NADPH in erythrocytes, which helps in the formation of reduced glutathione. This reduced form protects erythrocytes against oxidative stress.

G6PD deficiency is an X-linked inheritance disorder. Most patients with this condition are asymptomatic. But when exposed to oxidative agents, they are prone to develop acute hemolytic anemia. The various oxidative triggers include:

• Fava beans
• Infections
• Drugs such as primaquine, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin

A hemolytic attack can present with weakness and abdominal/ lumbar pain. Later, the patient can develop jaundice, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria. Investigations will show elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and low levels of plasma haptoglobin. Anisocytosis and spherocytes can be seen on peripheral smear. Acute renal failure is a complication seen in adults.

Other options:

Option A - Glycolysis, the main pathway of glucose, can occur either aerobically or anaerobically. A deficiency of the enzyme pyruvate kinase can present as hemolytic anemia. Fatigue can be the presentation when there is phosphofructokinase. Both these are enzymes of glycolysis.

Option B - Gluconeogenesis is the process by which non-carbohydrate precursors are used to synthesize glucose. Pyruvate carboxylase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, and glucose-6-phosphatase are the enzymes in the pathway. Glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency leads to von Gierke disease, which is a glycogen storage disorder. Defective gluconeogenesis results in hypoglycemia.

Option D - Luebering–Rapoport pathway is a shunt mechanism that generates and dephosphorylates 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG). 2,3-BPG mutase is the enzyme involved. A deficiency of this enzyme can cause erythrocytosis.
questions.learning: Hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway — The deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) enzyme, which is involved in the hexose monophosphate (HMP) pathway, could be the cause behind this presentation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of acquired systemic amyloidosis? 1. Tuberculosis 2. Multiple myeloma 3. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis 4. Chronic osteomyelitis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3 and 4

Systemic amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in various organs, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. The two major forms of acquired systemic amyloidosis are AL (light-chain) amyloidosis, associated with plasma cell disorders, and AA (secondary) amyloidosis, associated with chronic inflammatory or infectious diseases.

Why is D correct?

• 1. Tuberculosis: Chronic inflammation leads to increased Serum Amyloid A (SAA) protein, resulting in AA amyloidosis.
• 2. Multiple myeloma: Causes AL amyloidosis due to deposition of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains.
• 3. Untreated rheumatoid arthritis: A classic cause of secondary (AA) amyloidosis due to persistent inflammation.
• 4. Chronic osteomyelitis: Long-standing infection increases SAA production, leading to AA amyloid deposition.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3 and 4 Systemic amyloidosis is characterized by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils in various organs, leading to progressive organ dysfunction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman who has had 2 children through normal delivery presents with a dull aching pain over the abdomen, with irregular menses. Per vaginal examination revealed a mass felt through the posterior fornix. A USG showed a clear ovarian cyst of size 5 x 5 cm. What is the next best step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Follow up after 6 weeks

A clear ovarian cyst with size less than 7 cm in a woman of reproductive age group is most likely to be a functional ovarian cyst. The next best step in the management of this case is to follow up after 6–12 weeks and perform a repeat USG.

A simple unilocular cyst under 7 cm is often a functional cyst and should be observed. Most functional cysts resolve spontaneously within 4-6 months. A follow-up ultrasound will detect any persistent cyst, which may necessitate laparoscopic evaluation. To expedite resolution or to treat symptoms like pain and irregular menses, oral combined pills may be prescribed for 3-4 months in women of reproductive age.

Features of a functional cyst:

• Related to temporary hormonal variation
• Benign and rarely become complicated
• Usually 6–8 cm in diameter
• Usually asymptomatic
• Unilocular
• Contains clear fluid, unless hemorrhage occurs
• Lining epithelium corresponds to the functional epithelium of the unit from which they arise

Management of functional cysts in women of child-bearing age group is summarized in the flowchart attached below.

Other options:

Option A: Tumour markers such as CA-125 and CEA are particulary useful in postmenopausal women suspected of having a malignant epithelial cell tumor.

Option C: If the cyst does not resolve spontaneoulsy it can be removed laparoscopically or by laparotomy.

Option D: Imaging modalities such as CT scan and MRI help to detect ovarian neoplasms and assist in staging of ovarian cancers.
questions.learning: Follow up after 6 weeks — A clear ovarian cyst with size less than 7 cm in a woman of reproductive age group is most likely to be a functional ovarian cyst.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text:
Which of the following are seen in patients with chronic arsenic poisoning?

1. Raindrop pigmentation
2. Peripheral neuritis
3. Mees line
4. Luminous vomit
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1,2,3 are correct

Among the given options, raindrop pigmentation, peripheral neuritis, and mees line are seen in patients with chronic arsenic poisoning. Luminous vomit is a feature of yellow phosphorous poisoning.

Arsenic is an odorless, tasteless, metallic poison. Gastrointestinal features of acute arsenic poisoning include nausea and vomiting, colicky abdominal pain, and profuse diarrhea with rice water stools.

In chronic arsenic poisoning, skin symptoms include erythematous lesions, flushing, and can also lead to hyperkeratotic skin and desquamation. Pigmentation is patchy and resembles raindrops on a dusty road. In the distal parts of the body, hyperkeratosis is present.  Mees lines are transverse white striae of the fingernails, called striate leukonychia. Renal manifestations include chronic nephritis and urine contains albumin, casts, etc.

Arsenic can be detected in the bones for prolonged periods. Hence it can be found even in skeletonized remains of the body. Dimercaprol is the treatment of choice for acute arsenic poisoning.
questions.learning: 1,2,3 are correct Among the given options, raindrop pigmentation, peripheral neuritis, and mees line are seen in patients with chronic arsenic poisoning.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication for the insertion of the device shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trophoblastic disease

The given image shows a copper-containing IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device). Trophoblastic disease is an absolute contraindication for the insertion of this device.

In cases of uterine invasion like trophoblastic disease, there is an increased likelihood of complications related to IUCD such as perforation, misplaced device, and bleeding.

IUCDs are a type of long-term, reversible contraception. They are T-shaped devices that are inserted into the uterine cavity. These can either be copper-containing like CuT-380A and CuT-200, or hormone-containing IUCDs like Mirena.

The contraceptive action of IUCDs is because of foreign body reaction which leads to various changes in endometrial tissue that interfere with implantation. These changes include prostaglandin release that provokes uterine contractility and tubal peristalsis and leucocytic infiltration in the endometrium. It also interferes with the migration of spermatozoa.

The contraindications for insertion of IUCD include:

• Trophoblastic disease
• Distorted uterine cavity (fibroids, uterine anomalies)
• Ongoing pelvic infection
• Undiagnosed genital tract bleeding
• Suspected pregnancy
• Severe dysmenorrhea
• STIs — current or recurrent
• Wilson disease and copper allergy, for copper-containing IUCDs
• Breast cancer, for hormone-containing IUCDs

The different types of IUCD are shown below:

The timing of insertion of IUCD is as follows:

• Interval insertion (inter-conceptional period)- preferable to insert 2–3 days after menstruation, but it can be inserted at any time during the cycle. It can also be inserted during menstruation which has certain advantages like an open cervical canal and a distended uterine cavity
• Post-partum insertion is done at least 6 weeks after delivery when the uterus involutes to the normal size
• Postplacental insertion can be done immediately following delivery of the placenta
• Inserted within 5 days of coitus as an effective method of emergency contraception (Eg: incase of ruptured condom during intercourse)
questions.learning: Trophoblastic disease — The given image shows a copper-containing IUCD (intrauterine contraceptive device). Trophoblastic disease is an absolute contraindication for the insertion of this device.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department following a road traffic accident with complaints of intense superficial pain in his hand due to the injury. Considering the nature of this pain, which type of nerve fiber is primarily responsible for transmitting superficial pain and would be the appropriate target for selective pain relief?
questions.explanation: Pain sensation is transmitted by two main types of nerve fibers: A delta and C fibers. A delta fibers are small, myelinated fibers that transmit "fast pain". This is characterized as sharp, localized, and immediate pain, such as the acute superficial pain resulting from trauma in a road traffic accident. Targeting these fibers is the priority for alleviating the initial sharp discomfort. C fibers (Option D) are unmyelinated and transmit "slow pain," which is described as dull, aching, and poorly localized, typically arriving after the initial sharp sensation. A alpha fibers (Option C) are large and myelinated, primarily carrying proprioceptive information. A gamma fibers (Option B) are motor fibers involved in regulating muscle spindle sensitivity. Therefore, for the specific complaint of "severe superficial" sharp pain immediately following trauma, the A delta fibers are the primary neuroanatomical pathway involved in the transmission of the signal
questions.learning: Pain sensation is transmitted by two main types of nerve fibers: A delta and C fibers. A delta fibers are small, myelinated fibers that transmit "fast pain".

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 70-year-old female patient presents with pain in the thigh during walking. Investigation reveals the following finding as given below. What will be the best surgical management?

PTA- Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aortofemoral bypass

The symptom of pain in the thigh while walking and the given angiography image showing common iliac artery obstruction is suggestive of peripheral obstructive vascular disease with aortoiliac obstruction. The best surgical course, in this case, is to perform an aortofemoral bypass.

Clinical findings of aortoiliac obstruction are :

• Intermittent claudication is the debilitating cramp-like pain felt in the buttocks, leg, and thigh muscles due to reduced blood flow.
• Femoral and distal pulses are absent in both limbs.
• Arterial bruit is heard over the aortoiliac region.
• Impotence (Leriche syndrome) may occur. Buttock claudication is present.

As the disease progresses, rest pain, ulceration, gangrene, and slow capillary refilling may be seen.

CT angiography (CTA) and MR angiography (MRA) are specific investigations. Doppler ultrasound, duplex scanning, and digital subtraction percutaneous angiography (DSA) are the other available investigations.

An aortofemoral bypass is the choice of surgical intervention in aortoiliac obstruction. Dacron graft is a collagen-impregnated, knitted graft that is used to perform the proximal aortic anastomosis in aortofemoral bypass. It can also be used in aortic valve repair. In unfit patients, axillofemoral bypass may be done.

Other options:

Option A: Percutaneous Transluminal Angioplasty (PTA) is most useful in the treatment of isolated iliac stenoses (<4cm in length) than in occlusive disease.

Option B: Iliofemoral bypass is done in patients with unilateral occlusion of the distal common iliac or external iliac arteries.

Option D: Aortoiliac bypass more commonly known as the aortoiliac endarterectomy is rarely performed now a days because of greater blood loss associated with this surgery and greater sexual dysfunction caused, additionally it is difficult to perform.
Note: Aortofemoral bypass surgery has long-term patency of 70-80% at 10years and is often done bilaterally as the occlusion is more likely to be bilateral with one side affected more severely than the other. Bilateral aortofemoral bypass does not add to physiological stress and has equal benefits comparatively.
questions.learning: Aortofemoral bypass — The symptom of pain in the thigh while walking and the given angiography image showing common iliac artery obstruction is suggestive of peripheral obstructive vascular disease with aortoiliac obstruction.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Fluoroacetate is a component of pesticides. Which of the following metabolic pathways is inhibited by this compound?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. TCA cycle

Fluoroacetate inhibits the TCA cycle enzyme aconitase.

Fluoroacetyl CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to form fluorocitrate which inhibits aconitase, causing citrate to accumulate. This way it inhibits TCA cycle enzyme non-competitively.

Sources of fluoroacetate exposure:

• Fluoroacetate in some plants
• Fluorinated compounds (anticancer agents, industrial chemicals, and pesticides) are metabolized to fluoroacetate.
questions.learning: TCA cycle Fluoroacetate inhibits the TCA cycle enzyme aconitase. Fluoroacetyl CoA condenses with oxaloacetate to form fluorocitrate which inhibits aconitase, causing citrate to accumulate.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which medication is most appropriate for prophylaxis to reduce the frequency of future headache episodes in a 26-year-old woman who experiences unilateral, pulsating headaches associated with nausea, vomiting, and photophobia?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of unilateral, pulsating headaches with nausea and photophobia describes migraine. To reduce the frequency of future episodes (prophylaxis), propranolol is the drug of choice. Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker that has been well-validated for migraine prevention, with significant effects typically observed after four weeks of therapy. Alprazolam (Option B) and Diazepam (Option C) are benzodiazepines; while they may occasionally be used during acute attacks to induce sleep, they have no role in long-term migraine prophylaxis. Fluoxetine (Option D) is an antidepressant (SSRI); although sometimes used for chronic pain, it is not a first-line or standard agent for preventing migraine headaches. Therefore, for the specific goal of reducing attack frequency, propranolol remains the preferred pharmacological standard
questions.learning: The clinical history of unilateral, pulsating headaches with nausea and photophobia describes migraine. To reduce the frequency of future episodes (prophylaxis), propranolol is the drug of choice.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a 46XY female complete gonadal dysgenesis was noted. Complete gonadal dysgenesis is caused by what in the SRY gene?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Point mutation

Amongst the given options, a point mutation in the SRY gene is most likely to result in complete gonadal dysgenesis but this answer remains controversial as some other sources mention SRY deletion is more commonly associated. The most common cause attributable to about 85% of cases is still idiopathic.

Pure gonadal dysgenesis results from a point mutation in SRY/ SRY deletion or point mutations in another gene with testis-determining effects (DAXJ, SF-1, CBX2). This leads to underdeveloped dysgenetic gonads that fail to produce androgens or AMH. This is characterized by a normal prepubertal female phenotype and a normal mullerian system due to absent AMH.

The child usually presents with failure in the development of secondary sexual characteristics at puberty and amenorrhea. Investigations reveal the absence of estrogen production and they have elevated levels of FSH (>40 miU/mL) and low oestradiol levels (<25 pg/mL).

Women with streak ovaries are infertile, but they can bear children with oocyte donation. They must be treated with cyclic estrogen and progestogen to promote feminization and secondary sexual characteristics and prevent osteoporosis.
questions.learning: Point mutation Amongst the given options, a point mutation in the SRY gene is most likely to result in complete gonadal dysgenesis but this answer remains controversial as some other sources mention SRY deletion is more commonly associated.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of keratoconus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Haab's striae

The incorrect about keratoconus is Haab's striae. Haab's striae are seen in cases of buphthalmos where the intraocular pressure is raised and the eyeball is enlarged as a whole. The enlarged cornea is associated with tears in Descemet's membrane called Haab's striae.

Keratoconus or the conical cornea is a bilateral non-inflammatory progressive condition of the axial part of the cornea. Central or paracentral thinning of the cornea and apical protrusion of the anterior cornea are pathognomonic. This is attributed to mucopolysaccharide and collagen tissue synthesis defects.

Clinical features of the condition include defective vision due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism. Light sensitivity and ocular irritation may also be present. Complications include acute hydrops following the rupture of Descemet's membrane.

Slit-lamp examination reveals Fleischer's ring at the base of the cone formed. Deep, vertical stromal striae (Vogt lines) that disappear with external pressure are characteristic. Retinoscopy shows a scissoring reflex. The bulging of the lower lid in the downgaze, called Munson's sign, is shown in the image below.

The severity of the condition is graded based on keratometry. Corneal topography is a diagnostic modality with the highest sensitivity for early cases.

Intacs or intracorneal ring segments are useful in moderate cases due to their flattening effect. Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses, corneal collagen cross-linking with riboflavin, and keratoplasty are the other treatment modalities.
questions.learning: Haab's striae — The incorrect about keratoconus is Haab's striae. Haab's striae are seen in cases of buphthalmos where the intraocular pressure is raised and the eyeball is enlarged as a whole.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Riya was found to have a height of more than 95 percentile for his age and an arm-span to height ratio of more than 1.05. On further examination, she had flat feet, mild scoliosis, and long slender fingers. An image of her hand showing two characteristic signs is provided below. What is the most common ocular complication expected in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Subluxation of lens

The given features are suggestive of a diagnosis of Marfan's syndrome. Subluxation of the lens is the most common ocular complication.

Image (a) shows Walker-Murdoch (wrist) sign - the ability to join the thumb and fifth finger around the wrist.

Image (b) shows Steinberg (thumb) sign - thumb tip extends from the palm of the hand in a closed fist

Marfan’s syndrome is most commonly associated with superotemporal subluxation of lens.

Congenital subluxation of the lens is called ectopia lentis.

Features of Marfan's syndrome (Mnemonic: MARFAN’S)

* Mitral valve prolapse

* Myopia due to upward dislocation of the lens (bilateral ectopic lentis)

* Aortic root dilatation, Aortic regurgitation

* Retinal detachment

* Fibrillin 1 gene defect: Reduced fibrillin 1 production causing joint laxity

* Fifteen (Chromosome 15 is involved)

* Flat feet

* Arachnodactyly, Astigmatism, Air in lungs (Pneumothorax)

* Nearsightedness

* Subluxation of lens, Scoliosis, Speech disorders, Sleep apnea
