questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Zellweger syndrome is associated with which cellular organelle?
questions.explanation: Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome) is the most severe form of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders. It is characterized by the failure of the body to produce functional peroxisomes (Option A), leading to a toxic accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs). Peroxisomes are essential organelles responsible for lipid metabolism and the detoxification of hydrogen peroxide. Nucleosomes (Option B) are structural units of DNA packaging in the nucleus. Lysosomes (Option C) are involved in intracellular digestion, and their dysfunction leads to lysosomal storage diseases like Tay-Sachs. Ribosomes (Option D) are responsible for protein synthesis. Infants with Zellweger syndrome typically present with profound hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, hepatomegaly, and neurological dysfunction. There is currently no cure, and the condition is usually fatal within the first year of life. Understanding this relationship is fundamental for identifying the clinical manifestations of metabolic disorders related to organelle dysfunction

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is FALSE regarding deep second-degree burns?
questions.explanation: The false statement regarding deep second-degree (partial thickness) burns is that they are "painless." In reality, deep second-degree burns remain painful to pressure because the pressure-sensitive nerve endings in the deeper dermis are still functional, even if superficial pain receptors are destroyed. True "painless" burns are Third-degree (full thickness) burns, where all dermal sensory structures are completely destroyed. Other statements are correct: deep second-degree burns do result in damage to the deeper dermis (Option C); they show "less blanching" or delayed capillary refill because the superficial dermal vessels are damaged (Option B); and they frequently heal by scar deposition and may take 3 to 6 weeks to close (Option A) . Identifying the depth of a burn is essential for determining if a patient requires skin grafting or conservative dressing management. Because deep second-degree burns retain pressure sensation, labeling them as painless is medically inaccurate

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Blood cholesterol shown as mg/ml value is in which scale?
questions.explanation: Data in biostatistics is classified into different scales based on its nature. Blood cholesterol levels, measured as specific numerical values (e.g., in mg/ml or mg/dL), are an example of continuous data. Continuous data can take any value within a given range and can be measured with any degree of precision (including fractions or decimals). Nominal data (Option B) involves categories without an inherent order, like gender or blood group. Ordinal data (Option A) involves categories with a meaningful rank or order, such as stages of cancer or socio-economic status. Discrete data (Option C) involves whole number counts, such as the number of hospital beds or the number of children in a family. Understanding these scales is fundamental for choosing the correct statistical tests for data analysis. Continuous variables like cholesterol, blood pressure, and height are typically summarized using means and standard deviations and are analyzed using parametric tests like the t-test or ANOVA

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: After childbirth, how long does it usually take for a woman’s cardiac output to return to pre- pregnancy levels?
questions.explanation: During pregnancy, cardiac output (CO) increases by about 30–50% to meet the metabolic demands of the mother and fetus. Immediately after delivery, there is a transient further rise in cardiac output due to autotransfusion from the contracted uterus and mobilization of extracellular fluid. In the early postpartum period, cardiac output begins to decline gradually as blood volume decreases and vascular resistance normalizes. Most physiological adaptations reverse over time. Typically, cardiac output returns to pre-pregnancy levels within about 10 days postpartum. This gradual normalization reflects stabilization of hemodynamic changes, including reduction in plasma volume and heart rate. Why other options are incorrect: (A) 2 days: Too early; CO is still elevated (B) 5 days: Declining but not yet baseline (C) 7 days: Still above pre-pregnancy level

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Surgical excision is carried out, and microscopic examination of the tumor along with molecular studies reveals abnormalities in cell cycle regulation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The 3-year-old boy presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) and a missing red reflex, which are the hallmark clinical signs of retinoblastoma—the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood. Disrupted cell cycle regulation (Option B) mentioned in the molecular analysis refers to the inactivation of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 13, which is the underlying genetic cause. Wilms tumor (Option A) is a kidney malignancy. Ependymoma (Option C) is a CNS tumor. Neuroblastoma (Option D) is an extracranial solid tumor. Microscopic examination of retinoblastoma classically shows small blue round cells with characteristic Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Because the clinical findings are exclusively intraocular and the genetic profile matches RB1 dysfunction, retinoblastoma is the correct diagnosis. Early detection is vital for preserving vision and the life of the child through therapies like chemotherapy, cryotherapy, or enucleation

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Lung malignancy is most commonly associated with?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asbestosis

Asbestosis is most commonly associated with mesotheliomas,  pleural malignancy.

Asbestos-related diseases include:

* Localized fibrous plaques or diffuse pleural fibrosis

* Pleural effusion

* Parenchymal interstitial fibrosis (asbestosis)

* Lung carcinoma

* Mesotheliomas

* Laryngeal, ovarian and colon carcinomas

Asbestosis:

* Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis that occurs after 5-10 years of exposure to asbestos. However, once established, it progresses even in the further removal of the worker from its contact. Asbestosis affects the basal part of the lung causing diffuse peribronchial fibrosis.

* Asbestos is of 2 types, i.e

* Serpentine

* Amphibole

* Sputum shows asbestos bodies, which are asbestos fibres coated with fibrin.

* They present with cough and exertional dyspnoea and predominantly affect the lower lobes of the lung, in contrast to other forms of pneumoconiosis, which affect the upper lobes.

* Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis typically shows a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.

* X-ray shows peripheral reticular opacities predominantly in the lower zones.

* HRCT shows:

* traction bronchiectasis

* subpleural fibrotic lines

* honeycomb pattern

* irregular opacities

* The complications that can occur are

* Pulmonary fibrosis

* Carcinoma of the lung

* Malignancy of the gastrointestinal tract

* Mesothelioma of the pleura

Preventive measures:

* Using a safer type of asbestos, like chrysolite and amosite

* Substituting other insulants like glass fibre, mineral wool, calcium silicate, plastic foams, etc

* Dust control

* Periodic examination of workers

* Continuing research

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the papillae from the given histological section.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Circumvallate

The given histological image is a section of the tongue showing circumvallate papillae, the largest papillae of the tongue.

Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures that are around 8-12 in number, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

They are arranged in a V-shaped row immediately in front of the sulcus terminalis (not on the sides of the tongue) on the dorsal surface of the tongue. It is narrower at its base than its apex.

Numerous taste buds (around 250 taste buds for each of the 8-12 papillae) are present within the papillary walls and they contain chemosensory cells that synapse with the gustatory nerves. Serous glands of von Ebner empty via the ducts into the base of the sulcus.

Identification: They can be identified by their characteristic dome-shaped structure lined by stratified squamous epithelium.

Other options:

Option A - Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, and red in color and are mainly present on the lingual margins and also on the dorsal surface of the tongue. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve.

Option C- Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections that are mainly present on the dorsal part of the anterior 2/3rd of the tongue. All except filiform papillae contain taste buds. They are covered by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. It is supplied by the lingual nerve.

Option D - Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges that are present bilaterally in two zones at the sides of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis. They are covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to the Indian health care guidelines, what is the recommended number of antenatal visits during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Traditionally, the ideal antenatal care (ANC) schedule in India is based on frequent monitoring throughout pregnancy rather than just the minimum required visits. According to this ideal schedule: 1. Up to 7 months: one visit every month 2. 8th month: one visit every 2 weeks 3. 9th month: one visit every week This adds up to approximately 13–14 visits, which is considered the recommended or ideal number of ANC visits for optimal maternal and fetal care. Important distinction: 1. Minimum visits (Government of India): 4 visits 2. WHO recommendation (2016): at least 8 contacts 3. Ideal Indian schedule:13 visits Why other options are incorrect: (B) 6 visits: Not a recognized standard (C) 8 visits: WHO guideline, but not the “ideal” Indian schedule asked here (D) 4 visits: Minimum requirement only Thus, in exam context, 13 visits represent the recommended ANC schedule

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An intubated patient in the ICU had a chest X-ray taken to evaluate for fever spikes over the last 24-48 hours. The radiograph is shown below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
options: Start antibiotics and send samples for culture
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ultrasound-guided aspiration

The given clinical history of an intubated ICU patient and the X-ray features point toward a diagnosis of pleural effusion. Ultrasound-guided aspiration is the next step in the management of the patient. Antibiotics should be started once the pleural tap has been done and infective etiology is suspected.

Options A and B: ET tube suctioning and chest physiotherapy are done to remove thick secretions out of the upper and lower respiratory tract. It wouldn't help in removing the fluid of a pleural effusion.

Pleural effusion is a common finding in the ICU setting and in intubated patients. Many factors contribute to the impairment of pleural fluid turnover in such cases as prolonged recumbency, ventilator-produced positive pressure, and reduced plasma oncotic pressure.

The diagnosis of pleural effusion may be made by clinical examination (dull note on percussion) or by imaging. A pleural tap for confirmation of diagnosis and to relieve breathing difficulty is now done under ultrasound guidance.

The CXR features of pleural effusion include:

• Obliteration of costophrenic angle on the side of pleural effusion
• Air-fluid interface (meniscus sign)
• Large effusions show: Complete opacification of the lung, mediastinal shift, and tracheal deviation away from the effusion

Differential diagnosis in an intubated patient with opacities on CXR might be pneumonitis secondary to gastric acid or food aspiration. But the X-ray would show patchy infiltration unlike the homogenous density seen in pleural effusion.
questions.learning: Ultrasound-guided aspiration — The given clinical history of an intubated ICU patient and the X-ray features point toward a diagnosis of pleural effusion.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: La belle indifference is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Conversion disorder

La belle indifference is seen in conversion disorder.

La belle indifference refers to a lack of concern towards the symptoms, despite the apparent severity of the disability. Although not pathognomonic of conversion disorder, it is often seen in association with it.

Conversion disorder is also known as functional neurological symptom disorder or dissociative disorder. It includes acute and temporary loss of motor or sensory function without any underlying neurological disease. Because the onset of such symptoms often coincides with psychological issues such as internal conflict, it was speculated that these issues converted to neurological symptoms. Conversion disorder can present with symptoms such as paresis, non-epileptic seizures (NES), blindness, and anesthesia of the extremities. One of the gait disturbances which can be seen is astasia-abasia — a wildly ataxic, staggering gait with gross and irregular truncal movements, and thrashing and waving arm movements. The patient often has a carefree attitude towards his illness as mentioned above.

Patients of conversion disorder achieve primary gain by keeping internal conflicts outside of their awareness. These conflicts manifest as physical symptoms. As a result of being sick, the patients are excused from obligations and receive support that might not otherwise have been available. This is referred to as secondary gain.
questions.learning: Conversion disorder La belle indifference is seen in conversion disorder. La belle indifference refers to a lack of concern towards the symptoms, despite the apparent severity of the disability.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The given type of population pyramid indicates all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Developed countries

The given image shows an age pyramid/population pyramid with a broad base and tapering top. The age pyramid is plotted as a younger age at the bottom and older age at the top. Hence this age pyramid represents a higher young population. This pyramid is typical of developing countries, and not developed countries.

This type of pyramid also indicates an increasing population because of high young population reflecting high fertility.

Pearl PF1861: Population Pyramid

* The age or population pyramid is used to represent the age/sex structure of a population.

* Below is the age pyramid of India (2017).

* The age pyramid of India has a broad base and a tapering top, as it is with most developing countries.

* As a nation develops the lower portion of the pyramid will start constricting and the upper portion will start increasing.

* Developed countries usually will have a bulge in the middle with a narrow base, as shown below in the age pyramid of Switzerland.
questions.learning: Developed countries — The given image shows an age pyramid/population pyramid with a broad base and tapering top. The age pyramid is plotted as a younger age at the bottom and older age at the top.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 43-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe headache, confusion, and visual disturbances for 3 days. He has poorly controlled hypertension. On examination Blood pressure is 224/115 mm Hg and Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema. Laboratory evaluation shows mildly elevated serum creatinine. An intravenous antihypertensive agent is started that causes arteriolar vasodilation, improves renal blood flow and Promotes natriuresis. Which of the following drugs is most likely being administered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fenoldopam

This patient has a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) with end-organ damage (papilledema, encephalopathy).

Fenoldopam is a dopamine D1 receptor agonist that:

• Causes arteriolar vasodilation
• Increases renal blood flow
• Promotes natriuresis and diuresis
• Is preferred in hypertensive emergencies, especially with renal involvement

Why not other options?

A. Esmolol → β1-blocker; reduces heart rate, not a primary renal vasodilator

C. Hydralazine → Arteriolar dilator but does not improve renal perfusion significantly

D. Nitroglycerin → Predominantly venodilator; used in ACS, not ideal here
questions.learning: Fenoldopam — This patient has a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) with end-organ damage (papilledema, encephalopathy). Fenoldopam is a dopamine D1 receptor agonist that: • Causes arteriolar vasodilation • Increases renal blood flow • Promotes…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the abdominal plane labelled 2?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper border of L3

The plane marked 2 in the given image is the subcostal plane. It is at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The subcostal plane is an anatomical reference plane used in clinical and surgical practice. It is defined as a horizontal plane passing through the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage bilaterally. The 10th costal cartilage corresponds approximately to the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

The costal cartilages are extensions of the ribs that articulate with the sternum anteriorly. The 10th costal cartilage is the cartilage of the 10th rib.

In the given image, structure 2 represents the subcostal plane, which corresponds to the level of the lower border of the 10th costal cartilage. Since the 10th costal cartilage is at the level of the upper border of L3, it indicates that the subcostal plane is also at the level of the upper border of L3.

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.
questions.learning: Upper border of L3 — The plane marked 2 in the given image is the subcostal plane. It is at the level of the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A man sufferred trauma to the eye from a punch while fighting with another person. What is the most common site of fracture in the orbit?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Floor

The most common site of an orbital fracture due to blunt trauma is the floor of the orbit as it is relatively weak.

The floor consists of three bones: the zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones. The posteromedial portion of the maxillary bone is relatively weak and may be involved in a "blowout" fracture.

Isolated fracture of the orbital floor when a large blunt object strikes the globe is called blowout fracture. The orbital contents herniate through the antrum.

Clinical signs: periocular swelling (early stage), enophthalmos, ecchymosis and subconjunctival hemorrhage (later stages).

Investigations:

* X-Ray (Water's view) shows a teardrop opacity

* CT scan is used for confirmation of the diagnosis

Treatment:

Initial treatment consists of observation, oral antibiotics, ice packs, and nasal decongestants. Subsequent treatment is aimed at the prevention of vertical diplopia and cosmetically unacceptable enophthalmos.

Indications of surgery:

* Enophthalmos greater than 2 mm

* Persistent and progressive diplopia in the primary position

* Entrapment of orbital contents

* Fractures involving more than half of the orbital floor with or without herniation will develop enophthalmos if not corrected
questions.learning: Floor — The most common site of an orbital fracture due to blunt trauma is the floor of the orbit as it is relatively weak. The floor consists of three bones: the zygomatic, maxillary, and palatine bones.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding vasectomy?
options: The procedure is done under local anesthesia.
Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure.
A no-scalpel technique is being widely used now.
The vas deferens is the structure that is divided in the procedure.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure.

Option B is incorrect as sperms can remain in the reproductive tract for up to 3 months and thus sterility is not immediate. It can take up to 3 months after the procedure and during this time period, the couple must abstain from intercourse or use other methods of contraception.

Vasectomy:

Vasectomy is done under local anaesthesia. A small incision is made in the scrotum. The vas deferens are divided on both sides which disrupts the passage of sperms.

The no-scalpel technique has been now adopted. One single incision is made with special forceps and skin stitch is not required. Clips and plugs can be applied over the vas instead of cutting.

Approximately, 20 ejaculates clear the semen of all sperms. Two semen analysis reports must confirm the absence of sperms before the man can be declared sterile.
questions.learning: Sterility is achieved 3 weeks after the procedure. Option B is incorrect as sperms can remain in the reproductive tract for up to 3 months and thus sterility is not immediate.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: 27-year-old female came for treatment of infertility to OPD. Bromocriptine was prescribed. What could be the possible reason?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hyperprolactinemia

The patient is likely to be suffering from hyperprolactinemia.

Prolactin inhibits the secretion of GnRH, which leads to the decreased secretion of LH and FSH resulting in infertility. Bromocriptine acts on Dopamine D2 receptors to reduce prolactin secretion.
questions.learning: Hyperprolactinemia — The patient is likely to be suffering from hyperprolactinemia. Prolactin inhibits the secretion of GnRH, which leads to the decreased secretion of LH and FSH resulting in infertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman attends a routine gynecological visit and expresses concern about her family history of cancer. During counseling, the gynecologist explains that oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) have a protective effect against certain malignancies. Which type of cancer is not reduced in risk by the use of OCPs?
questions.explanation: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are known to provide a protective effect against endometrial cancer. Their use lowers the risk of developing this cancer, and the protection becomes stronger with longer duration of use, persisting even after discontinuation. This benefit is due to the hormonal action of OCPs, which helps regulate the menstrual cycle and reduces prolonged exposure of the endometrium to unopposed estrogen, a key factor in endometrial carcinogenesis. In contrast, OCPs do not significantly influence the risk of cervical cancer, although preventive measures like Pap smear screening and HPV vaccination are effective. The association with breast cancer is variable, with some studies showing a slight temporary increase in risk that declines after stopping OCPs. Similarly, bladder cancer risk is unrelated to OCP use and is more strongly associated with factors such as smoking, chemical exposure, and chronic irritation
questions.learning: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are known to provide a protective effect against endometrial cancer. Their use lowers the risk of developing this cancer, and the protection becomes stronger with longer duration of use, persisting even after discontinuation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presented with dysuria and increased frequency of micturition. He has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections with Proteus species. The radiographic image is given below. Identify the calculi shown.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Calcium Phosphate

The given clinical scenario and X-ray KUB showing a homogenous huge density with the smooth edge seen in the bladder is suggestive of struvite calculi, which is formed due to the precipitation of calcium, magnesium, and ammonium phosphate.

Struvite stones (triple phosphate stones)  are usually seen in a setting of infection with urease-producing bacteria like Proteus, Pseudomonas, and Staphylococcus. They can grow very large and form a cast of the renal pelvis and calyces resulting in staghorn calculi. Production of urease enzyme by Proteus, which hydrolyses urea to ammonia causes alkalinization of urine. Alkalinization of urine leads to precipitation of organic and inorganic compounds which contributes to the formation of Struvite stones.

Almost 90% of the renal stones are radio-opaque and the remaining 10% are radiolucent. The investigation of choice for renal stones is NCCT.

Struvite stones are usually managed with percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) as it is usually larger in size and associated with Urinary tract infections.

Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL) is a non-invasive method that generates shockwaves outside the body, which are focused on the stones. It is the most common method of treating urinary tract stones nowadays. Stones up to approximately 1.5 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.

PCNL is indicated in:

• Staghorn calculi - Stone >2 cm
• Multiple stones - >1 cm
• Proximal ureteral stone - >1 cm

Other options:
Option A: Patients with cystinuria (an autosomal recessive disorder) are at risk for Cystine stones. These stones are hexagonal.

Option C: Xanthine stones are seen in inborn errors of metabolism like Lesch Nyhan syndrome and cases of hyperuricemia. It is a radiolucent stone.

Option D: Calcium oxalate stones are seen in conditions causing high urine calcium such as primary hyperparathyroidism and chronic acidemia from distal renal tubular acidosis. Also seen in the condition of high urine oxalate which is seen during a low-calcium diet and in malabsorption syndromes(small bowel disease (eg, Crohn's disease), including a jejunoileal bypass for obesity (bariatric surgery), surgical bowel resection or diversion, or cystic fibrosis). Calcium oxalate monohydrate stones are usually dumbbell-shaped and Calcium oxalate dihydrate stones are usually envelope-shaped.
questions.learning: Calcium Phosphate — The given clinical scenario and X-ray KUB showing a homogenous huge density with the smooth edge seen in the bladder is suggestive of struvite calculi, which is formed due to the precipitation of calcium, magnesium, and ammonium phosphate.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Functioning pituitary adenoma most commonly arises from which one of the following cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lactotroph

Pituitary adenomas are benign tumors arising from the adenohypophysis (anterior pituitary). Functioning pituitary adenomas secrete excess pituitary hormones, and the most common functioning pituitary adenoma is a prolactinoma, which arises from lactotroph cells.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Somatotroph: ✗

• Secretes Growth Hormone (GH).
• Causes gigantism (children) or acromegaly (adults).
• Second most common functioning pituitary adenoma.

• C. Corticotroph: ✗

• Secretes ACTH.
• Causes Cushing disease.

• D. Thyrotroph: ✗

• Secretes TSH.
• Rare; causes secondary hyperthyroidism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements: Statement I: Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are more powerful predictors of subsequent risk of type 2 diabetes than Body Mass Index (BMI). Statement II: Central obesity is an important determinant of insulin resistance, the underlying abnormality in most cases of type 2 diabetes. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct but Statement II is not the correct explanation of Statement I
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I

Central (abdominal/visceral) obesity is a stronger predictor of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) than overall obesity measured by Body Mass Index (BMI). Measures such as waist circumference (WC) and waist-to-hip ratio (WHR) better reflect visceral fat, which is closely associated with insulin resistance, the key pathogenic mechanism in T2DM.

• Statement I: Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are more powerful predictors of subsequent risk of type 2 diabetes than Body Mass Index (BMI): ✓

• Waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio are better predictors of future T2DM risk than BMI because they assess abdominal fat distribution rather than total body weight.

• Statement II: Central obesity is an important determinant of insulin resistance, the underlying abnormality in most cases of type 2 diabetes: ✓

• Central obesity promotes insulin resistance through increased release of free fatty acids, inflammatory cytokines, and adipokines from visceral adipose tissue.

• Statement II correctly explains Statement I because visceral fat is metabolically more active and strongly linked to insulin resistance.
questions.learning: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I Central (abdominal/visceral) obesity is a stronger predictor of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) than overall obesity measured by Body Mass Index (BMI).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25 year old male after high speed RTA is slightly hypotensive but eFAST is negative. He has a widened mediastinum, chest wall ecchymosis and a pulse deficit in the left radial artery. Which is the next most appropriate step?
options: Give a 2L fluid rush and obtain a CT angiography for the patient.
Proceed to do an emergent thoracotomy.
Initiate permissive hypotension and perform CT angiography.
Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids and perform a TEE immediately.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids and perform a TEE immediately.

High-speed deceleration trauma with widened mediastinum, chest wall ecchymosis, and upper-limb pulse deficit strongly suggests blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTAI). A negative eFAST does not exclude this diagnosis because eFAST primarily evaluates for hemoperitoneum and pericardial tamponade, not aortic disruption.

In suspected BTAI, the key priorities are:

1.   ATLS stabilization (airway and breathing first)

2.  Prevent worsening hemorrhage by avoiding aggressive fluid boluses and maintaining controlled blood pressure (“anti- impulse therapy”)

3.  Obtain urgent definitive imaging to confirm injury

For imaging:

• CT angiography (CTA) is the standard confirmatory test in stable patients
• If the patient is borderline unstable or CT transfer is unsafe, Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is preferred because it:

o    can be performed immediately at bedside

o    rapidly detects aortic transection/pseudoaneurysm

o    avoids delays and transport-related collapse

Therefore, in a slightly hypotensive trauma patient with strong signs of BTAI, the best next step is Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids, and perform immediate TEE.
questions.learning: Stabilize the airway, avoid excessive fluids and perform a TEE immediately. High-speed deceleration trauma with widened mediastinum, chest wall ecchymosis, and upper-limb pulse deficit strongly suggests blunt thoracic aortic injury (BTAI).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The afferent limb of the corneal (wisp) reflex is carried by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), specifically via the nasociliary nerve.
questions.explanation: The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective mechanism that triggers bilateral eyelid closure when the cornea is stimulated. The Trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically the ophthalmic division (V1), is responsible for the afferent limb of this reflex. Sensory fibers from the cornea travel via the nasociliary branch of V1 to the trigeminal sensory nucleus in the brainstem. The Facial nerve (CN VII) (Option A) mediates the efferent limb, sending motor signals to the orbicularis oculi muscle to contract and close the eye. The Oculomotor nerve (CN III) (Option C) controls eyelid elevation and most extraocular muscles but is not part of this reflex pathway. The Abducens nerve (CN VI) (Option D) is responsible for lateral eye movement and is unrelated to the blink response. Clinically, testing this reflex is essential for assessing brainstem integrity and the function of cranial nerves V and VII
questions.learning: The corneal reflex (blink reflex) is a protective mechanism that triggers bilateral eyelid closure when the cornea is stimulated. The Trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically the ophthalmic division (V1), is responsible for the afferent limb of this reflex.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The quadruple test for antenatal screening of Down syndrome is performed in the second trimester of pregnancy, typically between 15 and 20 weeks of gestation (most commonly around 16–18 weeks).
questions.explanation: The Quadruple test is a vital biochemical screening tool for Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18), and neural tube defects. It is characteristically performed during the 2nd trimester, ideally between 15 and 20 weeks of gestation. The test measures four maternal serum markers: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG), unconjugated Estriol (uE3), and Inhibin-A. First trimester screening (Option A) typically involves the "Double marker" test (PAPP-A and free beta-hCG) combined with nuchal translucency ultrasound at 11–14 weeks. There is no standard "screening" for these conditions in the 3rd trimester (Option B) or a 4th trimester (Option D), as the window for diagnostic follow-up and clinical decision-making would be closed. The quadruple test provides a risk estimate; if the result is "screen positive" (high risk), the patient is offered definitive diagnostic testing via amniocentesis
questions.learning: The Quadruple test is a vital biochemical screening tool for Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (Trisomy 18), and neural tube defects. It is characteristically performed during the 2nd trimester, ideally between 15 and 20 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 27-year-old IT professional has presented to you with intense watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in the eye for the past 2 months. He took out his contact lens and applied eye lubricants to help alleviate his ailment, but it didn't provide any relief. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant papillary conjunctivitis

The clinical history of watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva, suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

Giant papillary conjunctivitis is a severe form of mechanically induced papillary conjunctivitis. It is most commonly associated with contact lens wear. It can also be associated with ocular prostheses, exposed sutures, and scleral buckles.

Patients usually present with redness, foreign body sensation, increased mucus production, itching, blurring, and loss of contact lens tolerance. On examination, giant papillae are seen on the upper tarsal conjunctiva with hyperemia. Focal apical ulceration and whitish scarring may develop on larger papillae.

Papillae are reddish, flat-topped, raised areas that give a red and velvety appearance to the tarsal conjunctiva. These are caused by the hyperplasia of the normal vascular system, with glomerulus-like bunches of capillaries growing into the epithelium.

The image below shows papillae in the tarsal conjunctiva.

Treatment includes the removal of the offending cause. Mast cell stabilizers, such as sodium cromoglycate, and drugs like azelastine and olopatadine, which have combined antihistamine and mast cell–stabilizing effects, are effective. Steroids can be used for resistant cases.

Other options:

Option A: In acute trachoma, sago-like follicles are characteristically seen. It is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. The SAFE strategy is used in the management of trachoma.

The image below shows sago-like follicles in trachoma.

Option B: In follicular conjunctivitis, follicles are seen. It is most commonly caused by herpes and adenoviruses. Follicles are greyish-white raised areas on fornices and palpebral conjunctiva. These are formed due to the localized aggregations of lymphocytes in the sub-epithelial adenoid layer.

The image shows follicles.

Option D: In spring catarrh (vernal catarrh), cobblestone appearance is a papillary reaction in the palpebral conjunctiva, ropy discharge, and Maxwell-Lyon sign are present. Horner-Trantas spots that are discrete, whitish, raised dots along the limbus can also be seen. It is more common during summer.

The image below shows Horner-Trantas spots.
questions.learning: Giant papillary conjunctivitis — The clinical history of watering, redness, and foreign body sensation in a contact lens user, along with the image showing giant papillae in the conjunctiva, suggests a probable diagnosis of giant papillary conjunctivitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient is admitted with fever and neck stiffness. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis reveals low glucose levels, elevated protein, and a predominance of neutrophils. What is the most appropriate treatment in this case?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, combined with CSF findings of decreased glucose, elevated protein, and neutrophilic pleocytosis, is diagnostic of bacterial meningitis. Ceftriaxone is the first-line, broad-spectrum antibiotic recommended for empirical treatment in adults. It effectively covers the most common pathogens, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Regarding the distractors, Ampicillin (Option A) is specifically added for Listeria monocytogenes in neonates or elderly patients but is not the primary choice for standard adult cases. Penicillin (Option C) is no longer used alone due to rising resistance. Vancomycin (Option D) is often used with Ceftriaxone to cover penicillin-resistant strains but is insufficient as monotherapy. Therefore, Ceftriaxone is the most appropriate first-line agent based on the provided clinical and laboratory profile
questions.learning: The classic triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity, combined with CSF findings of decreased glucose, elevated protein, and neutrophilic pleocytosis, is diagnostic of bacterial meningitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text:
A 40-year-old male presents with increased thirst and increased frequency and volume of urination. He has no other symptoms. His random blood sugar was 205mg/dl. What appropriate investigations should be done?

i) HbA1c
ii) Urine ACR
iii) Echocardiography
iv) Fundoscopy
v) ECG
vi) Serum protein electrophoresis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. i, ii, iv, v

This patient presenting with increased thirst(polydipsia), increased urination(polyuria) and a random blood sugar of 205 makes a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus likely. For a newly diagnosed case of diabetes, patients need to undergo other investigations to check for systemic progression of disease. These investigations include HbA1c, Urine albumin creatinine ratio, Fundoscopy, and ECG.

Diabetes can cause many microvascular and macrovascular complications and requires screening for these conditions.

• HbA1c is done to estimate the glycemic control over the last 3 months and helps guide further therapy. It should be done 2-4 times per year based on the previous values.
• Urine albumin creatinine ratio is done to check if there is progression to diabetic kidney disease. It should ideally be done annually to check for kidney disease.
• Dilated fundoscopy should be done annually in diabetics to rule out diabetic retinopathy. For a newly diagnosed case of T2DM, fundoscopy should be done at the time of diagnosis and then every year till there is no diabetic retinopathy.
• ECG should be done to check for resting electrolyte abnormalities in diabetics. Additionally, many diabetic patients also have co-existing hypertension so ECG is done to rule out left ventricular hypertrophy.
• Testing for diabetic neuropathy should be done annually with the monofilament test.
• BP screening 2-4 times a year
questions.learning: i, ii, iv, v This patient presenting with increased thirst(polydipsia), increased urination(polyuria) and a random blood sugar of 205 makes a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus likely.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the condition in the image?
questions.explanation: The image is a Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU), the gold standard for evaluating the anterior urethra. It shows a clear, focal area of narrowing (stricture) in the bulbar segment. Urethral strictures in the bulbar region are commonly caused by "straddle" injuries or instrumentation. A membranous urethral injury (Option B) or tear (Option C) is usually associated with pelvic fractures and would show extravasation of contrast rather than a clean narrowing. Benign Prostate Hyperplasia (Option D) affects the prostatic urethra (much more proximal) and would show an elongated, narrowed segment or a "J-shaped" ureter on IVP, rather than a focal anterior stricture. Patients with bulbar strictures typically present with a poor urinary stream, straining, and incomplete emptying. Treatment options include urethral dilation, internal urethrotomy, or definitive urethroplasty. Identifying the exact location and length of the stricture on RGU is essential for planning the correct surgical approach
questions.learning: The image is a Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU), the gold standard for evaluating the anterior urethra. It shows a clear, focal area of narrowing (stricture) in the bulbar segment.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient came to OPD with complaints of passing loose bulky stools that were associated with abdominal pain for the past 2 weeks. Stool examination reveals an organism with 4 pairs of flagella exhibiting falling leaf motility. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Giardia lamblia

The given clinical history and microscopy of an organism with 4 pairs of flagella and falling leaf motility is suggestive of giardiasis caused by Giardia lamblia.

Histopathology of the duodenum in giardiasis reveals several heart-shaped or pear-shaped trophozoites, with 2 equally sized nuclei and 4 pairs of flagella. It exhibits slow oscillating motility that resembles falling leaf motility.

Giardia lamblia, also called Giardia duodenalis, is the causative agent of giardiasis. It is a common pathogenic protozoan found in the duodenum and jejunum of humans.

Infection occurs by the ingestion of mature cysts in contaminated water and food. and may also be transmitted by the fecal-oral route.

It is weakly pathogenic in humans. Hence, giardiasis usually occurs in immunosuppressed, agammaglobulinemia, or malnourished individuals.

Clinical features:

* Diarrhea

* Fat malabsorption

* Dull epigastric pain

* Belching and flatulence

* Iron deficiency and growth stunting.

* The stool will have excess mucus and fat but no blood.

Detection of antigens by ELISA is more sensitive and specific than microscopy. Entero test /string test is also used in the diagnosis.

Other options:

Isospora belli is a coccidian parasite that can cause protracted diarrhea in immunocompromised patients. The oocyst is not easily seen on stool-wet mounts. It may be visible after stool concentration and staining with acid-fast stain, as shown below.

Cryptosporidium parvum, commonly causes diarrhea in immunocompromised individuals. The oocysts in the stool can be visualized by modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining. It appears as red acid-fast spheres. It can also be used for specimens such as sputum and bronchial wash. The image given below demonstrates uniformly acid-fast oocysts of Cryptosporidium parvum.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A female patient presented with acne that is not resolving on oral isotretinoin and antibiotics therapy. Which of the following is the next best investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Evaluate for hyperandrogenism

The next best step for a female patient with acne that is resistant to oral isotretinoin is to check for hyperandrogenism.

Hyperandrogenism usually manifests as hirsutism, acne, and/or androgenic alopecia. Acne that is persistent, moderate to severe, or late-onset raises concern for PCOS or other causes of hyperandrogenism.

The pathogenesis of acne vulgaris involves

• Blockage of the follicular opening by hyperkeratosis
• Sebum overproduction
• The proliferation of commensal Propionibacterium acnes
• Inflammation

Management is directed at minimizing inflammation, decreasing keratin production, antibiotics, and antiandrogens to diminish sebum production.

Other options:

Option A: Looking for dietary triggers could be considered, but there is limited evidence to support a direct relationship between specific food items and acne.

Option C: Since the patient has not shown improvement even with antibiotic therapy, it is reasonable to consider checking for antibiotic resistance. However, evaluating for hyperandrogenism should be prioritized due to its potential role in the patient's condition.

Option D: Looking for drug triggers may be relevant in some cases, but it is less likely to be the primary cause of acne that is not responding to isotretinoin and antibiotics. Drug-induced acne typically resolves once the offending drug is discontinued.
questions.learning: Evaluate for hyperandrogenism — The next best step for a female patient with acne that is resistant to oral isotretinoin is to check for hyperandrogenism.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The maternal mortality ratio is defined as?
options: Maternal Deaths per 10,000 women in reproductive age group
Maternal Deaths per 100,000 women in reproductive age group
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Maternal Deaths per 100,000 live births

Maternal mortality ratio is defined as the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births during a given time period.

Maternal mortality rate is the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 women of reproductive age in a given time period.
questions.learning: Maternal Deaths per 100,000 live births Maternal mortality ratio is defined as the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births during a given time period.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
All of the following cause a right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, except ___.

HbF- Fetal hemoglobin

2,3 BPG- 2,3 Bisphosphoglyceric acid
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased HbF

Increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin) causes a left shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:

This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the percentage saturation of Hb with O2. It is normally sigmoid in shape. If the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the right, it means that the affinity of Hb for O2 has become less, which favors O2 delivery. This means a higher P50, which implies that a higher PO2 is required to maintain 50% saturation (R - Right shift Releases oxygen). If the curve is shifted to the left, it means that affinity has increased for O2 ( which favors O2 binding ) i.e. lower P50 value ( L-Left shift Leashes oxygen ).

Causes of the right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:

• Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - metabolically active tissues utilize O2 and tissues produce CO2
• ↓ pH - Secondary to increased CO2 production
• ↑ in temperature
• ↑ in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis
• Growth hormone, thyroid hormone, androgen - by increasing 2,3 DPG
• Sickle cell anemia - reduced affinity for O2
• Exercise

Causes of the left shift of oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve:

• ↑ pH (alkalosis)
• ↓ PCO2
• ↓ 2,3-DPG
• ↓ Temperature
• HbF
• Carboxyhemoglobin

Bohr's effect- The decrease in the O2 affinity of hemoglobin when the pH of the blood falls
questions.learning: Increased HbF Increased HbF (fetal hemoglobin) causes a left shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve: This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the percentage saturation of Hb with O2.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the initial step when an immunization survey is being conducted?
options: Completing the cluster and summary forms
Calculating the total fertility rate of the area
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cluster identification

Among the following options, finding a cluster is the first step to be done in an immunization survey.

The five major steps of an immunization survey are as follows:

* Plan the survey

* Conduct the survey

* Tabulate data

* Analyse data

* Take action

1. Planning the survey includes selecting the children based on age groups, finding clusters among the population, and deciding how many interviewers are needed for the survey.

2. Conducting the survey includes the actual process in which interviewers visit houses and get information on the immunization status of the children or the clusters.

3. Data tabulation includes completing the cluster forms and summary forms that organize the data collected.

4. Analysis of the data procured occurs next which can evaluate immunization status and the reasons for immunization failure if any.

5. The last step includes taking action on the reports made by evaluating the data.

An immunization survey gives information on the total coverage of the population and areas where the immunization services can be improved. Actions can be done by increasing the immunization programs if the coverage is low or targeting a specific population or cluster to improve their immunization status.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions could be associated with a middle-aged man working in sandblasting who presents with hemoptysis, productive cough, and a chest X-ray suggestive of tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario of a sandblaster presenting with symptoms of tuberculosis (TB) is a classic association for silicosis (Option B). Inhalation of fine silica dust during sandblasting causes chronic pulmonary fibrosis. Crucially, silica is directly toxic to pulmonary macrophages, the body's primary defense against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Consequently, patients with silicosis have a significantly increased risk (roughly 30-fold) of developing tuberculosis, a condition known as silicotuberculosis. Asbestosis (Option A) is linked to construction and shipyard work and increases the risk of mesothelioma. Anthracosis (Option C) is "coal worker's pneumoconiosis" and is generally less fibrogenic. Siderosis (Option D) results from iron dust and is usually a benign, non-fibrotic condition. The pathognomonic X-ray finding in silicosis is "eggshell calcification" of hilar lymph nodes. Therefore, because of the specific occupational exposure and the established predisposition to TB, silicosis is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical scenario of a sandblaster presenting with symptoms of tuberculosis (TB) is a classic association for silicosis (Option B). Inhalation of fine silica dust during sandblasting causes chronic pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.text: The structure not passing through the aortic opening of the diaphragm is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vagal trunk

The vagal trunk does not pass through the aortic opening of the diaphragm.

It passes through the esophageal opening at the level of T10 vertebra.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: What is correct regarding transfusion of the blood received from blood bank?
options: It should be started within 4 hours of receiving it from the blood bank.
It should be completed within 4 hours of receiving from the blood bank.
No such time restraint and can be done anytime.
It should be completed within 6 hours of receiving from the blood bank.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It should be completed within 4 hours of receiving from the blood bank.

Blood received from blood bank should be completely transfused within 4 hours of receiving.

Principles of blood administration:

• All blood products should be given through an appropriate blood administration set containing a filter.
• A careful aseptic technique should be practised at all times.
• Vital signs should be documented before and after transfusion and as clinically required. For the first 15 minutes after the infusion has begun, the patient should be kept under close observation to detect any signs of a serious transfusion reaction. If none is observed, the infusion rate may be increased.
• One unit of red cells is often given in 1 to 4 hours, depending on the amount to be transfused and on the patient’s cardiovascular status. Infusion of a unit for longer than 4 hours is not recommended, as there is a risk of bacterial proliferation because the opened unit is at room temperature.
• No other solution and no medication should be added to or infused through the same tubing as a blood product.
• Ringer’s lactate or other solutions containing calcium must never be added to a blood product because the calcium present leads to coagulation.
• After the transfusion has been completed, the transfusion tag or record should become part of the patient’s chart.
questions.learning: It should be completed within 4 hours of receiving from the blood bank. Blood received from blood bank should be completely transfused within 4 hours of receiving.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with a long-standing history of diabetes is found to have cataract formation. Which metabolic by-product is mainly responsible for the development of cataracts in this condition?
questions.explanation: In patients with chronic diabetes, high blood glucose levels overwhelm the normal glycolytic pathway, leading to increased activity of the enzyme aldose reductase. This enzyme converts glucose into sorbitol via the polyol pathway. Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol that is poorly metabolized and slowly converted to fructose by sorbitol dehydrogenase in the lens. Consequently, sorbitol accumulates within the lens fibers. Because it is highly hygroscopic (osmotically active), it draws water into the lens, causing cellular swelling, oxidative stress, and the aggregation of crystallin proteins. This structural disruption results in the characteristic "snowflake" cataract of diabetes. Galactitol (Option B) is a similar osmotic product but is responsible for cataracts in patients with galactosemia, not diabetes. Fructose (Option D) is the end product of this pathway but does not cause osmotic damage. Thus, sorbitol is the primary metabolic culprit in diabetic cataractogenesis
questions.learning: In patients with chronic diabetes, high blood glucose levels overwhelm the normal glycolytic pathway, leading to increased activity of the enzyme aldose reductase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In the diagram showing the development of ovarian follicles, which structure is indicated at this stage of follicular progression?
questions.explanation: The diagram illustrates the sequential development of follicles within the ovary. The structure indicated by the arrow—characterized by a large, fluid-filled cavity—is an antral follicle (also known as a secondary or Graafian follicle) . This cavity, the antrum, is filled with follicular fluid containing high concentrations of hormones. Primordial follicles (Option C) are the quiescent microscopic clusters seen at the beginning of the cycle. Primary follicles (Option A) are slightly larger but lack an antrum. The corpus luteum (Option D) is the solid glandular structure that forms after ovulation occurs, visible in the "Luteal phase" section of the diagram. Because the visual shows a mature follicle containing an obvious central fluid space just prior to the ovulation marker, it is definitively the antral stage. Recognizing these stages is fundamental for understanding the hormonal regulation of the menstrual cycle
questions.learning: The diagram illustrates the sequential development of follicles within the ovary. The structure indicated by the arrow—characterized by a large, fluid-filled cavity—is an antral follicle (also known as a secondary or Graafian follicle) .

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not a symptom of severe dehydration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thirsty child

A thirsty child signifies some dehydration, not severe dehydration.

Clinical features of severe dehydration in a child include:

• Drowsy, lethargic, or unconscious, with deeply sunken eyes and absent tears
• Sunken fontanelle
• Drinks poorly or not able to drink
• Deep breathing
• Skin pinch goes back very slowly (recoil in >2 seconds)
• Tachycardia, with bradycardia in most severe cases
• Weak, thready, or impalpable pulse
• Prolonged capillary refill
• Cold, mottled, and cyanotic extremities
• Minimal urine output

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Observe the following curves, which of the following is a true statement about sensitivity and specificity when the curve changes from green to pink?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Both sensitivity and specificity increase

Both sensitivity and specificity are higher in the test represented in pink (Test B) compared to the test represented in green (Test A).

Sensitivity is the proportion of all people with the disease who test positive. It is the probability of the test being positive when the disease is present.

Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN) or Sensitivity = 1 – false-negative rate.

Specificity is the proportion of all people without the disease who test negative. It is the probability of the test being negative when the disease is absent.

Specificity= TN / (TN + FP) or specificity= 1 – false-positive rate.

Test B has an increased number of true positives and true negatives and decreased number of false positives and negatives, compared to Test A.

Hence leading to increased sensitivity and specificity.
questions.learning: Both sensitivity and specificity increase Both sensitivity and specificity are higher in the test represented in pink (Test B) compared to the test represented in green (Test A).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following best describes 'Neuropraxia'?
questions.explanation: Neuropraxia represents the mildest form of nerve injury according to Seddon's classification. It involves a temporary physiological conduction block caused by focal demyelination (damage to the nerve sheath) while the underlying axon remains completely intact. Because the axon is not severed, there is no Wallerian degeneration, and recovery is typically complete within six weeks once the sheath heals. Axonotmesis (Option B) involves a damaged axon within an intact connective tissue framework, leading to distal degeneration and a longer recovery period. Neurotmesis (Option C) is the most severe grade, characterized by complete disruption of both the axon and the supporting nerve sheaths; spontaneous recovery is impossible in these cases and surgical repair is mandated. Therefore, neuropraxia is specifically defined by the preservation of axonal continuity despite localized myelin dysfunction, leading to a favorable prognosis
questions.learning: Neuropraxia represents the mildest form of nerve injury according to Seddon's classification. It involves a temporary physiological conduction block caused by focal demyelination (damage to the nerve sheath) while the underlying axon remains completely intact.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. A diagnosis of fistula-in-ano is made. What is the gold standard investigation for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. MRI

In cases of fistula-in-ano, MRI is the gold standard investigation.

A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin, lined with granulation tissue. It may follow the drainage of a perianal abscess or may be seen in association with diseases like tuberculosis or Crohn's disease.

Clinical features are perianal pain, swelling, and intermittent purulent discharge, which might be blood-stained. On examination, one or more external openings may be visible.

Goodsall’s rule can be used as a guide in determining the location of the internal opening of the fistula. Fistulas with an external opening anteriorly connect to the internal opening by a short, radial tract. Fistulas with an external opening posteriorly track in a curvilinear fashion to the posterior midline.

However, exceptions to this rule often occur. Fistulas with an anterior external opening greater than 3 cm from the anal margin usually track to the posterior midline.

The investigations done for fistula-in-ano can include a fistulogram, endoanal ultrasound with hydrogen peroxide, MRI, and computed tomography (CT) scan. An MRI is the gold standard investigation for fistula imaging. It helps us to identify the secondary extensions of the track, which when missed may cause persistence of the fistula.

Surgical management includes fistulotomy, fistulectomy, ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), setons, or advancement flaps.
questions.learning: MRI — In cases of fistula-in-ano, MRI is the gold standard investigation. A fistula-in-ano is an abnormal connection between the anal canal and the perianal skin, lined with granulation tissue.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents since birth with ptosis and a right eye positioned in a “down and out” posture. Which cranial nerve palsy is most likely responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: The "down and out" eye position is the classic sign of an oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. CN III supplies the superior, inferior, and medial recti, as well as the inferior oblique. When these are paralyzed, the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) act unopposed, pulling the eye outward and downward. The accompanying ptosis results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris, also supplied by CN III. 4th nerve palsy (Option A) causes vertical diplopia and an "up and in" eye position. 6th nerve palsy (Option C) results in an "inward" deviation (esotropia) due to medial rectus action. 7th nerve palsy (Option D) affects facial expression and eye closure but not eye position. Thus, the "down and out" triad with ptosis confirms CN III involvement
questions.learning: The "down and out" eye position is the classic sign of an oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy. CN III supplies the superior, inferior, and medial recti, as well as the inferior oblique.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are the important parameters to be maintained in a patient with head trauma? 1. MAP 70–80 mm Hg 2. Intracranial pressure < 20 mm Hg 3. Cerebral perfusion pressure > 60 mm Hg 4. Na > 140 mEq/L Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

• In a patient with severe head trauma, the key goals are to maintain adequate cerebral perfusion and prevent secondary brain injury.
• The key targets shown for a head-injured patient in neurointensive care include: (Ref: Bailey-Love Surgery)

| Key parameters to maintain in head-injured patients in neurointensive care

| --------------------------------------------------------------------------

• PaCO₂ = 4.5–5.0 kPa
• PaO₂ > 11 kPa
• MAP = 80–90 mmHg
• ICP < 20 mmHg
• CPP > 60 mmHg
• [Na⁺] > 140 mmol/L
• [K⁺] > 4 mmol/L

High-yield:

• CPP = MAP − ICP.
• Maintaining adequate MAP while limiting ICP ensures sufficient cerebral perfusion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A female patient has a history of three miscarriages. Identify the investigation that was done from the image shown below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hysterosalpingography

The investigation shown in the given image is hysterosalpingography. The given hysterosalpingogram shows a unicornuate uterus.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is an imaging modality in which radiopaque contrast is injected through the cervical canal to assess the endometrial cavity, the fallopian tubes, and the endocervical canal.

HSG should be done between days 5 and 10 of the menstrual cycle, in the preovulatory phase, as an outpatient procedure. Leech Wilkinson cannula, Rubin's cannula, or Foley's catheter no.14 is introduced into the endometrial cavity through the cervical os, and the contrast is injected. The uterine cavity and fallopian tubes are then visualized and X-rays are obtained.

HSG can be used for the following:

• To assess tubal patency in infertility
• To detect uterine anomalies, synechiae, and polyps
• To detect incompetence of the cervical os

Contraindications to HSG:

• Acute pelvic infection
• Active uterine bleeding
• Pregnancy/ suspected pregnancy
• Contrast allergy
• Premenstrual phase

HSG is a safe procedure, however, complications such as ascending spread of infection, chemical peritonitis, allergic reaction to the dye, or pelvic endometriosis may occur.

Other options:

Option A: Hysteroscopy is an operative procedure in which the uterine cavity can be visualized by passing a fiberoptic telescope via the cervix. It can be diagnostic or therapeutic. A hysteroscopic image of a uterus with carcinoma is shown below.

Option B: Saline infusion sonography is a procedure where normal saline is injected into the uterine cavity and the uterus is imaged with transvaginal sonography. It is shown in the image below.

Option D: Transvaginal ultrasonography is a noninvasive imaging technique using the transvaginal approach. It provides a more detailed evaluation of the pelvic organs as compared to the transabdominal approach.
questions.learning: Hysterosalpingography — The investigation shown in the given image is hysterosalpingography. The given hysterosalpingogram shows a unicornuate uterus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 74-year-old man with congestive heart failure (CHF) on intravenous furosemide develops acute kidney injury (AKI) with serum creatinine rising from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. Laboratory findings show: Urine Na⁺: 45 mEq/L Urine creatinine: 55 mg/dL Which of the following tests best distinguishes prerenal azotemia from acute tubular necrosis (ATN) in the setting of diuretic use?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea)

In patients receiving loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), the fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) becomes unreliable because diuretics increase urinary sodium excretion.

In this setting, fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea) is preferred to distinguish:

• Prerenal azotemia → FeUrea < 35%
• Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) → FeUrea > 50%

Urea reabsorption occurs mainly in the proximal tubule and is less affected by diuretics, making FeUrea the best test to differentiate prerenal AKI from ATN when diuretics are used.
questions.learning: Fractional excretion of urea (FeUrea) — In patients receiving loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide), the fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) becomes unreliable because diuretics increase urinary sodium excretion.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman develops wheezing and breathlessness after taking aspirin for a headache. In addition to these symptoms, which other clinical features are most likely to be present in this condition?
questions.explanation: The patient is presenting with Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease (AERD), also known as Samter's Triad. This condition is defined by a characteristic clinical triad: Aspirin sensitivity, Asthma (manifesting as wheezing and breathlessness), and the presence of Nasal polyps. Therefore, finding a nasal polyp (Option B) is highly likely in this patient. AERD is not an IgE-mediated allergy (Option A); instead, it results from an imbalance in arachidonic acid metabolism, specifically an overproduction of leukotrienes when the COX-1 pathway is inhibited by aspirin. It is a form of intrinsic, not extrinsic (Option C), asthma. While this is a reaction to a drug, "Nasal polyp" is the specific clinical entity belonging to the diagnostic triad. On examination, these polyps are typically bilateral, pale, and insensitive to pain. Management involves a strict avoidance of NSAIDs, the use of leukotriene modifiers (like montelukast), and often surgical removal of the polyps if they cause significant nasal obstruction
