questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the surgical step shown in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Capsulorrhexis

Capsulorrhexis is the step shown in the given image.

Capsulorrhexis is a method of anterior capsulotomy, where an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens. It is one of the steps involved in conventional extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE).

Anterior capsulotomy can be done by one of three methods - can opener's technique, linear capsulotomy or envelope technique, or continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis.

Continuous curvilinear capsulorrhexis (CCC), is considered to be superior to all the preexisting methods because when done correctly, it does not leave any edges or tears. Trypan blue dye can be used to stain the lens capsule for better visibility.

In ECCE, a portion of the anterior capsule of the lens is removed, allowing extraction of the lens nucleus and cortex. This leaves the remainder of the anterior capsule, the posterior capsule, and the zonular support intact. The intact lens nucleus is then removed from the eye through a limbal incision.

An anterior capsulotomy is followed by hydro dissection using a balanced salt solution. This helps to separate the corticonuclear mass from the capsule. Removal of lens nucleus and aspiration of the cortex is done using a two-way irrigation and aspiration cannula. An intraocular lens (IOL) is then implanted and the incision is then closed.

Some of the IOLs used are shown in the image below.
questions.learning: Capsulorrhexis Capsulorrhexis is the step shown in the given image. Capsulorrhexis is a method of anterior capsulotomy, where an opening is made in the anterior capsule of the lens.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge?
questions.explanation: Intraductal papilloma is a benign tumor that forms within a milk duct and is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge. It typically presents in women aged 35–55 as a small, palpable lump near the nipple accompanied by clear or bloody discharge. Breast cancer (Option A) can also cause bloody discharge but is statistically less common than papilloma. Fibroadenoma (Option B) typically presents as a firm, painless, mobile mass in younger women and does not cause discharge. Duct ectasia (Option D) involves inflammation and dilation of the ducts; while it can cause greenish, blackish, or occasionally bloody discharge, it remains less frequent than papilloma. Diagnosis involves clinical examination, mammography, and biopsy to rule out malignancy. Management is usually surgical excision of the affected duct
questions.learning: Intraductal papilloma is a benign tumor that forms within a milk duct and is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge. It typically presents in women aged 35–55 as a small, palpable lump near the nipple accompanied by clear or bloody discharge.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl presents with primary amenorrhea. She has been reared as a female, shows no breast development, and ultrasonography reveals absence of the uterus. Karyotype analysis demonstrates a 46,XY chromosomal pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia that prevents the production of sex steroids (androgens and estrogens). In a 46 XY individual, the lack of testosterone results in female external genitalia, but the presence of anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) means the uterus is absent. Furthermore, the lack of estrogen prevents breast development. Swyer syndrome (Option C) would feature an XY karyotype but would have a uterus present because the streak gonads fail to produce AMH. MRKH syndrome (Option B) is 46 XX with normal breasts. Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (Option A) would show normal breast development due to the peripheral conversion of testosterone to estrogen. Thus, 17-hydroxylase deficiency is the only condition matching all findings
questions.learning: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency is a rare form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia that prevents the production of sex steroids (androgens and estrogens). In a 46 XY individual, the lack of testosterone results in female external genitalia, but the presence of…

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is punishable under the MTP Act?
options: Non-entry in MTP-register, not sending report to DDHS
questions.explanation: The MTP Act is a strictly regulated piece of legislation designed to provide safe and legal abortion services. Performing an MTP up to 24 weeks (Option A) for specified categories of women is legal. Performing it at an authorized center (Option B) by a qualified Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) (Option C) are the basic requirements for a legal termination. However, the Act also mandates strict administrative compliance. Failure to maintain the MTP register or failure to send the required monthly report to the Director of Health Services (DDHS) is a punishable offense. These administrative requirements are designed to prevent illegal or "back-alley" abortions and to ensure that all terminations are tracked for public health and safety purposes. Violations can lead to fines, imprisonment, and the closure of the facility. Maintaining confidentiality and proper documentation is a legal and ethical duty of the performing RMP
questions.learning: The MTP Act is a strictly regulated piece of legislation designed to provide safe and legal abortion services. Performing an MTP up to 24 weeks (Option A) for specified categories of women is legal.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient is brought to the casualty following a road traffic accident. On examination, the patient is conscious, BP is 90/60 mm Hg, respiratory rate is 40 breaths per minute, and pulse rate is 120 bpm. The X-ray is shown below. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chest tube insertion

The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax. The next best step in the management is chest tube insertion.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed while waiting for radiological confirmation. Imaging modalities used are ultrasound–extended focused assessment with sonar for trauma (eFAST), chest x-ray, and spiral CT.

A tension pneumothorax develops when there is a tear either in the parietal or visceral pleura. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e., air enters from the lung or chest wall through it during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration. This ultimately leads to the collapse of the affected lung.

It usually occurs following penetrating or blunt chest trauma, iatrogenic lung injury, or mechanical positive pressure ventilation.

It is characterized by:

• Chest pain
• Tachypnea and acute dyspnea
• Sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness)
• Neck vein distention
• Tracheal deviation away from the side of the injury
• Decreased chest movements on the affected side
• Hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side
• Absence or decreased breath sounds on the affected side

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing to the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Management of tension pneumothorax:

• Immediate management- needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line
• Definitive management- tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety, identified as a triangle that lies anterior to the midaxillary line above the nipple, below, and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

The images below show the triangle of safety and technique of chest drain insertion.

Other options:

• Pericardiocentesis is done in cases of cardiac tamponade which is characterized by the presence of hypotension, distended jugular veins, and muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad). The breath sounds are absent in tension pneumothorax while they are present in cardiac tamponade.
• Surgery for pneumothorax can be performed by video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or as an open procedure (thoracotomy) in cases of spontaneous pneumothorax failing to settle despite chest drainage. Pleural adhesion is achieved by chemical pleurodesis where talc is used and is insufflated into the chest cavity.
questions.learning: Chest tube insertion — The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The life cycle given below is of which of the following:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Entamoeba histolytica

The given life cycle is of Entamoeba histolytica.

Its life cycle includes 2 stages - the motile trophozoite and the non-motile cyst, both of which are seen in the image shown above. The transmission is primarily by the fecal-oral route. There is no animal reservoir. The most frequent site of systemic disease is the liver.

The ingested cysts differentiate into trophozoites in the ileum which invade the colonic epithelium. The trophozoites penetrate the submucosal layer and form abscesses which break down to form flask-shaped ulcers.

The trophozoites multiply by binary fission and produce cysts, and both stages are passed in the feces. Trophozoites are rapidly destroyed outside the body. Cysts survive in the external environment and are responsible for transmission.

Note: The genus Entamoeba has four morphologically identical species - E. histolytica, E. dispar, E. bangladeshi, and E. moshkovskii. E. moshkovskii which was initially thought to be non-pathogenic has recently been shown to be a causative agent of non-invasive diarrhea.
questions.learning: Entamoeba histolytica — The given life cycle is of Entamoeba histolytica. Its life cycle includes 2 stages - the motile trophozoite and the non-motile cyst, both of which are seen in the image shown above.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: On centrifugation of a cell, LDH will get deposited in the __? LDH- Lactate Dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cytoplasm

On centrifugation of a cell , the cell organelles can be seperated and then detected by specific marker enzymes. LDH is a marker enzyme of cytoplasm and hence will get deposited in the cytoplasm itself. LDH levels in cytoplasm are clinically significant as they leak into plasma whenever there is cell damage or necrosis, making it a useful diagnostic marker.

Other options:

Option A) Mitochondria are organelles responsible for cellular respiration and energy production. They contain enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle) and the electron transport chain. LDH is primarily found in the cytoplasm, not within mitochondria. While some LDH isoforms have been reported in the mitochondria of certain cell types, the bulk of LDH activity is in the cytoplasm.

Option B) Lysosomes are membrane-bound organelles containing various hydrolytic enzymes involved in cellular digestion and waste processing. LDH is not typically found in lysosomes.

Option D) Proteins and fats are sorted, altered, and packaged for transportation by the Golgi complex, also known as the Golgi apparatus.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used to describe the period between the entry of an organism into the human body and the point of its maximum infectivity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Generation time

Generation time is defined as the interval between the entry of an infectious agent into the host and the point at which the host reaches maximum infectivity.

It reflects the speed with which an infection can spread in a population and is especially important in epidemic modeling.

Generation time helps in:

In contrast, the incubation period measures time to symptom onset, while the serial interval refers to time between successive cases.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A child with a history of intubation presented to the OPD with shortness of breath while playing, approximately six weeks later. X-ray finding is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute laryngotracheobronchitis

The diagnosis in this child with a history of intubation and shortness of breath with X-ray showing the 'steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing is acute laryngotracheobronchitis.

Acute laryngotracheobronchitis is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months to 6 years. The clinical features include barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and low-grade fever.

Management:

* Racemic epinephrine nebulization rapidly improves upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway oedema.

* Dexamethasone is administered by the least invasive route (Oral > IV > IM ) for all grades of croup.

* Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %).

Antibiotics are not indicated in acute laryngotracheobronchitis.

Other options:

Option A: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency presenting in children with a rapidly progressive course of fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and respiratory obstruction, followed by a toxic appearance and drooling. The neck is hyperextended and stridor is a late finding. Radiography shows a classic thumb sign as given in the image below.

Option C: In children with acute bronchitis, chest radiographs typically show minimal to non-specific findings. The most common radiological features include hyperinflation of lung fields, indicating air trapping and bronchial wall thickening.

Option D: Laryngomalacia is a congenital laryngeal anomaly presenting in children with low-pitched inspiratory stridor exacerbated by exertion. The laryngoscopy image showing omega-shaped epiglottis is given below.

Pearl PF0104: Acute stridor/ Noisy breathing

Stridor indicates an upper airway problem. Look for a history of foreign body aspiration and signs of toxicity.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents to the dermatology outpatient department with the skin condition shown. Based on her pregnancy status and the clinical appearance, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, which is the pathognomonic presentation of Chloasma (Option D). Also known as melasma or the "mask of pregnancy," it is a common physiological skin change occurring in up to 70% of pregnant women. It is caused by the stimulatory effect of pregnancy hormones (estrogen, progesterone, and MSH) on melanocytes, exacerbated by sun exposure. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A) presents with a "malar rash" that is typically erythematous and spares the nasolabial folds, unlike the brown pigmentation seen here. Viral infections (Option B) and rosacea (Option C) would present with redness, pustules, or systemic symptoms rather than isolated pigmentation. Therefore, chloasma is the most probable diagnosis. It is benign and usually fades after delivery as hormone levels normalize
questions.learning: The clinical image shows blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, which is the pathognomonic presentation of Chloasma (Option D).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 55-year-old man with hypertension is prescribed verapamil. Which skeletal muscle feature explains its resistance to this medication?
options: Little dependence on extracellular calcium influx
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Little dependence on extracellular calcium influx

Skeletal muscle contraction is relatively resistant to calcium channel blockers such as verapamil because it relies primarily on intracellular calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum rather than extracellular calcium influx. In contrast, cardiac and smooth muscle require extracellular calcium entry through L-type calcium channels, making them sensitive to calcium channel blockade.

• In skeletal muscle, depolarization of the T-tubule activates the dihydropyridine receptor (DHPR).
• DHPR is mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
• This direct coupling triggers massive calcium release from intracellular stores.
• Therefore, skeletal muscle contraction has minimal dependence on extracellular calcium influx, explaining its resistance to verapamil.

Why not the others?

• A. Calmodulin-independent excitation-contraction coupling → True for skeletal muscle, but this does not explain resistance to calcium channel blockers.
• B. Decreased troponin affinity to calcium → Not the mechanism responsible for verapamil resistance.
• C. Elaborate T-tubular system → Facilitates excitation-contraction coupling but does not explain the lack of dependence on extracellular calcium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A drowsy man was brought to the casualty with minimal response. He had a progressive history of weakness of the body for 2 days. A CT scan was taken which is shown below. Which vessel is likely to be thrombosed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Middle cerebral artery

The middle cerebral artery supplies the entire motor area except for the leg area. Thus, a lesion in the middle cerebral artery causes contralateral hemiparesis, sparing the leg area.

Anterior cerebral artery:

* It is the smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.

* It runs in the sagittal fissure and anastomoses with the posterior cerebral artery.

* It supplies the medial surface of the cerebral cortex and parts of lentiform, caudate nuclei, and the internal capsule.

Middle cerebral artery:

* It is the larger terminal branch of the internal carotid artery.

* It runs in the lateral sulcus.

* It supplies the entire lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere except for a narrow strip (supplied by the anterior cerebral artery) and the occipital pole and the inferolateral surface (supplied by the posterior cerebral artery).

Posterior cerebral artery:

* It is the terminal branch of the basilar artery.

* It supplies the occipital lobe, inferolateral and medial surfaces of the temporal lobe, and parts of the brainstem.
questions.learning: Middle cerebral artery — The middle cerebral artery supplies the entire motor area except for the leg area. Thus, a lesion in the middle cerebral artery causes contralateral hemiparesis, sparing the leg area.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young patient presents with a large retroperitoneal hemorrhage. He also gives a frequent history of intermittent swelling of knees on strenuous exercise. There is no history of any mucosal bleed. Which among the following clotting factors is responsible for the above-mentioned condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Factors VIII and IX

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario hemophilia A. The clotting factors responsible for the above-mentioned condition are factors VIII and IX.

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. It occurs due to a deficiency of clotting factor VIII, which causes inadequate thrombin generation and results in the inability to form a tight fibrin clot to support the platelet plug.

Symptoms include easy bruising, intramuscular hematomas, hemarthroses, hematuria, and bleeding from minor traumatic lacerations of the mouth can persist for hours or days. Retroperitoneal hemorrhages can accumulate large volumes of blood and may cause a hypovolemic shock.

Laboratory findings in hemophilia A:

• Factor VIII - reduced
• Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) - prolonged
• Platelet count - normal
• Bleeding time - normal
• Prothrombin time - normal

Mild cases of hemophilia are treated by the administration of desmopressin acetate. Moderate to severe cases need the replacement of deficient clotting factors (factor VIII in hemophilia A). Monoclonal antibody emicizumab can restore activated factor VIII activity in patients with hemophilia.

Other options:

Option B: Factors XI and XII - Deficiencies of these factors are not associated with the clinical presentation described in the question. Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) can cause mild bleeding disorders, but it is generally not associated with severe hemorrhages or joint swelling. Factor XII deficiency is typically asymptomatic and not associated with bleeding disorders.

Option C: Von Willebrand factor - A deficiency in von Willebrand factor results in von Willebrand disease, which can cause excessive bleeding similar to hemophilia. However, von Willebrand disease usually presents with mucosal bleeding (e.g., epistaxis, menorrhagia, and gum bleeding), which is not described in this case.

Option D: Lupus anticoagulant - This is an acquired condition seen in antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS), which can cause thrombotic events rather than bleeding. It is not associated with retroperitoneal hemorrhage or joint swelling upon strenuous exercise.
questions.learning: Factors VIII and IX — The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario hemophilia A. The clotting factors responsible for the above-mentioned condition are factors VIII and IX.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a true statement regarding telomerase?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Involved in DNA repair

The false statement is that telomerase is involved in DNA repair.

Telomeres are the end of chromosomal DNA. Since prokaryotic DNA is circular, it does not have free ends and hence no telomeres. Thus, telomeres are present only in eukaryotes  Telomeres have TG- rich repeats and usually do not code for any proteins. With every DNA replication during cell division, telomere shortening occurs. Once telomeres are almost negligible or non-existent in length, the DNA is unable to replicate and the cell dies. Hence, there is a limit to the number of times a cell can divide.

In stem cells and cancer cells, an enzyme telomerase having reverse transcriptase activity (RNA dependent DNA polymerase) adds telomeres to the chromosome ends, thereby preserving chromosomal length. It allows the stem cells and cancer cells to multiply a lot more number of times than a normal adult cell.
questions.learning: Involved in DNA repair — The false statement is that telomerase is involved in DNA repair. Telomeres are the end of chromosomal DNA.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient on follow-up for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) undergoes endoscopy, which reveals a nodule in the second part of the duodenum. Elevation of which hormone is most likely suspected in this case?
questions.explanation: A nodule in the second part of the duodenum in a patient with GERD symptoms raises strong suspicion for a gastrinoma, the hallmark of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Gastrinomas are neuroendocrine tumors that secrete excessive amounts of the hormone gastrin. This hypergastrinemia leads to massive gastric acid secretion, resulting in severe gastroesophageal reflux disease and refractory peptic ulcers. The "Gastrinoma Triangle" includes the junction of the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum, where such nodules are frequently located. Inulin (Option B) is not a hormone but a marker used to measure glomerular filtration rate. VIP (Option C) is elevated in VIPomas, which cause watery diarrhea and achlorhydria rather than acid hypersecretion. Glucagon (Option D) is raised in pancreatic glucagonomas, presenting with diabetes and skin rashes. Therefore, given the specific location of the nodule and the presence of GERD, gastrin is the definitive hormone suspected to be elevated
questions.learning: A nodule in the second part of the duodenum in a patient with GERD symptoms raises strong suspicion for a gastrinoma, the hallmark of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with a hypopigmented lesion on his back. On examination, there is a complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensation over the lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hansen's disease

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy/ Hansen's disease.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve, followed by the ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion, which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule.

Ridley-Jopling classification of leprosy:

*

* Tuberculoid (TT)

* Borderline tubercular (BT)

* Borderline (BB)

* Borderline lepromatous (BL)

* Lepromatous (LL)

Indeterminate (IL)

One or a few hypopigmented or faintly erythematous, ill-defined to well-defined macular lesions with mild to moderate impairment of touch and/or thermal sensations. No thickening of peripheral nerves.

Borderline tuberculoid (BT)

Macular or plaque-type lesions numbering three to nine or more and asymmetrically located on any part of the body, with variable sizes and contours. Satellite lesions may be present. Loss of sensation is less intense than it is in TT lesions.

Several peripheral nerves are likely to be enlarged in an asymmetrical pattern, with sensory and motor deficits. Increased susceptibility to develop Type 1 leprosy reaction.

Tuberculoid (TT)
Well-defined, hypopigmented macule or as a raised, erythematous/brown/copper-colored plaque with a well-defined edge up to three in number.

Complete loss of fine touch and temperature sensations over the lesion.

Larger corresponding cutaneous nerves are thickened in a limited number of case

Mid-borderline (BB)

An unstable form of leprosy. Multiple plaque lesions and macular lesions; lesions are of various shapes and sizes, are bilateral, and usually occur in a more or less symmetrical. Minimal loss of sensation over the lesions.

Many nerves may be thickened, and this effect may be asymmetrical.

Borderline lepromatous (BL)

Numerous bilateral, round or oval, macular, diffusely infiltrated, erythematous, or hypopigmented lesions with moderately defined borders. Some loss of sensation may be detected, particularly over older lesions.

Widespread but asymmetrical thickening of peripheral nerves

Lepromatous (LL)

Innumerable bilateral, symmetrically distributed, diffusely indurated, erythematous, copper-colored, or skin-colored patches or plaques. There is no loss of sensation over these lesions.

Bilateral earlobe thickening and eyebrow loss occur. Coarse induration on the face gives rise to leonine facies.

Involvement of peripheral nerves occurs late and is bilateral and symmetrical, with sensory loss in a “glove-and-stocking” distribution.

Cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy:

* Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.

* Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.

* Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases with low bacterial load.
questions.learning: Hansen's disease — The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy/ Hansen's disease. Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Longest lag period in bacterial growth is associated with:
questions.explanation: The term “lag period” in this context refers to the delay before observable antibacterial effect occurs after drug exposure. Among anti-tubercular drugs, Ethambutol is a bacteriostatic agent that inhibits arabinogalactan synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall. Unlike bactericidal drugs, it does not rapidly kill bacteria, but rather slows their growth. Because of this mechanism, the onset of its visible effect is delayed, producing the longest lag period among the listed drugs. Ethambutol primarily prevents multiplication rather than causing immediate bacterial death, so cultures may take longer to show a decline in bacterial load. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Rifampicin: Rapidly bactericidal; acts on RNA synthesis → quicker effect (B) INH: Strong early bactericidal activity → minimal lag (C) Streptomycin: Bactericidal against actively dividing bacilli → faster action

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In an experimental study, norepinephrine was administered to guinea pigs, leading to an increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure along with a reduction in heart rate. Which physiological mechanism best explains this response?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine (NE) is a potent -adrenergic agonist that causes widespread vasoconstriction, leading to a significant increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Although NE also stimulates -receptors in the heart (which would normally increase heart rate), the rapid rise in systemic blood pressure stretches the baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. This baroreceptor stimulation triggers a reflex vagal (parasympathetic) response from the medulla, which overrides the direct cardiac effect and causes a compensatory decrease in heart rate (reflex bradycardia). Option A and B are incorrect because NE is an agonist, not a blocker. Baroreceptor inhibition (Option D) would result in a faster heart rate due to a loss of parasympathetic tone. Thus, the paradox of increased blood pressure coupled with a decreased heart rate is entirely explained by the baroreceptor reflex
questions.learning: Norepinephrine (NE) is a potent -adrenergic agonist that causes widespread vasoconstriction, leading to a significant increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure.

Lab investigations in vitamin D-dependent rickets will reveal normal/decreased serum calcium, decreased phosphorous, elevated PTH, and increased ALP levels.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 is due to 1 α hydroxylase deficiency resulting in decreased hydroxylation of 25 hydroxy vitamin D leading to increased levels of 25 OH vitamin D and decreased levels of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 is due to the resistance of the vitamin D receptors to vitamin D in both bone and intestine. Here, the levels of 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D are raised, but despite this, the serum calcium and phosphate levels are low due to the lack of action of vitamin D.

Decreased vitamin D leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased PTH production. PTH tries to normalise the calcium and further decreases the phosphate because of renal elimination. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH) occurs because of a defect in the PHEX gene. Since the PHEX gene is responsible for inactivating FGF-23, there is an increased FGF-23 in XLH. Increased FGF-23 inhibits phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney and causes phosphaturia. It also inhibits 1-α-hydroxylase, leading to decreased production of activated vitamin D.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following regulate body temperature?
questions.explanation: The Hypothalamus serves as the body's master thermostat and primary center for thermoregulation. It contains specialized thermosensitive neurons that monitor both the core blood temperature and signals from peripheral skin receptors. The anterior (preoptic) hypothalamus primarily coordinates heat loss mechanisms, such as sweating and vasodilation, while the posterior hypothalamus coordinates heat conservation and production mechanisms, such as shivering and vasoconstriction. Basal ganglia (Option B) are involved in motor control and habit formation. The thalamus (Option C) acts as a major relay station for sensory information to the cortex. The limbic system (Option D) is primarily responsible for emotional processing and memory. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic set-point is the physiological basis of fever, where cytokines induce prostaglandin E2 production, leading the hypothalamus to perceive normal core temperatures as cold and initiating heat-generating responses. This regulatory function is critical for maintaining metabolic homeostasis within a narrow temperature range
questions.learning: The Hypothalamus serves as the body's master thermostat and primary center for thermoregulation. It contains specialized thermosensitive neurons that monitor both the core blood temperature and signals from peripheral skin receptors.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Based on the clinical image shown, which nerve is most likely involved?
questions.explanation: The provided clinical image shows "winging of the scapula," where the medial border of the scapula protrudes abnormally from the back. This condition is caused by paralysis of the serratus anterior muscle, which is specifically innervated by the long thoracic nerve (C5-C7). The long thoracic nerve is vulnerable to injury due to its long, superficial course along the lateral thoracic wall, often during radical mastectomy or trauma. Paralysis of the serratus anterior prevents the scapula from being held against the rib cage and severely impairs the patient's ability to abduct the arm above the horizontal plane. The thoracodorsal nerve (Option A) innervates the latissimus dorsi, and its injury would weaken arm extension. The axillary nerve (Option B) supplies the deltoid, leading to loss of rounded shoulder contour. The intercostal nerves (Option C) supply the thoracic wall muscles. Therefore, the pathognomonic finding of scapular winging confirms long thoracic nerve injury

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A healthy couple's first child has nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets. During preconception counseling, they ask the recurrence risk for the next child. The risk can be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Can’t say

• Nutritional vitamin D deficiency is an environmental disorder, not a Mendelian genetic disease.
• Therefore, there is no fixed genetic recurrence risk.
• Adequate maternal vitamin D supplementation prevents recurrence.
• Infant vitamin D prophylaxis is recommended.
• Exclusive breastfeeding without supplementation increases risk.
• Sunlight exposure also contributes to prevention.
• Genetic forms (vitamin D–dependent rickets) have defined inheritance patterns.
• This question specifically refers to vitamin D deficiency rickets.
• Hence recurrence is preventable rather than inherited.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In which class of shock is there an initial decrease in urine output?
questions.explanation: In the clinical classification of hemorrhagic shock, Class III shock is considered moderate shock. It is typically associated with 30–40% blood loss. At this stage, compensatory mechanisms such as tachycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction become inadequate to maintain effective organ perfusion. A key and early physiological marker of moderate (Class III) shock is a significant decrease in urine output (oliguria, usually <30 mL/hour), reflecting reduced renal blood flow and the onset of systemic hypoperfusion. In mild or compensated shock (Class I–II), renal perfusion is generally preserved, and urine output remains near normal. In contrast, severe shock (Class IV), with >40% blood loss, is characterized by minimal or absent urine output (anuria) due to profound circulatory collapse. Thus, the initial decrease in urine output is most characteristic of moderate (Class III) shock, making Option B the correct answer
questions.learning: In the clinical classification of hemorrhagic shock, Class III shock is considered moderate shock. It is typically associated with 30–40% blood loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a known history of rheumatic heart disease is found on imaging to have an aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: A coronary artery aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm (10–20 mm) is classified as a large aneurysm. Such lesions carry a high risk of complications, including intraluminal thrombosis and distal embolization, which can lead to myocardial infarction. The standard of care for long-term thrombotic risk reduction in these patients is lifelong low-dose aspirin therapy. Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with Clopidogrel (Option B) is typically reserved for acute coronary syndromes or giant aneurysms rather than stable large ones. A 3-week course of aspirin (Option C) is insufficient because the risk of clot formation persists as long as the aneurysm is present. IV antibiotics (Option D) are only indicated if there is evidence of an infected (mycotic) aneurysm or active endocarditis. Thus, permanent antiplatelet protection is the cornerstone of management
questions.learning: A coronary artery aneurysm measuring 1–2 cm (10–20 mm) is classified as a large aneurysm. Such lesions carry a high risk of complications, including intraluminal thrombosis and distal embolization, which can lead to myocardial infarction.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young sexually active female patient presented to the outpatient department with complaints of lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. On examination, the body temperature is 103 degrees Fahrenheit, pulse rate is 109 per minute and there is abdominal tenderness. Cervical motion tenderness is present on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic inflammatory disease

The likely diagnosis in this patient is pelvic inflammatory disease(PID).

Pelvic inflammatory disease is characterized by inflammation of the upper genital tract including the fallopian tubes as well as the ovaries. This disease is commonly seen in sexually active young women and is usually preceded by a sexually transmitted disease. Gonococcal and chlamydial infections are commonly associated with PID.

Patients present with lower abdominal pain, fever, vomiting, dysuria, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and vaginal discharge. The symptoms also vary depending on the causative organism. On examination, there is a fever of around 103- 104°F, abdominal tenderness, tachycardia, and pelvic mass. Chronic PID is associated with sequelae such as chronic pelvic pain, menorrhagia, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility.

Acute PID is diagnosed if uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness, or cervical motion tenderness is present and other etiologies are excluded or unlikely. One or more of the following can be used to diagnose PID on the clinical findings:

* Oral temperature >38.3°C (101.6°F),

* Mucopurulent cervical discharge or cervical friability,

* Abundant WBCs on saline microscopy of cervical secretions,

* Elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP), and

* Presence of cervical N gonorrhea or C trachomatis

Depending on the extent of tissue involved, PID can be classified into five stages

Stage I
Acute salpingitis without peritonitis - No adhesions

Stage II
Acute salpingitis with peritonitis - purulent discharge

Stage III
Acute salpingitis with superimposed tubal occlusion or tubo ovarian complex

Stage IV
Ruptured tuba ovarian abscess

Stage V
Tubercular salpingitis

Other complications of chronic pelvic inflammatory disease:

* Hydrosalpinx

* Chronic pyosalpinx

* Chronic interstitial salpingitis

* Tubo ovarian cyst

Other options:

Option B: Endometriosis is a condition characterized by ectopic benign endometrial tissue that occurs outside the uterine cavity. Patients present with dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, menorrhagia, and infertility. There is no foul-smelling vaginal discharge or fever hence this option is incorrect.

Option C: Adenomyosis is seen in multiparous women >40 years. The most common symptom involves menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea. Per-Vaginal examination reveals symmetrical enlargement of the uterus corresponding to <12 weeks of pregnancy.

Option D: Migrating abdominal pain from the periumbilical area to the right iliac fossa is classic for appendicitis. The abdominal pain also causes nausea and vomiting. Other nonspecific signs of appendicitis include low-grade fever, abdominal tenderness, guarding, and rebound tenderness.

Pearl PF1533: Organisms Responsible for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease

Sexually transmitted: Gonococcus, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Trichomonas
Aerobes: Staphylococci , Streptococci ,E. coli

Anaerobes: Bacteroides fragilis, Peptococcus, Clostridium, Actinomyces (IUD)

Others: Tubercular salpingitis
questions.learning: Pelvic inflammatory disease — The likely diagnosis in this patient is pelvic inflammatory disease(PID). Pelvic inflammatory disease is characterized by inflammation of the upper genital tract including the fallopian tubes as well as the ovaries.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A cancer patient undergoing radiotherapy is given a dose of 1.8 to 2 Gy once daily for 5 days per week for a duration of 6 to 8 weeks. What is this type of brachytherapy called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Regular Fractionated radiotherapy

Since the patient is given a dose of 1.8-2.0 Gy per day for 5 days a week, for 6 to 8 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

Radiotherapy:

The total dose of radiation needed for a tumor is usually given as fractions over the entire treatment period as it maximizes the effects of the radiation on the malignant cells and minimizes the damage to the healthy cells.

The reasons for this are due to :

1. Re-distribution: Cells are more resistant to damage in the late S2 phase while sensitive in the M and G2 phase. Only some tumor cells will be in the sensitive phase of the cell cycle when the radiation is given. Hence, giving another dose at a later time helps in killing the other cells that were in the resistant part of the cell cycle, thus increasing the success rate of the therapy.

2. Re-oxygenation: Hypoxic cells are less sensitive to the indirect effects of radiation. The tumor cells which are closer to oxygen sources are killed first and in the intervening time, the other relatively hypoxic cells can improve their oxygenation so that the next fraction of radiation is effective on them.

3. Repair: The ability to repair DNA is more for healthy cells than malignant cells and thus when a radiation dose has been received, the healthy cells repair their DNA faster than the malignant cells. The malignant cells whose DNA is not fully repaired are highly susceptible to the next dose of radiation.

Types of fractionation:

Standard Fractionation: Radiotherapy(RT) is given once daily for 5 days/week, not more than 2 Gy/fraction.

Accelerated Fractionation:(Option C) Any fractionation schedule that gives >10 Gy/week. Subtypes include:

* Pure accelerated fractionation (2 Gy/fraction, 6–7 fractions/week)

* Accelerated hypofractionation (>3 Gy/fraction)

* Accelerated hyperfractionation (>1 fraction/day)

Hypofractionation: Increased fraction size, with or without a decreased number of fractions/week.

* Stereotactic Radiation (SRS/SBRT/SABR): RT delivered with stereotactic localization techniques in five fractions or less.

* Fractionated Stereotactic RT (FSRT): RT delivered with stereotactic techniques and more than five fractions.

Hyperfractionation: Decreased fraction size with more than one fraction per day (BID or TID). (Option B)

Concomitant Boost (CB): Two fractions per day with one fraction to a large field and the other to a boost volume.

Simultaneous Integrated Boost (SIB): One fraction per day with a higher dose to a boost volume and a lower dose to the large field.

Note: Brachytherapy(Option D) is a method of treatment in which sealed radioactive sources are used to deliver radiation at a short distance by interstitial, intracavitary, or surface application.
questions.learning: Regular Fractionated radiotherapy Since the patient is given a dose of 1.8-2.0 Gy per day for 5 days a week, for 6 to 8 weeks, it is called Regular/Conventional Fractionated Radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman who presented to the clinic with a lump in her right breast is diagnosed to have breast carcinoma. All of the following are favorable prognostic markers except ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Her2 overexpression

The clinical scenario explains breast carcinoma and HER2 overexpression is associated with poor survival.

The main importance of HER2 status is as a predictor of response to agents that target this receptor. Luminal A subtype i.e well-differentiated, ER-positive, HER2-negative, and low proliferation, has the most favorable prognosis.

The proliferative rate can be measured by mitotic counts or by immunohistochemical detection of Ki67 proteins. Carcinomas with high proliferation rates have a poorer prognosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not a characteristic of the inactive phase of otosclerosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Excessive osteoclast activity

Otosclerosis has two histopathological phases: Active (otospongiosis) and inactive (sclerotic) phase.

Inactive (sclerotic) phase features

• Dense, sclerotic, mineralized bone
• Minimal bone remodeling
• Hypocellular, avascular bone
• Replacement of earlier spongy bone with hard sclerotic bone

Excessive osteoclast activity is NOT seen in the inactive phase as it is a feature of the active otospongiotic phase, where bone resorption and vascular spongy bone formation occur.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following pathogens is least likely to be responsible for causing croup?
questions.explanation: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) is a common viral respiratory illness in children characterized by a "barking" cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness. The most common and classic causes are the Parainfluenza viruses, with Parainfluenza type 1 (Option A) being the leading cause, followed by Parainfluenza type 2 (Option B) and type 3. Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) (Option D) is also a significant cause of croup, particularly in infants, though it more famously causes bronchiolitis. Rhinovirus (Option C) is the primary cause of the common cold (acute nasopharyngitis); while it can cause upper respiratory infections, it is least likely to cause the specific subglottic swelling and stridor that define croup. Other occasional causes include influenza and adenovirus. In exams, Parainfluenza is the "always" answer for croup etiology, and Rhinovirus is the "always" answer for the common cold. Therefore, Rhinovirus is the correct outlier for this condition
questions.learning: Croup (Laryngotracheobronchitis) is a common viral respiratory illness in children characterized by a "barking" cough, inspiratory stridor, and hoarseness.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a class of 100 students, 80% are immunized against measles. Despite this, 12 students develop the disease. What is the secondary attack rate in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The secondary attack rate (SAR) measures the spread of a disease among susceptible individuals following exposure to a primary case. It is calculated as the number of secondary cases divided by the total number of susceptible individuals, multiplied by 100. In this scenario, out of 100 students, 80% are immunized, meaning 80 students are protected and 20% (20 students) are susceptible. Given that 12 students were affected (secondary cases), the calculation is , which equals 60%. Option B (80%) refers to the immunization coverage rather than the attack rate. Option C (70%) and Option D (50%) are mathematically incorrect based on the provided data. SAR is a critical epidemiological tool used to assess the infectivity of a pathogen and the effectiveness of control measures like vaccines in a community setting. Thus, 60% accurately represents the transmission rate among the vulnerable population in this class
questions.learning: The secondary attack rate (SAR) measures the spread of a disease among susceptible individuals following exposure to a primary case. It is calculated as the number of secondary cases divided by the total number of susceptible individuals, multiplied by 100.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy had received a full course rabies vaccine taken in December 2018. His pet dog which has been fully vaccinated now (November 2019) bit him on the toe. Bleeding was present at the site of the bite. What would be the line of treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2 doses of vaccine on Day 0 & 3

This boy should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

Management of a new dog bite in a previously immunized individual with either pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) or post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is as follows:

• Category I: Wound treatment only
• Category II/ III:

• Wound treatment with soap and running water for 15 min and apply antiseptic
• Receive Anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) 2 doses ID (0.1 ml, 1 site)/ 2 doses IM (1 VIAL, 1 site) on days 0 and 3.

*Note: In developing countries like India, the vaccination status of animals alone, doesn't play a significant role in determining the initiation of prophylaxis in humans.
questions.learning: 2 doses of vaccine on Day 0 & 3 This boy should receive 2 doses of vaccine on days 0 & 3 as he has received a prior course of post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) > 3 months ago.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent abdominal pain and a history of blood in stools. On examination, there are dark pigmented spots on his lips and oral mucosa. Endoscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome

Classic Triad of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome

1. Hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine (especially jejunum)

2. Mucocutaneous pigmentation

• Dark spots on lips
• Oral mucosa
• Perioral skin

3. Adolescent onset with GI bleeding or abdominal pain

These findings together are diagnostic of PJS.

The hamartomatous polyps can cause:

• GI bleeding
• Recurrent abdominal pain
• Intussusception (very common complication in PJS)

The pigmentation occurs due to melanin deposition in mucocutaneous areas.

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is caused by mutation in the: STK11 (LKB1) tumor suppressor gene

Inheritance pattern: Autosomal dominant.

A) Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP)

• Caused by APC gene mutation
• Hundreds to thousands of adenomatous polyps
• No mucocutaneous pigmentation

C) Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome

• Hamartomatous polyps but mainly in colon
• No characteristic mucocutaneous pigmentation

D) Cronkhite–Canada Syndrome

• Non-hereditary
• Occurs in older adults
• Associated with alopecia, nail changes, and diarrhea
questions.learning: Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome Classic Triad of Peutz–Jeghers Syndrome 1. Hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine (especially jejunum) 2.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the most common defect in a ventricular septal defect?
options: Non-development of the perimembranous part of the septum
questions.explanation: The most common type of ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the membranous (or perimembranous) defect, accounting for approximately 80% of all cases. These defects occur in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, located below the crista supraventricularis. Muscular (trabecular) defects (Option A) are also common, particularly in infants, and may present as multiple defects known as "Swiss cheese" VSDs; they have a high rate of spontaneous closure. Inlet defects (Option C) represent about 8% of all VSDs and are frequently associated with Trisomy 21. Outlet or infundibular defects (Option D) are located below the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary) within the outlet septum of the right ventricle. VSDs generally result from the incomplete development or fusion of various septal components during embryonic cardiac formation. While muscular defects are prevalent, the membranous type remains the most frequently encountered in clinical practice and carries a high potential for spontaneous closure

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient, 36 hours after cataract surgery, presents with complaints of pain and visual disturbance. His eye is as shown below. What is the management of this condition?
options: Bandage and padding of the eye
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intravitreal antibiotics

A post cataract surgery patient presenting within 36 hours of surgery with inflammation, congestion and hypopyon as seen in the image, is suggestive of acute bacterial endophthalmitis. The treatment of acute bacterial endophthalmitis is intravitreal antibiotics.

Endophthalmitis is an intraocular inflammation affecting the inner structures of the eyeball. Acute postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis occurs within 1-7 days after cataract surgery and the most important factor to prevent it is preoperative administration of 5% povidone iodine. The cardinal features of endophthalmitis are pain, swelling of the lid, and a decrease in vision. The patient classically shows inflammation of the eye, corneal edema and a hypopyon due to the pouring of exudates in the vitreous cavity, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber.

Once the endophthalmitis sets in it is important to treat all the cases empirically with a combination of antibiotics and steroids from the beginning. The various drugs, routes and surgical management used to treat endophthalmitis are as follows:

1. The mainstay of treatment is intravitreal injections of antibiotics.

• First choice: Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus ceftazidime 2.25mg in 0.1ml.
• Second choice:Vancomycin 1 mg in 0.1 mL plus amikacin 0.4mg in 0.1ml.
• If there is no improvement, a repeat intravitreal injection should be given after 48 hours

2. Topical antibiotics are started immediately and used frequently.

• Vancomycin (50mg/ml) or cefazolin (50mg/ml)
• Amikacin (20mg/ml) or tobramycin

3. Systemic antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice.
4. Steroid therapy includes:

• Intravitreal injection of dexamethasone (0.4mg in 0.1ml) which is started along with antibiotics.
• Topical dexamethasone (0.1%)

5. Oral steroids such as prednisolone are started after 24 hours of intensive antibiotic therapy.
6. Supportive therapy includes:

• Cycloplegics such as atropine 1%
• Anti-glaucoma drugs such as oral acetazolamide or timolol in patients with raised intraocular pressure

7. Pars plana vitrectomy is done if the patient does not improve with the above therapy in 48-72 hours or   when the visual acuity is reduced to hand movements near the eye

Other options:

Option A: Steroids are given in endophthalmitis to reduce the inflammation of the tissues. The preferred route of administration is either by intravitreal injections, topical concentrations or oral route. Intravenous route (option A) of administration of steroids is not used in endophthalmitis.

Option B: Systemic administration (intravenous) of antibiotics have a limited role in the treatment but are commonly used in practice as an add on.
questions.learning: Intravitreal antibiotics — A post cataract surgery patient presenting within 36 hours of surgery with inflammation, congestion and hypopyon as seen in the image, is suggestive of acute bacterial endophthalmitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Slow waves are generated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Interstitial cells of Cajal

The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ion channels that periodically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generate slow-wave activity.

Interstitial cells of Cajal are the pacemaker cells of the GIT that initiate the basic electrical rhythm (BER). These are stellate mesenchymal pacemaker cells with smooth muscle-like features.

In the stomach and the small intestine, these cells are located in the circular smooth muscle layer near the myenteric plexus. In the colon, they are at the submucosal border of the circular muscle layer.

The slow waves usually do not by themselves cause muscle contraction in most parts of the gastrointestinal tract, except perhaps in the stomach. Instead, they mainly excite the appearance of intermittent spike potentials, and the spike potentials in turn actually excite the muscle contraction.

Note: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal.
questions.learning: Interstitial cells of Cajal — The interstitial cells of Cajal undergo cyclic changes in membrane potential due to unique ion channels that periodically open and produce inward (pacemaker) currents that generate slow-wave activity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the affinity of carbon monoxide to hemoglobin in comparison to oxygen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 250

CO binds to hemoglobin with an affinity that is 250 times that of O2 to form carboxyhemoglobin.

CO also increases the O2 affinity of remaining free hemoglobin sites (causes left shift of the O2 - hemoglobin dissociation curve).

* Curve A - Myoglobin O2-dissociation curve

* Curve B - Normal Hb O2-dissociation curve

* Curve C- CO binds to hemoglobin and prevents O2 binding

* Curve D - Anemia

Carbon monoxide (CO) reacts with hemoglobin to form carbon monoxyhemoglobin (carboxyhemoglobin or COHb). The affinity of hemoglobin for CO is 210 times its affinity for O2, and COHb liberates CO very slowly. An additional difficulty is that when COHb is present, the dissociation curve of the remaining HbO2 shifts to the left, decreasing the amount of O2 released.

Treatment of CO poisoning consists of ventilation with oxygen since oxygen hastens the dissociation of carboxyhemoglobin.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn is brought to the pediatric clinic with early-onset jaundice and abnormal ocular findings. Ophthalmologic examination shows multiple small, white, punctate opacities clustered in the central part of the lens, consistent with an oil-drop cataract. Considering the combination of neonatal jaundice and this characteristic lens opacity, which underlying metabolic disorder is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of neonatal jaundice and an oil drop cataract is the classic diagnostic indicator for Galactosemia. As established in Q.221, this metabolic disorder leads to the accumulation of toxic galactose metabolites, specifically galactitol, within the lens, which draws water in and creates a characteristic drop-like opacity. Early jaundice results from hepatic toxicity and impaired bilirubin conjugation. Phenylketonuria (Option A) leads to intellectual disability and "mousy" odor but not primary cataracts. Maple syrup urine disease (Option B) presents with severe ketoacidosis and a burnt-sugar odor in the urine. Wilson's disease (Option D) involves copper deposition, which causes "Kayser-Fleischer rings" in the cornea and "sunflower cataracts," but it typically presents in older children and adults, not neonates. Therefore, given the immediate neonatal presentation of jaundice and this specific lens finding, Galactosemia is the pathognomonic diagnosis

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following studies progresses from cause to effect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cohort Study

A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study. A well-designed cohort study is considered the most reliable means of showing an association between a cause or suspected risk factor and subsequent disease (or effect).

Types of epidemiological studies:

* Observational studies - allow nature to take its course, the investigator measures but does not intervene.

* Descriptive studies - limited to the description of the occurrence of a disease in a population- (hypothesis formulation).

* Analytical studies - go further by analyzing the relationship between health status and other variables- (hypothesis testing).

* Ecological studies

* Cross-sectional studies

* Case-control studies

* Cohort studies

* Experimental studies or intervention studies involve an active attempt to change a disease determinant or the progress of a disease and are similar in design to experiments in other sciences- (hypothesis confirmation).

* Randomized controlled trials

* Field trials

* Community trials

Other options:

Option A: Although case-control studies are inherently analytical, they are not longitudinal. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.

Option C: A randomized control trial is an experimental study in which an intervention is given to a group of patients participating in the study and compared to another group of patients with similar characteristics who are not given that intervention to be studied. It uses patients as the unit of study.

Option D: An ecological study is a type of analytical study that analyzes the health status and its relation with other variables. It is also called a correlational study, and it uses the population as a unit of study. Longitudinal studies involve the collection of variables about a subject over an extended duration.
questions.learning: Cohort Study — A cohort study is a type of analytical study, which progresses from cause to effect, as exposure has occurred but not disease. It is also known as a forward-looking study, incidence study, prospective study, and longitudinal study.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the ulcer shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Venous ulcer

The image of a healing ulcer with a sloping edge in the Gaiter's area indicates a venous ulcer.

Venous ulcers due to chronic venous insufficiency are most commonly seen in the lower ⅓ of the leg and foot. They usually lie just proximal to the medial or lateral malleolus.

Ambulatory venous hypertension is the most acceptable theory in the pathophysiology. They have a sloping edge and the floor contains granulation tissue covered by slough and exudate. Marjolin’s ulcer is a type of squamous cell carcinoma seen in chronic long-standing venous ulcers. These are accompanied by lipodermatosclerosis and hemosiderosis.

Management of venous ulcers:

1) Bisgaard's regimen (4Es)

* Education of the patient

* Elevation of the affected limb to reduce the edema

* Elastic compression stockings - The ideal interface pressure in venous ulceration is 35-40 mmHg.

* Evaluation

2) 4-layer bandaging system comprising of:

* Orthopaedic wool

* Cotton crepe

* Elastic bandage - first compressive layer

* Cohesive bandage - second compressive layer

3) Antibiotics are given only if the wound is infected.
4) Regular dressing.
5) Medical management by oral pentoxifylline is considered which helps in reducing the viscosity and improving circulation.
6) Surgical management by ulcer excision with pinch mesh grafting has a good outcome and helps in preventing recurrence.

Note: Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) is a negative pressure dressing. An occlusive dressing is placed over the sore and it is connected to VAC that generates -125mmHg of pressure. It is used in chronic non-healing ulcers, venous ulcers, diabetic ulcers, burn wounds, and bed sores.

Type of Ulcer
Ischaemic/Arterial
Venous
Neuropathic

Tuberculous

Underlying condition
Peripheral vascular disease mainly atherosclerosis, thromboangitis obliterans, and Raynaud's phenomenon
Varicose veins, previous deep vein thrombosis
Diabetes, peripheral neuropathy
Tuberculosis lymph nodes, cold abscess from bone and joint tuberculosis

Location
Toes, feet, legs, or even upper limb digits
Lower limb, commonly on the medial side of the ankle, never above the middle third of the leg
The plantar surface of the foot and toes
Neck, axilla, and groin

Characteristics
Deep, penetrates the deep fascia exposing the tendons, muscles, and underlying bone. The ulcer is painful, tender, and hyperaesthetic.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is the best indicator of chronic malnutrition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Height for age

Height for age is the best indicator of chronic malnutrition.

Nutritional status is often assessed in terms of anthropometry:

* Low height for age, or stunting, indicates chronic malnutrition. This is the best indicator of long-term nutritional status in the pediatric population.

* Low weight for height, or wasting, indicates acute malnutrition.

* High weight-for-height indicates overweight.

* Low weight for the age indicates acute or chronic malnutrition. It does not differentiate between wasting and stunting. Hence, it has limited clinical significance.

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is an age-independent parameter used for the screening of wasting in children.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What hormonal mechanism is responsible for lactational amenorrhea, the temporary absence of menstruation during the postpartum period in breastfeeding women?
questions.explanation: Lactational amenorrhea is a physiological state of infertility that occurs after childbirth while a woman is breastfeeding. The primary driver is "increased prolactin secretion" from the anterior pituitary in response to the infant's suckling stimulus. High levels of circulating prolactin exert a negative feedback effect on the hypothalamus, leading to the suppression of pulsatile Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) secretion. In turn, this results in low levels of LH and FSH, preventing the development of ovarian follicles and ovulation. Increased GnRH (Option B) would lead to menstruation. Decreased prolactin (Option C) occurs when breastfeeding stops, leading to the return of menses. Increased progesterone (Option A) is characteristic of pregnancy or the luteal phase, not the lactational period. This mechanism is the basis for the Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) of contraception. However, its effectiveness as a contraceptive depends on exclusive breastfeeding and the absence of any menstrual bleeding since delivery
questions.learning: Lactational amenorrhea is a physiological state of infertility that occurs after childbirth while a woman is breastfeeding. The primary driver is "increased prolactin secretion" from the anterior pituitary in response to the infant's suckling stimulus.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 78 year old male presented with complaints of fatigue,breathlessness and palpitations.He has no co-morbidities and does not smoke or drink. On examination there was pedal edema and vitals were: PR-55, BP-100/70, Spo2-94%. An ECG was taken which showed no abnormalities after which he was given oxygen and an ECHO revealed restrictive cardiomyopathy. The physician in doubt of a disease did a cardiac biopsy which showed apple-green birefringence when viewed under polarized light after staining with Congo red stain. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiac Amyloidosis

The clinical scenario of breathlessness, pedal edema,ECHO finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy and the apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain is suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis.

Cardiac amyloidosis:

* Amyloidosis of the heart can develop as a consequence of systemic amyloidosis or localized amyloidosis restricted to the heart, particularly in the aged (senile cardiac amyloidosis).

* It is seen in individuals 70 years and older, and it has a far better prognosis than systemic amyloidosis.

* Senile cardiac amyloid deposits are largely composed of transthyretin, a normal serum protein synthesized in the liver that transports thyroxine and retinol-binding protein.

* Cardiac amyloidosis most frequently produces restrictive cardiomyopathy. But, it can also be asymptomatic, manifest as dilation or arrhythmias, or mimic ischemic or valvular disease.

* Another presentation of cardiac amyloidosis is congestive heart failure due to systolic dysfunction, generally a later finding.

* In approximately 10% of patients with amyloidosis, orthostatic hypotension occurs and is presumed to be a result of amyloid infiltration of the autonomic nervous system.

* Morphology: The chambers are usually of normal size, but can be dilated and have thickened walls. Small, semitranslucent nodules resembling drips of wax may be seen on the atrial endocardial surface, particularly on the left.

* Histologically, hyaline eosinophilic deposits of amyloid may be found in the interstitium, conduction tissue, valves, endocardium, pericardium, and small intramural coronary arteries.

Image: Congo red stain viewed under polarized light, in which amyloid shows characteristic apple-green birefringence in the heart

Other options:

Option C- Hemosiderosis is characterized by deposition of hemosiderin, which is a hemoglobin-derived golden-yellow colored pigment. The deposition may occur in any organ or tissue. It is seen in conditions associated with iron overload.

Option D-Dystrophic calcification:When the deposition of calcium occurs in dead or dying tissues, it is called dystrophic calcification. This occurs in the absence of derangements in calcium metabolism, i.e the calcium levels are normal. Dystrophic calcification is seen in areas of necrosis of any type including coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive, and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.
questions.learning: Cardiac Amyloidosis — The clinical scenario of breathlessness, pedal edema,ECHO finding of restrictive cardiomyopathy and the apple-green birefringence when stained with Congo red stain is suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient presented with a midline neck swelling. He later developed cervical node enlargement. The histopathology of the lesion is shown below. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?
options: Excellent prognosis is associated with this condition
Nuclear characteristics are used for identification
Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is not diagnostic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is not diagnostic

The given scenario of a male patient with a midline swelling, cervical lymph node enlargement, and the histopathology showing branched papillae with orphan Annie eye nuclei is suggestive of papillary thyroid carcinoma. The false statement regarding the condition is that FNAC is not diagnostic.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common thyroid malignancy. It is more commonly seen in women between the ages of 30 and 50. Radiation exposure and family history of thyroid malignancies are the common etiologies. Genetic abnormalities in either the RET gene or the BRAF gene can be seen in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Clinical features include an asymptomatic thyroid swelling with cervical lymph node enlargement. In advanced disease, there may be features like hoarseness, dysphagia, cough, or dyspnea.

An ultrasound scan accurately assesses the size and number of nodules, as well as categorizes the lesions as benign, indeterminate, or malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is a diagnostic test, helpful in investigating an indeterminate or malignant lesion.

Histopathology shows the following features:

• Branching papillae
• Orphan Annie eye nuclei: optically clear nuclei with fine nuclear chromatin
• Pseudo inclusions: invaginations of the nuclear membrane
• Psammoma bodies: concentric calcifications in the core of the papillae.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is known to spread via lymphatics, hence lymph node metastasis is commonly seen.

Management is by thyroidectomy with neck dissection (central or local depending upon the site involved) followed by lifelong levothyroxine supplementation. Radioactive iodine is also useful.

The disease has an excellent prognosis, with a high survival rate.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A non-smoker patient with a history of cardiac disease suddenly develops chest pain and breathlessness. An X-ray is performed and given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema

The given chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings, vascular redistribution, and alveolar oedema in a butterfly pattern points to a diagnosis of pulmonary oedema.

Acute severe hypertension, acute myocardial infarction, or exacerbation of chronic heart failure are some of the common causes of cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. It can be precipitated by the discontinuation of medications (non-compliant patient), excessive salt intake, or tachyarrhythmias.

It presents with severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum production, diaphoresis, and cyanosis. Auscultation reveals rales and rhonchi in all lung fields. Cardiomegaly might be seen in cases of chronic heart failure.

Management of pulmonary oedema includes the use of diuretics, nitrates, and morphine to decrease the preload. Nitroglycerin and isosorbide dinitrate have a rapid onset of action and can be given sublingually. If there is a persistence of pulmonary oedema and no hypotension, it can be administered intravenously.

Oxygen therapy to maintain a saturation of >92% is recommended. If saturation is not maintained even with supplemental oxygen, positive-pressure ventilation through a face mask or endotracheal intubation is required. A sitting position with legs hanging by the side of the bed can be used to reduce venous return in patients without hypotension.

Non-cardiac causes of pulmonary oedema are high altitude, sepsis, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.

Heart failure is a manifestation of most chronic cardiac conditions such as hypertension, valvular heart disease, and coronary artery disease. Symptoms such as shortness of breath, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea point to left heart failure due to pulmonary congestion. In contrast, symptoms such as pedal oedema, weight gain, early satiety, and hepatic congestion are characteristic of right heart failure.

Chest X-ray shows increased interstitial markings, vascular redistribution, and alveolar oedema in a bat wing/ butterfly pattern as given in the image below.

Summary of Pathogenesis of Major Findings in Congestive Heart Failure

Abnormality

Cause

Left ventricle output inadequate to perfuse muscles; especially, failure of output to rise with exercise

Ankle, sacral edema

Increased peripheral venous pressure →increased fluid transudation.

Hepatomegaly

Increased peripheral venous pressure →increased resistance to portal flow.

Pulmonary congestion

Increased pulmonary venous pressure →pulmonary venous distention and transudation of fluid into air spaces

Dyspnea on exertion

Failure of left ventricular output to rise during exercise → increased pulmonary venous pressure

Paroxysmal dyspnea, pulmonary edema

Probably a sudden failure of left heart output to keep up with the right heart output →acute rise in pulmonary venous and capillary pressure →transudation of fluid into air spaces.

Orthopnea

Normal pooling of blood in lungs in supine position added to the already congested pulmonary vascular system; increased venous return not put out by the left ventricle. (Relieved by sitting up, raising the head of the bed, lying on extra pillows.)

Cardiac dilation

Greater ventricular end-diastolic volume.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: 6x6x6 strategy under Anemia Mukt Bharat includes all except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Coordination/Ministries

Anemia Mukt Bharat scheme implements 6 x 6x 6 strategy which focuses on six target beneficiary groups, through six interventions and six institutional mechanisms to achieve their target by 2022.

The Anemia Mukt Bharat scheme is an initiative that aims to strengthen the existing mechanisms and foster newer strategies for tackling anemia.

Interventions include:

* Prophylactic iron and folic acid supplementation.

* Deworming.

* Intensified year-round Behaviour Change Communication Campaign (Solid Body, Smart Mind) including ensuring delayed cord clamping in newborns.

* Testing of anemia using digital methods and point-of-care treatment.

* Mandatory provision of Iron and Folic Acid fortified foods in government-funded health programs.

* Addressing non-nutritional causes of anemia in endemic pockets, with a special focus on malaria, hemoglobinopathies, and fluorosis.

IFA tablet distribution under Anemia Mukt Bharat:

* Lactating mothers of 0 to 6-month-old children are given a daily dose of red color IFA tablet containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid.

* Weekly doses of red color IFA tablets containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid are given to women of reproductive age (non-pregnant, non-lactating), between 20-49 years of age.

* Children between 5-9 years of age are given pink color sugar-coated tablets containing 45 mg of elemental iron and 400 mcg of folic acid tablets once a week.

* Blue color tablets containing 60 mg of elemental iron and 500 mcg of folic acid can be given to school-going adolescent girls and boys of 10-19 years and out-of-school adolescent girls of age 10-19 years.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding from the ear following a fall. What is the investigation of choice in this scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. CT temporal bone

In a patient with ear bleeding following trauma, the investigation of choice is CT temporal bone, as it is the best modality to detect temporal bone fractures.

·  CT temporal bone (HRCT) provides detailed visualization of:

o    Bony structures of ear (external, middle, inner ear)

o    Fracture lines (longitudinal/transverse)

o    Ossicular disruption, facial canal involvement

·  Helps classify fractures and identify complications such as:

o    CSF leak

o    Facial nerve injury

o    Hearing loss

Why not other options:

·   MRI brain: Better for soft tissue and intracranial complications, not first-line for fractures

·   CBP: Irrelevant

·   X-ray skull: Low sensitivity, largely obsolete

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 52-year-old male diabetic presents with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. On examination, Pulse: 84 beats/minute, BP: 160/100 mm Hg, Chest and CVS examination unremarkable. Which of the following antihypertensive should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Propranolol

In patients with diabetes mellitus and recurrent hypoglycemia, non-selective β-blockers, particularly propranolol, should be avoided because they mask the adrenergic warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremors, palpitations, anxiety) and delay recovery by inhibiting glycogenolysis. In contrast, ACE inhibitors and ARBs (e.g., Telmisartan) are the preferred antihypertensive agents in diabetic patients due to their reno- and cardioprotective effects.

• A. Propranolol: Non-selective β-blocker that masks hypoglycemic symptoms and may prolong hypoglycemia.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Telmisartan: An ARB and a first-line antihypertensive in diabetes, especially in patients with albuminuria or diabetic kidney disease. It does not mask hypoglycemia.
• C. Torsemide: A loop diuretic used for edema and hypertension; although it may cause electrolyte disturbances, it is not contraindicated because of hypoglycemia.
• D. Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker with no effect on hypoglycemia awareness.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following investigations are useful for diagnosis of unresponsive endometrium as a cause of primary amenorrhoea? 1. Karyotype 2. Progesterone challenge test 3. Hormonal studies 4. Hysterosalpingography Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Primary amenorrhea due to an unresponsive endometrium occurs when the endometrium fails to respond to normal hormonal stimulation, most commonly because of outflow tract abnormalities (e.g., Asherman syndrome, genital tuberculosis) or endometrial destruction.

• 1. Karyotype ✗

• Karyotyping is useful for chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., Turner syndrome, androgen insensitivity syndrome), not for diagnosing an unresponsive endometrium.

• 2. Progesterone challenge test ✓

• Assesses whether the endometrium has been adequately primed by estrogen.
• No withdrawal bleeding suggests either:

• Hypoestrogenism, or
• Endometrial/outflow tract abnormality.

• 3. Hormonal studies ✓

• Serum FSH, LH, estradiol, prolactin, and TSH help determine whether the cause is ovarian, pituitary, hypothalamic, or uterine.

• 4. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) ✓

• Evaluates the uterine cavity and helps diagnose intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome) or congenital uterine abnormalities causing an unresponsive endometrium.
